United finished fourth in the Women’s Super League last season and reached the quarter-finals of the Women’s Champions League, as well as the League Cup final.

Matt Johnson, United’s director of women’s football, said: “Eva is an outstanding coach with an incredible determination to succeed. Her remarkable achievements at Heart of Midlothian showcased her ability to maximise the potential of individual players, whilst also implementing an exciting style of football.

“Eva is the perfect coach to lead us into an exciting new era. She shares our commitment to developing exciting homegrown and young players, a tradition deeply embedded in our club’s history and culture, as well as improving established senior internationals, both of which form an integral part of our vision for long-term, sustainable success.”

Sports.title: Infantino is getting his karmic kicking, but why did football take so long to rebel against Fifa? | Jonathan Liew
Sports.content:
In recent decades the city of Salé, just across the river from Rabat on Morocco’s Atlantic coast, has undergone a remarkable transformation. At the start of this century it was a gritty working-class area, whose old town was still weathered enough to serve as a body double for the Somali capital Mogadishu in the film Black Hawk Down. But in recent decades, under the country’s autocratic government, the area has been transformed beyond measure, and largely beyond control.

The population has trebled in the space of 40 years. Slums have been cleared, often forcibly, to make way for grand megaprojects: a new tram system, luxury tourist spaces, a sparkling marina, a blue-chip business park called Technopolis, and – since last July – the African headquarters of Fifa. And in a way, this hub of disruption and avarice, unshakeable volition and rampant capitalism, feels like the perfect location from which a besieged warlord might choose to make his desperate last stand.

According to reports in the Times, Gianni Infantino has been “holed up” in Salé this week as he tries to save his presidency. Apparently Infantino’s aides have been feverishly calling Fifa Legends – the organisation’s paid ex-player ambassadors – to persuade them to offer Infantino their public support. On Wednesday one of them, Luís Figo, decided to break his silence. “Infantino must go,” he said, condemning his plan to sell off a stake in the World Cup to private investors as “the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed.” That’ll be a no, then.

Meanwhile, the leaders of Uefa, Concacaf and the Asian Football Confederation are massing forces at the gates. A “governance boycott”, in which members refuse to attend meetings or ratify Fifa decisions, is one idea. A rival World Cup-style competition – which would in effect translate to secession – is the nuclear option. And yes, in the moment this feels good, stirring, cathartic, karmic. We should all take a certain satisfaction in seeing Infantino get his long-deserved kicking. For all this, a pertinent question should also pose itself. Why now? And why like this?

It is, after all, almost eight years since Fifa first proposed selling off a slice of its commercial legacy. In 2018 Infantino agreed in principle a deal with the Japanese firm SoftBank – whose main financial backer just so happened to be the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia – for an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League. The scheme eventually sputtered to a halt, but with virtually none of the screaming and apocalyptic threats seen over the past fortnight.

It is four years since the soiled, blood-soaked Qatar World Cup, and the “today I feel gay” speech that turned the sport’s most important administrator into a figure of ridicule. Two years since Saudi Arabia were handed the 2034 tournament in a bidding process no other country appeared to be prepared for. Three years since the Club World Cup was coerced into existence over a chorus of player welfare concerns. Two months since Omar Artan was summarily denied entry to a World Cup in which he was supposed to be refereeing. One month since Folarin Balogun had his suspension overturned in a supposedly independent process.

View image in fullscreen Apparently Gianni Infantino’s aides have been calling Fifa Legends – the organisation’s paid ex-player ambassadors – to persuade them to offer the president their public support. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

For the men and women who – as it turned out – held Infantino’s fate in their hands all along, none of this appeared to be a red line. For years the injustices, the indignities, the reputational and environmental damage, the ruptures to rules and structures, the stitch-ups and dead migrant workers, have been waved through by acclamation. And so it is worth wondering whether anything has materially changed here, beyond the fleeting opportunity for ambitious footballing executives to claim the keys to Infantino’s empire.

It is more than a decade since the late Lord Triesman, the former FA chair, described Fifa as a “mafia family”, and nothing about that description feels less true today. This is in many ways a supralegal body operating beyond the boundaries of conventional politics or economics, operating under its own rules and its own moral code, tied together not through popular consent but through a feudal system of tribute and protection, which changes not through legislation or overthrow but by occasional mob-style decapitation.

The moral objections to Infantino’s investment plan are manifest, but perhaps more striking still – for a president who has staked everything on his ability to drive revenue – is the economic illiteracy. One hand-picked buyer (Joshua Kushner), one made-up number ($20 billion) and an artificial countdown clock (19 September). Is this really how to fetch the best price for your asset? Or is it how you act when you want to secure a bigger piece of the largesse you have so selflessly created, but are statutorily bound to one more term in your current job?

And in hindsight, it seems clear that Infantino’s thirst for bending rules and breaking conventions was a kind of loyalty test, his Yakuza tattoo, a way of demonstrating to the billionaire investor class that he truly was one of them. No wonder his first instinct on finding himself cornered was reportedly to appeal to Donald Trump: his roof, his protection, his kindred spirit.

It is often said that Infantino is the symptom and Fifa is the disease. In fact Fifa too is the symptom; the disease is capitalistic fascism, a simple disdain for humanity, a belief that some are born to rule and others are bound to follow. And this is a cancer that will remain embedded in so many of our institutions long after Infantino has taken his last celebrity selfie, long after “45/47” has chowed down his last Oval Office Big Mac, long after the new Fifa regime has swept in through the door wearing the pageant sash of reform.

Football, the greatest mass pursuit ever invented, will of course endure. In a way its ingenuity, its ability to adapt and not be crushed by adaptation, is its beauty and its curse. Like the Salé skyline, it warps and shifts and grows and gentrifies and swells beyond recognition. This is still recognisably the same land, the same turf, upon which its ancestors once stood. But the old waterfront is gone for ever.

Sports.title: ‘There is a clear vision’: Matthias Jaissle installed as Newcastle head coach
Sports.content:
Matthias Jaissle has described Newcastle “as an incredibly compelling place to be” after finally formalising his managerial move from Saudi Arabia’s Al-Ahli.

The 38-year-old German has been with his new players at their training camp in La Manga, southern Spain, since last Saturday but, despite also falling under the ownership of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Al-Ahli took time to provide Newcastle with some vital paperwork regarding the release of a head coach they were extremely reluctant to lose.

Jaissle won two Asian Champions Leagues at the Jeddah-based club and, having enjoyed earlier success during a much-vaunted stint in charge of RB Salzburg, is regarded as one of the brightest young coaches in football. He will be installed as the head coach at St James’ Park.

Nonetheless, the task of succeeding Eddie Howe with the start of the new season only a fortnight away is considerable – and particularly as Newcastle have lost three key players this summer in Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and, now, the Arsenal-bound Bruno Guimarães.

Jaissle remains undaunted. “When Newcastle United come your way you take notice,” he said. “The ambition of the club, the vision for the future and the opportunity ahead made this an incredibly compelling place to be.

“I am incredibly excited about the future. I fully and unreservedly believe in this project, the ambition and the direction the club is taking. There is a clear vision, strong leadership and an exceptional platform to build on.”

Under Howe, Newcastle’s motto was “intensity is our identity” and Jaissle suggested he would be following a similar path. “My teams are built on togetherness, hard work and a passion to improve every single day,” he said.

“I believe there is enormous potential within this squad and throughout this football club. I give my complete commitment and total energy to bringing further success to Newcastle.”

With Howe’s coaching staff having departed with him, Jaissle is assembling a new backroom team but it seems David Hopkinson, Newcastle’s chief executive, and Ross Wilson, the sporting director, have full faith in his ability to revive the fortunes of a club that finished a disappointing 12th in the Premier League last season. “Matthias is one of the most exciting and highly regarded young coaches in football and I’m thrilled to welcome him to Newcastle,” Hopkinson said.

Wilson said: “Matthias’s leadership style and football philosophy are strongly aligned with our sporting vision. His teams play high-energy football and we could feel his passion during all our discussions throughout the recruitment process.”

Sports.title: ‘Punch to the gut’: Indian football thrown into chaos with Jamshedpur withdrawal from ISL
Sports.content:
“Please don’t let this be the final whistle for Jamshedpur FC,” the defender Pratik Chaudhari said, looking into the camera as teammates looked on disconsolately. “We would like to say on behalf of all the players, please do rethink about this. Because if this happens, this is not just a loss for Indian football … this is a big loss for all of India.”

In addition, fans of the Indian Super League club marched in protest, petitions were launched, and the Indian football legend Sunil Chhetri said it was a “punch to the gut” and joined others in begging for a rethink.

The target of all these pleas was the Jamshedpur owner Tata Steel, which surprisingly pulled the plug on the club on 31 July. After the problems of the 2025-26 campaign, which started five months late and lasted just 13 games, the new season’s big kick-off on 4 September was to be a new start. The positivity and optimism before the new season, fragile though it was, disappeared along with JFC.

And understandably so as it is a huge blow, for players, staff and fans but also for the league. Jamshedpur had solid support and won the ISL shield in 2022, five years after the club was formed. Steve Coppell was the first head coach with Scott Cooper, Aidy Boothroyd and Owen Coyle all following in his footsteps.

Baljit Rihal of Inventive Sports was the agent who took Coppell to the city in the eastern state of Jharkhand. “To be quite frank, after all the uncertainty Indian football has faced over the last couple of seasons, Jamshedpur FC would have been one of the last clubs I expected to pull out,” he told the Guardian.

The club was founded by the Tata Group, which has been involved with Indian football at various levels for decades. “When an institution with that history decides it can no longer continue at the highest level, it says something very serious about the current state of the game,” Rihal said.

The league is also losing a major corporate backer, one which insists, however, that the decision is not about money. “At Tata Steel, sports have never been evaluated through a profit-and-loss lens,” the company’s vice-president and the club’s chairman, Sundara Ramam, told the Guardian.

View image in fullscreen Jamshedpur FC won the Indian Super League shield in 2022 Photograph: Courtesy of ISL

“Our decision to exit professional club football has nothing to do with Tata Steel’s financial position. In fact, the resources that would have been spent on the club will continue to be invested in grassroots sports development. Our sports budget is not decreasing. It will continue to grow. As chairman of Jamshedpur FC, I can say clearly that this decision was driven by our desire to focus more intensely on grassroots development and not by financial considerations.”

Yet if others follow suit then there may not be much of a professional pathway for young talent. This latest episode shines a light on the league once more. In the club’s original letter sent to the All India Football Federation, concerns were expressed about the financial model of the ISL, which recently changed. Reliance Industries was the federation’s commercial partner from 2010 but, when that agreement expired in 2025, a new deal was not made and a new partner not found, hence the shortened season.

This time, the AIFF looks after governance and administration with the clubs taking on the commercial and marketing side. “The old model meant clubs had very little say in how the league was packaged and sold,” Ravi Puskur, the chief executive of Goa FC, said last month.

“Now the clubs hold the broadcast and sponsorship rights directly. It puts the incentive to grow the league’s commercial value in the hands of the people who are most invested in it growing.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

A member of Jamshedpur’s staff told the Guardian that the decision was because of concerns over the new arrangements. “I believe Tata are not interested in the club-led model,” he says. “There had to be a commitment of four years and the AIFF was asking for an initial payment of around £43,000 from all 14 clubs to be made by 31 July. Tata might have thought it’s better to stop rather than get dragged into unknown waters.”

View image in fullscreen The former Crystal Palace manager Steve Coppell was the club’s first head coach in 2017. Photograph: The India Today Group/Getty Images

It is a worrying exit as this is not the only corporate departure from Indian football of late. “Reliance stepping away from its central role was significant,” Rihal says. “City Football Group leaving Mumbai City was another warning.” That happened in December, in the middle of the problems last season. “Tata now withdrawing from Jamshedpur FC feels different again because of the group’s deep-rooted history in Indian football. These departures have happened for different reasons, but collectively they represent a major loss of confidence in the professional game.”

Now there is fear that others may follow and there will be some relief if all 13 remaining clubs kick off the season. “Indian football can recover, but we should not underestimate the scale of the challenge,” Rihal says.

“The priority now must be the people affected, followed by urgent clarity over the league’s structure and future. Players, staff and supporters cannot continue living from one period of uncertainty to the next. They deserve much better.”

There is still hope that Tata could have a rethink. “I understand that some tough decisions in sport are down to what makes sense in the boardroom,” Chhetri said. “But I can only request and hope that the thinktank at Tata picks their heart over head and reconsiders this call. It might be a poor business decision, but it will be the one Indian football needs the most at this hour.”

Sports.title: Mohamed Salah’s story of success and sacrifice: ‘Chasing a dream I had to reach’
Sports.content:
The entrance to Al Mokawloon Al Arab’s youth sector feels imposing. At first it is confusing to pinpoint the reason. Is it the facade; a mesh of thick concrete slabs, a marble-like trim that alters in colour depending on the light, and the no-nonsense black steel gate? Perhaps it is the stately signage of white block letters in Arabic juxtaposed against the dark background, with satellite pieces of information and announcements signifying importance. But to stop and pay attention to buildings around Nasr City in eastern Cairo is to notice that the blend of functional and decorative elements of the entrance, down to even the font and array of notices, is not unique.

The building’s aura can be explained by the main image above its gates, and the knowledge that to walk through them is to follow the footsteps a history-maker took from the age of 14. Mohamed Salah’s face has pride of place above the gates; it is a reminder of where he’s been, but more pertinently, of why it is important to marry talent with discipline and determination. The truth is he has achieved the impossible.

Hamdi Nouh, Salah’s first coach at Al Mokawloon and who he has referred to as a “second father”, knows that is because “he was ready to sacrifice everything, he wanted to work hard, and liked to learn”. It sounds simple, until you start drilling at the heart of what it means for a boy from Nagrig to endure a nine-hour round trip five days a week simply to train in Cairo. Salah’s route has become so well known, you can read the tale of the minimum four buses he needed to take each way in Chinese, Spanish and every other major language. One from the T-junction at the edge of his village to reach Basyoun. The transfer from there to the capital of the Gharbia Governorate, Tanta. The great slog of around 100 kilometres to reach the rush of Ramses Square. A connection from Cairo’s chaotic central transport hub to Nasr City. And, on the luckier days, a ride close to the club’s gates to spare Salah having to run almost two kilometres up a steep hill, to be on time for his training session. After four hours at the centre, he would leave to do that all again in reverse.

The problem with summarising the journey in this way, as it has been done since 2017 when Salah started shifting the parameters for greatness in the Premier League, is that it omits the reality of what this daily grind truly entailed. When Nouh underlines sacrifice, part of it was Salah giving up his youth to sit shoulder slammed into shoulder, bodies filling up every available inch of the microbus and often even hanging off it, racing to the next stop and against the anxiety of missing a connection in a schedule that had no rhyme nor reason, with only enough cash for the exact journey. He was too respectful to ask his father for more, even though there was no margin for error. Salah weirdly enjoyed rather than endured the stressful odyssey. “I didn’t feel tired travelling when I was young,” he would reflect in 2022. “It’s because I was doing something I wanted, chasing a dream I had to reach. I wasn’t seeing my situation, I was seeing my goal. These are days I sit and think about, I’ll never forget them and I still smile now when I remember everything.”

View image in fullscreen Egyptian boys in Nagrig look up to Mohamed Salah and hope to follow in his footsteps. Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/Alamy

It is not the same for Umm Mohamed (the Mother of Mohamed), who was averse to her eldest son spending only two hours at school, between seven and nine in the morning, and venturing so far away from his village, when lanes were seen as a mere suggestion and dangerous driving was the only type. Her memories were of worry and fear prompted by the high number of crashes involving microbuses. One major accident along her son’s route provoked sheer panic, which only increased as his phone rang unanswered. She tried calling over 20 times, and while Salah insists exhaustion didn’t grip him during his great trek, he didn’t pick up because he was fast asleep. She was also concerned if he had enough money, as was her husband, Salah Ghaly, who worked as a government administrator and traded in jasmine, Nagrig’s greatest export. He funded Salah’s football path, first to Ittihad in Basyoun, which was only a half-hour trip, then on to the Othmason club in Tanta, 90 minutes away, all before he became a teenager, followed by the almighty mission to Al Mokawloon.

Salah was eight when he started training there and rushed at opponents with the fearlessness of a microbus driver. “He was small, but his left foot and his shots were powerful,” Ghamri Abdel-Hameed el-Saadani, who was the juniors coach at the youth centre, says. “He was fast and could do things with the ball the other boys couldn’t.” Salah’s father knew it, and despite his own apprehensions about the big city and how it could swallow and spit out young hopefuls, he told Umm Mohamed they were doing the right thing.

Back to the entrance of Al Mokawloon’s youth sector, and just behind the black steel gates, lies a story that hasn’t travelled the world like the bus trip. One of Salah’s teammates had suggested they could stay at his uncle’s house in Greater Cairo for the week. It was located in the 10th of Ramadan City and it took plenty of convincing for his parents to green-light the sleepover. Salah’s father gave him 60 Egyptian pounds and he set off. When they arrived at the house, in the black of the night, his friend’s uncle was not there. They were stuck, with not enough money or knowledge to find other lodgings.

All Salah knew of Cairo were the roads through it to train at Al Mokawloon. His friend, whose name he doesn’t want to reveal to avoid the media frenzy that accompanies any detail about his life, suggested the house of someone else he knew not too far away. When they got there, Salah encountered a bigger problem. The dwelling was in a cemetery, a saddening – and scary – symptom of Cairo’s severe housing shortage and high population density. Salah was not going to stay in the necropolis. His friend had one final plan: he knew an on-site administrator at Al Mokawloon who could let them in. Right behind the steel gate, they laid out the sheets they had packed on the floor into two makeshift beds.

View image in fullscreen Mohamed Salah began his career at Al Mokawloon in 2010 before moving to Europe. Photograph: Courtesy of Al Mokawloon

Salah used his shoes as a pillow and set his alarm for 6am so the pair could be up before anyone caught them and the administrator got in trouble. They packed up their bedding and headed off, returning to the complex at 9am as though they had just arrived. The sleeping arrangement stayed secret but needed to be amended; there was too much jeopardy being so close to the entrance. The next day, the duo slept on Field 2 of the four pitches, in the open under the cold night sky. In the morning, they would again go into covert mode and Salah enjoyed that he could be early for training.

Salah had already packed in a lifetime’s worth of sacrifice, effort and lessons by his 18th birthday. The moment he will never forget, however, was when he joined the first team group and moved into the Al Mokawloon’s residences. “Not everyone could stay there, so psychologically I felt like I became someone, like a star,” Salah would recall. “I used to see players finish training and go upstairs, while I would leave to take the journey back to Nagrig. I’d think, ‘One day I’ll go up there’.” He would go higher than any other Egyptian footballer in history.

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino REFUSES to resign as FIFA president: Under-fire chief apologises and vows to fight on as he breaks cover after being forced to abandon World Cup sale plans
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino REFUSES to resign as FIFA president: Under-fire chief apologises and vows to fight on as he breaks cover after being forced to abandon World Cup sale plans

See more Daily Mail on Google - save us as a Preferred Source

Shameless Gianni Infantino has been given the ‘full support’ of FIFA’s top brass - and is set to remain as president - after summoning execs to crisis talks in Morocco.

At the end of another extraordinary day in the World Cup sell-off scandal, which saw Luis Figo become the latest high-profile name to call for Infantino’s head in a blistering attack in Daily Mail Sport, a FIFA statement suggested its under-fire supremo survives, for now.

In a searing 601-word assault Figo had described Infantino’s now-aborted plan to flog a stake in the World Cup to private investors as the ‘lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed’ and a ‘grubby, underhand plot’.

His explosive words ramped up the pressure on Infantino, who had called a crisis meeting in Rabat as he attempted to cling to power.

It would now appear, however, that he has managed to do so. A lengthy statement from FIFA late on Wednesday night admitted mistakes were made, but said they have now apologised in a letter to the various football associations and that a ‘review’ will be carried out.

The statement said that, following the meeting, FIFA’s secretary general Mattias Grafstrom, who had criticised Infantino, and other management board members in attendance ‘reaffirmed their full support for the president’.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (right) and FIFA secretary general Mattias Grafström (left) appeared in high spirits while watching a women's AFCON game on Wednesday night

For good measure, it added: ‘FIFA will no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process and will take all necessary measures to protect and safeguard its name and reputation.

‘There are always lessons to be learned, and FIFA will continue to improve its processes in light of this experience. In this instance, however, it is important to stress that, although mistakes were made, everything that was done was done in full compliance with the FIFA regulatory framework.’

Figo, the former Barcelona and Real Madrid star, who initially backed Infantino in 2015, branded the Swiss a ‘relic who should have no part in football’s future’ and accused him of ‘a litany of abuses’.

Aside from the World Cup sell-off, he referenced the decision to suspend the ban for USA striker Folarin Balogun after his red card at the World Cup and the half-time show during the final which ‘broke the laws of the game’.

‘Infantino has debased the office of FIFA president he promised to elevate,’ he wrote.

‘He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve.’

Figo’s comments came after an attack by UEFA, which said it had lost confidence in Infantino, calling his proposal to flog commercial and event operations a ‘shabby, back room, opaque deal’.

Amid heavy criticism and calls for Infantino to go, Grafstrom sent an all-staff memo describing the situation as ‘sad and reproachable’ and adding ‘individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go.’

However, second-in-command Grafstrom was pictured laughing and joking with Infantino at a women’s Africa Cup of Nations game following the meeting, ahead of the release of the statement.

Should he survive, Infantino would face re-election in March, and would need 106 votes from Fifa's 211 members to win another term in charge of the global game.

Infantino arrived at the crunch meeting in Morocco earlier on Wednesday amid mounting pressure.

He had summoned senior FIFA officials to the Moroccan city of Sale for crisis talks after plans to sell £3.1billion in World Cup stakes leaked last week

The Swiss football administrator has since scrapped the proposals after widespread opposition – including an internal rebellion at FIFA.

UEFA and CONCACAF – the body for North and Central America and the Caribbean – are both calling for Infantino to step down, with Europe declaring a lack of confidence in the FIFA president.

Pressure grew further after Jordan FA president Prince Ali bin Hussein accused him of blackmail, becoming the first Asian nation to rebel against the FIFA president.

Jordan became the 91st member association to move against Infantino, assuming all UEFA and CONCACAF nations follow the stance set by their continental bodies. 106 nations are needed to depose Infantino as president.

FIFA President Infantino arrived at an emergency meeting in Sale, Morocco on Wednesday

Infantino is facing mounting pressure over his failed plan to sell off stakes in the FIFA World Cup

Football legend Luis Figo became the latest high-profile individual to call for him to resign, while Arsene Wenger distanced himself from Infantino's plans

A car carrying Infantino was seen arriving at FIFA's Africa regional office in Sale on Wednesday.

The meeting comes hours after Figo became the latest major name in football to demand his resignation.

In an explosive piece for Daily Mail Sport, which further ramped up the pressure on the under-fire FIFA chief, the Portuguese legend described his now aborted World Cup sell-off as the ‘lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed’ and a ‘grubby, underhand plot’.

Across 600 no-holds-barred words Figo, who had initially backed Infantino in 2015, brands the disgraced exec a ‘relic who should have no part in football’s future’ and accuses him of ‘a litany of abuses’, also referencing the now-infamous suspension of the ban behind Folarin Balogun’s red card and the half-time show at the World Cup final which ‘broke the laws of the game’.

‘Infantino has debased the office of FIFA President that he promised to elevate,’ the former Real Madrid, Barcelona and Inter Milan star writes. ‘He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve.’

Figo, now 53, is viewed by many as a potential successor to Aleksandr Ceferin, head of UEFA which is leading the war against Infantino.

Figo and Jordan's Prince Ali had both previously stood against former FIFA president Sepp Blatter in the 2015 elections.

Figo ultimately withdrew from the process, while Prince Ali pulled out after the second round of voting. Blatter announced his resignation four days after re-election amid a vast backlash.

Infantino is facing his own backlash following his World Cup plans, with FIFA’s chief operating officer Kevin Lamour saying he was ‘deceived’ by the project and others, including chief of global football development Arsene Wenger, have distanced themselves from the hastily dropped plan.

Figo branded Infantino as a ‘relic who should have no part in football’s future’ in an explosive article for Daily Mail Sport

Figo, who had initially backed Infantino in 2015, claimed the Swiss official has 'debased the office of FIFA President'

With morale among staff said to be ‘rock bottom’ according to insiders, secretary general Grafstrom sent an internal email to staff citing ‘a sad and reproachable series of events’ and perhaps tellingly pointing out that ‘individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go’.

Figo, a former FIFA presidential candidate, starts: ‘I could write 10,000 words on the problems at FIFA. But the solution needs only three: Infantino must go.’

He adds: ‘I have loved football all my life. I was a professional player for 20 years. And believe me, I have met some rogues in my time in the game. But what I have seen exposed in the last ten days is the lowest, most deceitful and cravenly self-interested behaviour I have ever witnessed. The man who would do that - the man who would try to force through such major changes just to enrich himself and his friends - is a relic of the game’s past and should have no part in its future.’

The Portuguese, who won 127 caps for his country, then rounds on Infantino for a lack of transparency. ’If it was such a good idea, why not tell your members when you had them all in a room before the World Cup Final?’ he asks.

‘If it was such a robust plan, why not tell your members the risks as well as what you describe as the benefits?

‘If the scheme was a no-brainer, why not be honest about the fact that it was going to give you a $30m a year job at the end of it?’

Figo adds: ‘None of this was done. Because it’s not a good idea. It’s not robust when you fail to be transparent about the crippling returns that private equity always seek.

‘It’s not bold when you fail to explain that once you have sold your share it is gone forever and you have disinherited your successors from ownership of the World Cup.

FIFA legends have reportedly declined to publicly support Infantino amid the backlash to his plans

‘And it’s not honest when you fail to mention that, after you have delivered the head of the World Cup on a platter to your mates in DC, they are going to give you a job worth five times your current salary.’

Figo then highlights FIFA’s staggering level of wealth, asking how many shares the $5billion in its reserves ‘could buy in this grubby, underhand plot’.

‘Infantino has debased the office of FIFA President that he promised to elevate,’ he writes. ‘He has lied, deceived and tried to feather his own nest at the expense of the game he is supposed to serve…he should go. Now.’

According to The Times, allies of Infantino had been trying to persuade 'FIFA legends' to publicly support Infantino, but have been unsuccessful.

The FIFA legends are among former international players who have been paid to appear at the governing body's events.

Sports.title: Inside the fall of the Hundred: Attendances down, prices up and locals snubbed as counties fear massive divide once IPL windfall wears off. 'We've seen this all before - it was called LIV Golf. Is the Hundred even going to be here in three years?'
Sports.content:
Inside the fall of the Hundred: Attendances down, prices up and locals snubbed as counties fear massive divide once IPL windfall wears off. 'We've seen this all before - it was called LIV Golf. Is the Hundred even going to be here in three years?'

Unlock more of the best of our cricket coverage with a DailyMail+ subscription - brilliant exclusives, in-depth insight and the writers you love every day

When Harry Brook was wowing those at Headingley on Tuesday night with a no-look six during a record-equalling 50, it felt in that particular moment that everything might at last be coming together for the Hundred.

A competition with multiple launches but a recurring marketing campaign promising to take a new audience to new places – what better than a shot that wasn’t even a thing when 100-ball cricket was dreamt up? – was doing so through one of its homegrown pin-ups.

Undoubtedly, Brook’s 15-ball half century at Headingley just past the midpoint of the Hundred’s sixth season ticked all the boxes, fulfilling the pledges to make this competition second only to the Indian Premier League in short-form stature and to feature England’s premier players at its forefront.

The strength of the attack the 27-year-old was up against spoke of the quality on show this year: six of the London Spirit bowlers were internationals and the seventh was James Coles, the Hundred’s most expensive auction purchase ever at £390,000.

Yet that snapshot also exposed two sporting spheres colliding. In South Asia and North America – the territories from which this year’s new money in a £975million Hundred upgrade has come – franchises pop up, move cities and disband with minimal fuss while supporters are more willing to change allegiance depending on where their favourite players move.

Here in the UK, though, we are a parochial bunch and one trick that the newly owned teams either missed, or brazenly disregarded, was signing local county players to their respective Hundred teams to boost identity.

When Harry Brook was hitting a no-look six during a record-equalling 50, it felt in that particular moment that everything might at last be coming together for the Hundred

Australia stars Marcus Stoinis (left) and Adam Zampa (batting) are two of the international stars cementing the Hundred as the second-strongest short-form competition behind the IPL

Nowhere in the country is as insular as Yorkshire and it felt wrong during the early stages of this year’s auction that SunRisers Leeds were not going all out to recruit one of Joe Root, Jonny Bairstow or Adil Rashid. It left Brook and his former Burley-in-Wharfedale club mate Matthew Revis as the only familiar faces to relate to on Tuesday.

Southampton-based Southern Brave have just one Hampshire player in their ranks in teenager Manny Lumsden, a squad player rather than a first-choice pick and could not retain their local hero and captain James Vince in this season’s auction.

Somerset’s England Twenty20 international Tom Banton has played for three Hundred franchises, but has spent the past three seasons at Trent Rockets and admits continuity in squads is needed to deepen connections with fans.

‘If they're coming every year and there's new faces, I guess it's hard for people to get behind the team and support, isn't it?’ says Banton. ‘Whereas if you've been playing for a few years, they can kind of relate to you, get to know you and want to come and watch you.’

In contrast to the majority of their new-money rivals, the table-topping Rockets have also maintained the same colours and badge following the tournament’s unofficial relaunch. Five seasons of familiarity has been removed elsewhere.

Until recently, Headingley was full of purple-shirted Northern Superchargers fans. Overnight, following the complete buyout of Yorkshire’s stake in the competition by Sunrisers Hyderabad, they were being asked to form an orange army, and support Leeds rather than band together as the North. Best of luck.

Colours and identities are important to a British supporter base. Recall the anger when Cardiff City switched from blue to red shirts and ditched the bluebird for a dragon or when Hull City’s former owner Assem Allam applied to change the club’s name to Hull Tigers.

The Sunrisers are one of three teams to have changed names, along with Oval Invincibles becoming MI London and the Manchester Originals being renamed Manchester Super Giants. All have badges and kits to reflect their IPL links, although MI have retained the colours of the reigning three-in-a-row champions Invincibles for training.

‹ Slide me ›

Oval Invincibles won the last three men's titles wearing a turquoise strip, before being taken over by Mumbai Indians and becoming MI London, playing in royal blue

‹ Slide me ›

Meanwhile, the Old Trafford-based franchise have gone from being Manchester Originals in black kits to Manchester Super Giants in red and navy stripes

Southern Brave have gone from green and black to blue and red. Birmingham Phoenix have moved from orange shirts to black. To their credit, both Manchester and Leeds teams have begun schemes to make the switch easier, giving out replica shirts to every ticket holder at their early matches.

MI London launched a shirt amnesty in which turquoise 2025 Oval Invincibles shirts could be exchanged for the new royal blue ones. Additionally, they produced a club T-shirt for £20 under their ‘Twenty’s Plenty’ campaign.

Vikram Banerjee, the Hundred’s managing director, says that 40 per cent of those through the turnstiles are Under 16s and that ‘as we look to deepen and accelerate fandom, merchandise sales are a great barometer. Southern Brave and London Spirit are already having to restock, and nearly 40,000 fans are wearing the new jerseys of Manchester Super Giants or SunRisers Leeds.’ Presumably referencing the freebies.

Filling their grounds with a shirt-donning, flag-waving, family-oriented crowd has been championed as a success by the host counties too, but there are sceptics from within the county game about the real impact underneath the veneer, with one executive telling Daily Mail Sport: ‘The rebranding is utterly ridiculous. They’ve alienated the local people, and now they've whacked the prices up that nobody can afford it. And the sales are through the floor.

‘I don't know about anybody else, but I'm just looking at the Hundred right now and thinking we've seen this before – it was called LIV Golf. So, is the Hundred even going to be here in three years’ time?’

Whether it is the impact of the cost-of-living crisis, increased ticket prices or the rebranding that has proved a turnoff remains to be seen, but the Hundred is proving a hard sell in 2026. The first block of matches saw attendances down around 20 per cent on last year, the second block dropping by 27 per cent.

Crowds have generally picked up across the competitions since, but with ticketing operations now run by the organisations themselves rather than centrally, entrance fees hitting a high of £55 is an issue, even if you do get access to both parts of the men’s and women’s double-header for your money.

That is some hike for a competition that spent its first iteration between 2021-25 dishing out complimentary seats to its target audience of mums and kids. The problem with freebies, though, comes when you ask people to start paying instead.

The first block of matches saw attendances down around 20 per cent on last year, the second block dropping by 27 per cent

Brook’s blockbuster knock was watched by just over 9,000 spectators this week, a few hundred down on the 9,438 that turned out for the Leeds v Manchester contest. By comparison, the established Roses Twenty20 Blast fixture, promoted with a fraction of the budget, drew 11,300 at Headingley in June.

Kaviya Maran, part of the Sun Group that owns the SunRisers said the first signs at Headingley were ‘a good beginning’, adding: ‘Obviously it's a new brand for them.’

It was a similar story across the Pennines at Old Trafford, scene of a 16,500 sellout for the reverse Blast match. The cheapest tickets were £30 with £8 concessions for that, and while those for Super Giants matches cost less, starting at £24 and £5 in advance, their average men’s Hundred crowd has been under 12,000.

There have been some misjudgments. A huge proportion of Yorkshire fans will refuse to support a team with Leeds in its name, especially after the woeful attempt to incorporate Leeds United’s Marching On Together as the club song via a (swiftly deleted) social media post.

There have been highs, such as Welsh Fire setting attendance records for any women’s match in Wales and in the men’s competition on July 25 for the visit of the MI London teams. And the women’s game is benefitting with a higher percentage of people turning up earlier to stadia. Eighty per cent of fans that watched Southern Brave’s men on July 27 had been there early doors to see the women’s game too.

While the cash-rich Hundred stumbles, the county game it has kicked into the side verges has witnessed a series of triumphs. Helped by the presence of Ben Stokes, Durham sold out Jesmond when hosting Glamorgan in the MetroBank One-Day Cup and had to warn ticketless supporters not to turn up on matchday. There were 2,300 present to witness a thrilling match that saw Durham recover from 97 for six to knock off their 327-run target with three balls to spare.

Stokes was also in the Durham team that played to almost 5,000 in defeat by Yorkshire at York last week, 48 hours after the same venue accommodated 4,500 for the visit of Worcestershire.

Gloucestershire have had to expand their capacity for their visits to Cheltenham this year because of demand and although these numbers are more modest than the Hundred, full outgrounds are aesthetically pleasing to see and provide a county’s emerging players with an entry level for professional cricket.

By contrast, the Roses T20 Blast match drew a sell-out crowd of 16,500 - despite prices being higher than the Hundred

Peter Matthews, chairman of Gloucestershire, is an advocate of taking 50-over cricket to venues ‘that don't normally see cricket,’ adding: ‘It has echoes for those of a certain generation of some of the Sunday League grounds. Gloucestershire used to play a Sunday League game at a number of different grounds – Lydney, Moreton-in-Marsh, Gloucester – which we can't do now because it doesn’t work economically.’

Matthews says the lack of an obvious Hundred competitor in the region has helped footfall during the period between the World Cup and the start of the Premier League in a fortnight. And non-host clubs like his have been able to plan for more sustainable futures thanks to the £25million individual windfalls from the ECB’s big sell-off.

In addition to paying off their debts – ‘we got ourselves into a bit of a muddle,’ says Matthews – Gloucestershire ploughed £3million into a project codenamed Dressing Rooms, which drastically improved player and match official facilities plus general infrastructure at their Nevil Road headquarters.

Leicestershire are another to have been dragged out of the red by the Hundred’s millions, and they have begun feasibility studies on adding further non-cricket earnings to their annual income.

They have already been creative in this space on a smaller scale, holding drive-in cinema days last weekend and planning to install a 4G multi-sports pitch alongside the country’s largest playing area to be hired out during the winter. Their decision to allow children in free this month has resonated with their following, coming during the school holidays.

Chief executive Emma White says: ‘We're in the middle of a cost of living crisis, so I think there’s a ridiculous squeeze on the leisure pound. Are we getting a true reflection of the Hundred effect? I'm not entirely sure we are, if I'm totally honest. We're seeing a true reflection of the fact that people can't afford to do much at the moment.

‘The massive positive is that it's given quite a lot of counties more than you would imagine, the breathing space needed to kind of reset a little bit and almost future-proof cricket in their area by investing in revenue-generating projects.’

With the £25million lump sums viewed as a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to become less reliant on ECB annual handouts, counties – particularly the non-hosts – are taking their time to assess how best to invest. Durham recently received planning permission for an on-site hotel that they first discussed pre-Covid and will now employ a project director to produce a report on profitability, given the rise of costs in the hospitality industry.

Counties – particularly the non-hosts – are taking their time to assess how best to invest. Durham received planning permission for an on-site hotel that they first discussed pre-Covid

But there is a fear that however smartly the money is used, the disparity between those that have taken the finite sum and those still with skin in the Hundred game is only going to widen

The IPL might be a behemoth now but it took the expansion of the league from eight to ten teams in 2011 to truly realise its potential

But there is a fear that however smartly the money is used, the disparity between those that have taken the finite sum and those still with skin in the Hundred game is only going to widen.

‘Host counties are going to become wealthier and more able to attract the best players,’ said one county chair. ‘Fundamentally you're talking about those grounds having tradition, history and scale. It's very difficult to argue against tradition, history, and scale. They’re always going to generate more revenue than elsewhere.’

To back up the theory, the Lord’s-based Spirit have been valued at £300million – two and a half times more than the field. Suspicion remains around the shires that while this year’s competition will not return profits for the new investors, they are biding their time until expansion. Teams based in Bristol and Chester-le-Street would be the most obvious additions.

It was not until the IPL increased from eight to ten teams that the original set hit a goldmine, as the fee paid for the rights to own a new franchise would be distributed among the rest of the existing teams. And that with half the teams now controlled by powerful IPL owners, it is only a matter of time before Indian players are allowed to feature in a league outside of their own, significantly increasing its value in television and commercial rights on the subcontinent.

At which point, Hundred teams would potentially need fewer Englishmen and counties would be re-stocked with some of their primary talents, opening the chance to play the County Championship throughout August once more and easing a schedule already past saturation point. Unlike Brook’s shot in Leeds, all eyes are on what direction the Hundred will go now.

Sports.title: Atletico lead chase for Cristian Romero, Aston Villa braced for fresh Arsenal bid for Ezri Konsa, Mikey Moore set for Cologne loan... and Mo Salah mobbed in Turkey: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:
It's that time of the year again – the transfer window is now open until September 1 and it's sure to be a busy period with clubs looking to make big signings ahead of next season.

Here are today's latest developments from Simon Jones and the Daily Mail Sport team...

Madrid wait for Vinicius Jr decision

Real Madrid are awaiting a response from Vinicius Jr after offering the Arsenal target improved terms in excess of £19million a year.

The Brazil international’s current terms with Madrid expire at the end of next season and Arsenal have made him aware they are willing to step in if he fails to find agreement with the Spanish giants.

Talks between the player’s agents, general director Jose Angel Sanchez and chief scout Juni Calafat took place in Madrid on Wednesday. Jose Mourinho also underlined that the 26-year-old is also firmly in his plans.

Atletico lead chase for Romero

Atletico Madrid are ready to firm up their interest in Tottenham defender Cristian Romero after he held talks with Inter Milan.

Atletico are in talks to sell left-back Matteo Ruggeri to Aston Villa in a deal worth £19.7m if the 24-year-old agrees to go. They are also selling Nahuel Molina to Roma and the combined fees will go towards a £30m bid for Romero.

Tottenham's Argentina defender Cristian Romero has suitors in Spain and Italy

Spurs yet to approach Liverpool about Gakpo

Tottenham remain keen to sign Cody Gakpo from Liverpool, as reported earlier this week, but, as of this afternoon, the Reds have yet to receive a formal approach.

Liverpool want to keep Gakpo but are exploring the possibility of signing Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris Saint-Germain as well as Bradley Barcola. But they are not in for Pedro Neto at Chelsea, who is a target for Manchester City.

Liverpool do not want to sell Cody Gakpo, with Spurs interested in a move

Toon working on replacement for Bruno

Newcastle are working to find a replacement for Bruno Guimaraes, who is set to have a medical at Arsenal after a £75m deal was agreed.

They have asked about Dortmund's Felix Nmecha, Angelo Stiller at Stuttgart and Luka Sucic at Real Sociedad, among others. as they try to find a solution swiftly with new boss Matthias Jaissle being announced tonight.

Norgaard's Everton move a done deal

Arsenal midfielder Christian Norgaard has completed a £7m move to Everton.

Ait Boudlal in talks with Fulham

Fulham have opened talks with Rennes for centre-back Abdelhamid Ait Boudlal. The 20-year-old Morocco international is valued in excess of £25m.

Spurs' Moore off to Germany

Tottenham winger Mikey Moore has accepted a loan move to Cologne in Germany. The 18-year-old spent last year on loan with Rangers.

Tottenham’s teenage striker Mason Melia has undergone his medical at Lincoln today ahead of finalising his loan move. The 18-year-old is a Republic of Ireland international.

Mikey Moore is set for another second loan spell after spending last year at Rangers

Villa working on £14m Ruggeri deal

Aston Villa are continuing to discussing a £14m deal with Atletico Madrid for Italian left-back Matteo Ruggeri but they are awaiting approval from the 24-year-old. Daily Mail Sport reported their interest yesterday.

Atletico looking to utilise funds towards their planned bid for Cristian Romero at Tottenham.

Burnley go for keeper Amos

Burnley have signed free agent goalkeeper Ben Amos.

The 36-year-old had taken part in the PFA training camp for free agents this summer after leaving Port Vale at the end of last season. He has signed a one-year deal with Burnley.

Amos has over 360 appearances with a host of EFL clubs after beginning his career at Manchester United.

Ben Amos spent time at Charlton, among several EFL clubs

Chalobah arrives for Como medical

Chelsea defender Trevoh Chalobah has arrived in Italy for his medical with Como. The deal is worth an initial £25.7m plus a further £5.1m in potential add-ons.

Spanish defender Pep Chavarria is in London to complete his £16m deal from Rayo Vallecano.

Trevoh Chalobah is closing in on a move to Como

Coventry aim to break transfer record AGAIN

Coventry are attempting to break their transfer record for the second time this week after offering nearly £26million for Ghana star Caleb Yirenkyi.

The midfielder, who plays for Danish club Nordsjaelland, represented his country at this summer’s World Cup as they drew 0-0 with England and exited at the first knockout stage.

Back in the top flight for the first time in 25 years, the Sky Blues have already signed goalkeeper Carl Rushworth for £22.5m as well as defender Aurele Amenda and winger Loum Tchaouna. They have also turned on-loan midfielder Frank Onyeka’s move from Brentford into a permanent switch.

TOM COLLOMOSSE

Caleb Yirenkyi featured for Ghana against England in the 0-0 draw at the World Cup

Arsenal set to come back for Konsa

Aston Villa are braced for a fresh bid from Arsenal for England defender Ezri Konsa amid attempts to tie him to a new contract.

Daily Mail Sport reported last month that Konsa was the Gunners’ top target for central defence though their initial proposal was well below Villa’s £60million valuation of the 28-year-old.

Konsa has remained on Arsenal’s radar since. He has two years remaining on his current deal at Villa Park and the club would like him to sign a new one.

Having already seen key men Morgan Rogers and Youri Tielemans depart this summer, and with Lucas Digne poised to join Paris Saint-Germain, Villa boss Unai Emery would have an even bigger rebuilding job were Konsa to depart.

Having recouped more than £140million for Rogers, who joined Chelsea, and Tielemans, who signed for Manchester United, Villa are not under financial pressure to sell Konsa and are unlikely to do so without a high-level replacement lined up.

But along with Bruno Guimaraes and Vinicius Junior, Konsa is a key target for Arsenal – especially with William Saliba facing a lengthy injury absence – and they are unlikely to give up hope.

TOM COLLOMOSSE

Ezri Konsa would join England team-mate Declan Rice if Arsenal can pull off a deal

Come in No 61! Salah on his way to Turkey

Mohamed Salah is travelling to Turkey ahead of negotiating final details to complete his free transfer to Trabzonspor.

The Turkish club have posted pictures and videos on social media of the former Liverpool forward in a Trabzonspor shirt wearing No 61 while on their private plane.

Salah is scheduled to arrive in Istanbul shortly before heading to Trabzon later on today.

Read more on this story HERE

Mo Salah is pictured in a Trabzonspor shirt ahead of his move to Turkey

£14m Vitek set for Boro

Manchester United have agreed a deal worth £14million with Middlesbrough for goalkeeper Radek Vitek.

The fee is inclusive of bonuses for the highly-rated 22-year-old and there is also a 35pc sell-on clause plus matching rights and a buy back option for the Czech.

Tottenham defender Ashley Phillips, 21, is also in talks over a move to Boro.

Kim Hellberg has brought in seven signings so far this summer, including Will Lankshear from Spurs in a deal worth up to £20m.

Meanwhile, two Boro players are due to have medicals ahead of moves away. Delano Burgzorg is heading to Preston in a £2m deal and Kaly Sene is joining Young Boys in Switzerland.

Bruno set for £75m Arsenal move

Arsenal are set to complete their protracted £75million move for Newcastle United captain Bruno Guimaraes.

Full agreement is now almost done, with the clubs agreeing a compromise to end the saga.

Guimaraes is waiting for permission to leave Newcastle's training base in La Manga, in Spain, to finalise the formalities of his move to Emirates Stadium.

Read more on this story HERE

Bruno Guimaraes is set to wave goodbye to Newcastle after four years at the club

Swansea's Wilson heads to Gent

Swansea City forward Kyrell Wilson has joined KAA Gent for an undisclosed fee, subject to the relevant clearance.

The 21-year-old former Chelsea academy graduate impressed on loan at Falkirk last season and links up with the top-flight Belgian side who secured European qualification last term.

Swansea, meanwhile, are close to agreeing a deal worth £5.2m for Valencia attacking midfielder Andre Almeida.

Talks are focusing on an initial fee of £3m, plus £2.2m in add-ons as well as a sell-on clause.

Almeida, 26, was left out of Valencia’s training yesterday and has still to agree personal terms with the Welsh club.

Kyrell Wilson (left) in action for Falkirk last season - he will now head to Belgium

Altay's off to Spain

Manchester United goalkeeper Altay Bayindir has been given permission to travel to Spain and complete his move to Celta Vigo.

As Daily Mail Sport reported on Saturday, the Turkey international is joining on an initial loan with option to buy around £3.5million.

Vigo will cover Bayindir salary in full and there are various performance-related bonuses.
