World.title: 1,000 complaints made to EU Commission’s anti-harassment team
World.content:
The Commission — which has a workforce of some 30,000 — hired a chief confidential counsellor, Lene Naesager, to deal with staff harassment issues, in May 2024. She has a team of 40 counsellors across the Commission and its executive agencies.

Since September 2024, the chief counsellor, who reports to Budget Commissioner Piotr Serafin, has received 960 reports from “colleagues feeling harassed, alleged harassers, witnesses, managers and HR correspondents,” according to a Commission spokesperson.

However, the chief counsellor “has no mandate to investigate and is not entitled legally to qualify the conduct as harassment as defined in the Staff Regulations,” the spokesperson explained.

To make a formal complaint, staff instead have to go to the Investigation and Disciplinary Office (IDOC) or to the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF). The Commission receives around 20 to 25 formal complaints per year, the spokesperson said.

The Commission said 14,000 staff have attended presentations on anti-harassment policy while 2,400 managers have attended mandatory training sessions in the last two years. This increased awareness about how to seek support in dealing with harassment has “generated a relatively high number” of reports to the chief confidential counsellor, the spokesperson said.

A Commission spokesperson said the institution was “committed to being a modern, respectful and attractive place to work,” pointing to a review launched by President Ursula von der Leyen into the Commission’s operations. An internal survey found 74 percent of staff rated the Commission an attractive employer, up six percentage points from 2023.

But a senior official said that same review will not include recommendations on anti-harassment policy, as the issue falls outside its “scope.”

World.title: Why people want a job at the European Commission — and why so many end up miserable
World.content:
Their experiences varied widely across the Commission’s 30,000-strong workforce — but the same complaints surfaced again and again. Some were granted anonymity to speak frankly about their workplace experiences.

“The conditions are more and more difficult,” said Nicolas Mavraganis, president of Union Syndicale Fédérale, an umbrella group linking roughly 20 staff unions across EU and international bodies. A Commission official since 1994, he has led the federation since 2019 and helps steer its representation of member unions in dealings with the institutions. “There is more and more workload, which means more and more pressure.”

As Brussels has taken on a more central geopolitical role — responding to Russia’s war against Ukraine, navigating tensions with China and managing an increasingly unpredictable United States — officials said there is a growing sense that every file matters.

Few of the complaints POLITICO heard — ranging from stressful projects and difficult bosses to endless bureaucracy and aging offices — are unique to the Commission, and similar stories can be found in ministries, law firms and consultancies across Europe. But officials said the combination of prestige, political pressure and the sheer scale of the institution makes the experience distinctive — and often difficult.

“It’s the EU’s executive so people have this weird God complex,” one official said.

A Commission spokesperson said the institution was “committed to being a modern, respectful and attractive place to work,” pointing to a review launched by President Ursula von der Leyen into the Commission’s operations. An internal survey found 74 percent of staff rated the Commission an attractive employer, up six percentage points from 2023.

World.title: Andy Burnham talks big on bills. Now for the hard part.
World.content:
Britain’s new prime minister has already made one bid to show voters he is serious about tackling the problem: Removing VAT from household electricity bills, something he announced on his first day in No. 10.

The move will knock less than £4 off the average monthly bill, ends after one year, and comes with a price tag of £850 million. Downing Street said it will be paid for through so-far unspecified Whitehall savings.

But Burnham and his new Energy Secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, promised that the intervention is just a start. Cutting VAT is a “down payment” ahead of the winter, Fahnbulleh said.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh arrives at 10 Downing Street for Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first cabinet meeting, on July 21, 2026 in London, England. | Dan Kitwood/Getty Images

That means ministers have just weeks before Burnham’s first budget this fall to figure out what, if anything, can really ease the burden — and how to pay for it.

Salami slicing

“The fiscal space is going to be a challenge, and that is the case for any government,” said Sam Alvis, associate director for environment, energy security, and nature at the Labour-aligned Institute for Public Policy Research think tank.

That’s because any intervention to bring down energy bills will have to be funded from already under-pressure Whitehall departments.

World.title: German anti-terror police investigate explosive drone found at Leipzig airport
World.content:
Officials told WELT — which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer group — that the device’s detonator failed to function, preventing an explosion. They also said the drone was found just meters from a Ukrainian Antonov transport aircraft. According to the report, it contained Semtex, the explosive used in the bomb that brought down Pan Am Flight 103 over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988, killing all 259 people on board and 11 on the ground.

Leipzig airport hosts the base of operations of NATO’s Strategic Airlift International Solution (SALIS), which gives participating countries access to Antonov cargo planes to transport military equipment. The airport is DHL’s largest European air hub and serves as an aircraft maintenance base for some Ukrainian Antonov aircraft.

According to WELT, security authorities have internally classified the incident as an attempted attack. No suspects had been detained as of Wednesday evening.

Germany’s Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt interrupted his summer vacation in Italy to meet officials in Leipzig.

Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster described the incident in a statement as “very serious security incident.”

Ukraine’s ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, assumed Moscow could be behind the incident. “I hope that all the authorities in Germany will now establish the facts as well. But who else could it have been besides Russia?” he posited on WELT TV.

Russia’s embassy to Germany didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Lennart Pfahler contributed reporting from Berlin. This article has been updated.

World.title: Starlite: the 'Disney' of music makes Marbella one of Europe's top experiential destinations
World.content:
For decades, Marbella has been one of the Mediterranean's leading tourist destinations, thanks to its beaches, its climate and its range of hotels. But over the past fifteen years, a new attraction has begun to draw visitors from all over the world: music.

 

It is not just about going to a concert. Those who travel each summer to Starlite Occident Marbella are looking for a complete experience that begins long before the stage lights go down and continues well into the early hours.

It is a new way of thinking about tourism, where the trip revolves around an experience rather than just a destination. Every summer it is held in the Cantera de Nagüeles, a spectacular natural amphitheatre carved into the rock just a few minutes from the centre of Marbella.

Starlite has become one of the most distinctive entertainment events in Europe. Unlike the big music festivals, which pack dozens of artists into a single weekend, here each night is devoted to a single concert.

Image of the venue provided by the festival. Starlite

This programme, which runs for almost three months, allows thousands of visitors to plan their holidays around the artist they want to see. "We are much more than a festival", its founder and CEO, Sandra García-Sanjuán, tells 'Euronews'. "Music is the common thread, but the experience begins long before the concert."

A destination with its own soundtrack. The transformation of tourism in recent years has led many travellers to prioritise experiences over traditional destinations. Starlite fits that trend perfectly.

The venue opens at around eight in the evening and stays busy for about ten hours. Before each performance, guests can dine in one of its five restaurants, explore different food areas, take part in cultural activities or simply enjoy the open-air atmosphere, surrounded by the quarry's rock walls.

When the concert ends, the experience goes on. The venue turns into a nightclub with DJ sets and live performances until dawn.

"Our visitors spend an average of between four and a half and five hours inside the venue. They come to have dinner, to enjoy themselves with friends, to experience the concert and then to carry on the night. That is all part of the Starlite experience", García-Sanjuán explains.

Closeness as the new luxury. With capacity for barely 3,500 people, the auditorium offers a completely different experience from a stadium or a giant festival.

While other events compete to pull in as many spectators as possible, Starlite has built its identity precisely on the opposite idea.

"We do not want to compete to be the biggest. We want to offer closeness", its founder says. That smaller scale allows for a much more direct relationship between artists and audience.

Everyone has a seat, they can get up to dance or step out for a few minutes without losing their place, and they enjoy a level of proximity that is rare at concerts by major international stars. For García-Sanjuán, this human connection is precisely one of the great strengths of the tourism of the future.

"We live surrounded by screens and artificial intelligence. It will be increasingly important to share real experiences, to look the artist in the eye, to feel the energy and to live something that no technology can replace", she says. A tourism engine for Marbella. The impact of Starlite goes far beyond the festival grounds.

According to a study by PwC, each edition generates around 315 million euros in economic impact for the Costa del Sol.

Image of the festival provided by the organisers Starlite

The length of the event largely explains that figure. For almost three months, thousands of visitors arrive from 93 countries, stay in hotels, spend in restaurants, visit beaches, play golf, go shopping and extend their stay for several days so they can attend one or several concerts.

"When a destination sells only sun and beach, visitors always think they can come back another summer. But when it also offers the chance to see an international artist in a unique setting, the trip takes on the feel of something unrepeatable", the Starlite CEO points out.

The organisation works with hotels and tour operators that sell specific packages for those who want to combine holidays and concerts, a model that has established itself as one of the leading examples of experiential tourism in Spain. A global brand. The success of the project has taken Starlite far beyond Marbella.

The company has already staged several editions in Madrid, conceived as the winter version of the concept, and is studying new international locations. Saudi Arabia, Mexico and other Latin American markets are among the destinations that have expressed interest in hosting the model.

Even so, García-Sanjuán insists that expansion will be limited. "We do not want to be everywhere. Disney is not everywhere either".

The comparison is no accident. "We are the closest thing to Disney, but with music", she says. Not because it aims to turn itself into a theme park, but because it wants to build a recognisable universe around an experience.

Just as millions of people travel to Disney to spend a few days immersed in a world of its own, Starlite wants each edition to become a destination worth travelling to in its own right, regardless of which artist is on stage that night.

The rise of emotion-based tourism. Starlite's evolution reflects a trend that is gaining ground in the global tourism industry: the rise of tourism built around emotions and experiences.

More and more travellers plan their trips around a major sporting event, a food festival, an exhibition or a concert. The destination still matters, but it is no longer the only reason for the trip.

In that context, Marbella has found a powerful tool to diversify what it offers beyond traditional sun-and-beach tourism.

Starlite does more than attract visitors. It produces audiovisual content that is distributed internationally, projects the image of the city in dozens of countries and fuels aspirational tourism: people who discover the festival on television or social media and end up travelling years later to live the experience for themselves.

But perhaps the real spectacle is seeing how a former industrial site, a stone quarry in the middle of the mountains, has managed to reinvent itself to become one of the most exclusive experiential destinations of the European summer. Because at Starlite the concert is only the beginning of the journey.

World.title: IDF to continue to 'operate proactively' in Gaza, Israeli military chief says
World.content:
The Israel Defense Forces will continue to "operate proactively" in Gaza, according to Eyal Zamir, the chief of the general staff of the Israeli military.

 

Zamir made the comments following an operational tour on Wednesday, during which he met with several senior Israeli commanders who briefed him on the situation on the ground, per a statement shared by the military.

“In the Gaza Strip, we have struck a blow against Hamas, significantly weakened it and altered the security situation,” Zamir said. “The IDF will continue to operate proactively and in accordance with the principle we have established – to eliminate threats and, in all circumstances, to defend the communities and their residents, and to safeguard their security".

His statement came after Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had not agreed to a US-backed plan for Gaza, which would see Israeli forces withdraw from territory and the disarmament of the Hamas militant group.

"President Trump and his team think they can get Hamas to disarm and demilitarise in Gaza," Netanyahu said in a video message on Tuesday.

"We are looking into that. They sent us a draft, we did not agree," he continued, adding: "It is not our draft. We sent our comments".

Trump announced last week that his Board of Peace had reached what he called a "historic" agreement on the "complete disarmament of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza," which he said would pave the way for the transition to a new Palestinian government.

According to Trump, the deal would see Israeli forces withdraw from Gaza while an International Stabilization Force would work with a new Palestinian police unit to run the territory.

Jennifer Gavito, a nonresident senior fellow with the Scowcroft Middle East Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council, said "external actors" would be "indispensable in the success of this proposal."

"Egypt and Qatar will have to continue to lean heavily on Hamas to fulfill its commitments," Gavito said, adding that Trump would also have to put "tremendous pressure on Netanyahu" in order for the plan to succeed.

The Israel-Gaza war broke out after Hamas's October 7 attacks on Israel in 2023, which killed more than 1,200 people and saw 251 others taken hostage into Gaza.

Israel launched a military campaign into Gaza in the wake of the attacks, which has killed more than 73,000 people, per Gaza's health ministry.

World.title: Europe’s biggest debates – Migration, Mercosur, and housing on The Ring
World.content:
Water Matters

Europe's water is under increasing pressure. Pollution, droughts, floods are taking their toll on our drinking water, lakes, rivers and coastlines. Join us on a journey around Europe to see why protecting ecosystems matters, how our wastewater can be better managed, and to discover some of the best water solutions. Video reports, an animated explainer series and live debate - find out why Water Matters, from Euronews.

World.title: Iran and Oman agree route for ships in Strait of Hormuz, Tehran says
World.content:
Iran and Oman on Wednesday finalised an agreement on what Tehran calls the geographical coordinates of a proposed shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz.

 

Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran and Oman are preparing a joint statement on the agreement which includes technical, legal, security and environmental points.

Separately, Iranian media quoted official sources saying that the reopening of the Strait would depend on the US ending its naval blockade of the country's ports.

The key aspect of such an agreement revolves around Tehran’s insistence to charge fees for passage as it claims sovereign control of the key waterway, in direct opposition with the United States and the Gulf countries who insist that navigation must remain free as stipulated by the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.

“Provided that certain third parties do not obstruct the process, a joint statement by the two countries outlining the main considerations and points agreed upon is also being reviewed and finalized,” Baghaei said referring to the US as a “third party”.

Baghaei however underlined that the Iran-Oman agreement in itself cannot guarantee the safety of navigation through Hormuz as long as “the US naval blockade and other actions against Iran and its interests remain in place.”

Tehran’s announcement comes amid several days of intense speculation on the two-month long negotiations between Iran and Oman, which Tehran insists are in line with the Memorandum of Understanding signed with the United States in June.

Contradictory comments on US-Iran talks

Earlier on Wednesday, Iranian state television reported that the Iran-Oman talks focus on setting up a “middle corridor” through the Strait of Hormuz, to be controlled by the two countries.

Another Iranian state media outlet reported that the agreement would not immediately result in the reopening of the strait due to what Tehran calls “US violations”, and that the negotiations “have nothing to do with the United States”.

“The reopening of the Strait of Hormuz depends on a change in US behaviour and the correction of its violations,” state TV channel IRIB said.

However, US President Donald Trump insisted in an interview with US broadcaster Fox News on Tuesday night that the US is part of the Hormuz negotiations, which are “moving along very nicely”.

“The Strait is going to be open very soon, or they are going to get hit very hard, and then the strait is going to be open,” Trump said.

The waterway, a crucial energy transit chokepoint that carries roughly a quarter of the global seaborne oil trade, was effectively closed by Iran after US and Israeli strikes in late February, sparking wild swings in energy markets.

Former head of Israel’s military intelligence research department Danny Citrinowicz commented on X that “from day one, it was clear that restoring the Strait of Hormuz to its pre-crisis status would have required either regime change in Iran or a sustained military effort to impose control over the waterway.”

“Neither option was politically or strategically acceptable to Washington, given the enormous costs and long-term commitments they would require. Sometimes, the least desirable option is the only realistic one,” Citrinowicz said.

World.title: Basque Country halves colon cancer deaths with screening programme
World.content:
Screening for colon cancer using a simple test for hidden blood in faeces can save thousands of lives. That is the conclusion of one of the largest studies carried out to date in Spain, which finds that this programme of early detection is associated with a 50% reduction in mortality from colorectal cancer among people aged 50 to 69.

 

The research, published this Wednesday in "JAMA Network Open (source in Spanish)", tracked how the disease evolved over 21 years in a population of almost 2.2 million people in the Basque Country. The findings show that the fall in deaths began just three years after the screening programme was introduced and has been sustained ever since.

As well as cutting mortality, the programme has made it possible to detect 70.8% of tumours at stages I and II, when the chances of cure are far higher and treatment is less aggressive.

The study, led by Dr Luis Bujanda, examined mortality data recorded between 2004 and 2024. Over that period there were 438,134 deaths from all causes, of which 16,298 were linked to colorectal cancer.

In the age group covered by the screening programme, 50 to 69 years, the mortality rate fell from 39.7 to 19.8 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants, a decrease of 50.1%. In the population as a whole, mortality also dropped, from 32.8 to 23.1 deaths per 100,000 inhabitants.

The researchers identified a turning point in 2012, just three years after the programme began, strengthening the link between screening and the reduction in deaths from colorectal cancer. They also estimate that, without the introduction of this early detection system, mortality among people aged 50 to 69 would have been 46.2% higher.

A simple test that can detect cancer before symptoms appear

The screening programme is based on the faecal immunochemical test (FIT), a non-invasive test that detects small amounts of hidden blood in faeces, one of the earliest signs of a possible cancer or precancerous lesions. In the Basque Country, this test is offered every two years to men and women aged 50 to 69 who have no symptoms. If the result is positive, a colonoscopy is carried out to confirm the diagnosis.

Over the study period, the programme led to the detection of 4,892 cases of colorectal cancer. More than seven in ten were diagnosed at stages I or II, when treatment options are more effective and survival is significantly higher.

Support for early detection programmes

Colorectal cancer is one of the most common tumours and a leading cause of cancer death in Spain and worldwide. However, detecting it early greatly increases the chances of cure and even makes it possible to remove polyps before they turn into a malignant tumour.

For the authors, the results support the long-term benefits of organised screening programmes using the faecal immunochemical test as a public health strategy to reduce mortality from colorectal cancer.

They nevertheless stress that this is an observational study. This means the results show an association between the rollout of the programme and the fall in mortality, but do not allow a cause-and-effect relationship to be established with the same degree of certainty as a clinical trial.

Even so, the scale of the decline observed and its persistence for more than two decades reinforce the value of screening as one of the main tools for tackling this type of cancer.

World.title: Moroccan prosecutors charge 25 over Ceuta migrant crossings
World.content:
Moroccan prosecutors have charged 25 people in connection with last Thursday's mass crossing of migrants into the Spanish territory of Ceuta.

 

The charges include organising illegal border crossings, transporting passengers without a license, overcrowding vessels, overstaying visas, insulting and assaulting security forces, and deliberately damaging public property. The Moroccan news outlet Hespress reported the developments this week.

On Monday, the Moroccan government denied that it had given in to "pressure or blackmail" during the crisis - which saw tens of thousands of migrants enter Ceuta - while expressing its "disappointment" at the reactions of several European leaders, accusing them of trying to use the migration crisis for domestic political gains.

Moroccan diplomatic sources also rejected claims that the country had eased border controls. Speaking to Spanish media, they insisted that anyone attempting to cross the border "knows that they will be sent back and that Morocco will accept their return". It is a commitment they said Rabat had upheld "for years."

Meanwhile, the Moroccan Association for Human Rights said this week that Moroccan authorities have prosecuted 52 people in the city of Nador over their alleged involvement in the recent crisis.

According to a statement from the organisation, 11 young people appeared before the Criminal Division of the Court of Appeal in Nador, while another 41 people have been brought before the city's Court of First Instance.

All remain in pre-trial detention and some face accusations of criminal offences, although AMDH has not specified the charges against them.

World.title: Scotland’s ‘Grand Canyon’ for sale: Beauty spot featured in Outlander hits the market
World.content:
It’s never too late to switch career paths. Plenty of people become lawyers in later life, or give up their desk job to pick up a pair of scrubs.

 

So, how about running a tourist attraction in Scotland made famous by Outlander?

Because if that sounds like your dream life, you might just want to check out this listing on Christie & Co.

Finnich Glen, dubbed Scotland’s “Grand Canyon”, has just gone up for sale. The 23-acre site centres on a sandstone gorge that reaches 80 feet deep in some spots.

Long a popular filming location, having appeared in King Arthur, Sherlock Holmes and Taggart, the glen shot to new-found levels of fame after The Devil’s Pulpit was used as the fictional St Ninian’s Spring in Outlander’s first season.

Located just 15 minutes south of Loch Lomond and 30 minutes north of Glasgow by car, around 70,000 people visit the glen each year. An added bonus for prospective buyers, the site has approved plans for a visitor centre with a café/restaurant, plus a dedicated car park and an event space, which would take the projected annual visitor number to more than 300,000.

Current owners David and Carole Young are selling up because they want to “pass the project onto somebody with the vision and enthusiasm to take it forward”.

“This opportunity will appeal to buyers who want to create a commercial business and unique visitor experience with national importance, against a stunning backdrop,” Mark Lavery, director of retail and leisure at Christie & Co, who is managing the sale process, said.

“Historically important, and already a tourist attraction with approved planning permission, the development opportunities are exciting, and we encourage interested parties to get in touch.”

Outlander’s impact on Scottish tourism

The Outlander book series follows Claire Randall, a British nurse who travels back in time to 18th-century Scotland after touching a stone circle while on her honeymoon in Inverness.

There, she meets Jamie Fraser, the dashing Highland warrior she initially clashes with before falling for.

Diana Gabaldon’s book series, having first been published in 1991, was already popular, but the TV adaptation, which ran from 2014 until earlier this year, took it to the next level.

The impact on Scottish tourism has been massive. While we can’t know the exact number of people heading to the country in the hopes of joining Clan Mackenzie, visitor numbers at attractions that feature in the show jumped by an average of 19%, according to Visit Scotland.

World.title: Copenhagen’s Noma restaurant to re-open under new leadership after abuse accusations
World.content:
René Redzepi had it all.

 

The Danish chef and co-founder of Noma led his restaurant to three Michelin stars and during his 23 years at Noma, the restaurant collected numerous accolades. These included topping the World's 50 Best Restaurants List not once, but five times.

On top of wowing the culinary world with his innovative "New Nordic" cuisine, he even created and starred in a TV series, Omnivore, which was released on Apple TV+.

Now, as the restaurant reopens, he's nowhere to be found.

Noma says it is beginning a “new chapter” with long-time chefs taking charge and a menu that will change monthly to focus even more on the seasonality of ingredients.

“It’s been crazy tough,” says new executive head chef Pablo Soto. “There’s been a lot of media attention and questions about what we’re doing, but we’re still here standing.”

What went wrong?

A woman enters fine-dining restaurant Noma's cafe and shop in Copenhagen, Denmark Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Abuse allegations

Redzepi had for years been dogged by reports of mistreatment of his staff, as well as his years long use of unpaid interns to staff the pricey restaurant.

Criticism came to a head just days before the opening of a Noma pop-up in Los Angeles. An article in The New York Times detailed several former employees’ accounts ranging from verbal abuse to physical assault at the hands of Redzepi and his deputies between 2009 and 2017.

The 48-year-old chef later apologised and announced his intention to “step away” in a tearful video posted to the restaurant’s Instagram page.

The restaurant declined to make Redzepi, who is now in a creative director role, available for an interview.

In an Instagram video, he said he was excited to see “fresh energy” come into the restaurant.

"What changes right now is the way he is allowing us to be more dynamic in the way we take decisions," explains Soto.

Chefs busily practice making dishes in fine-dining restaurant Noma's kitchen ahead of its new season in Copenhagen, Denmark Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Innovation and reinvention

Tom Sietsema, food correspondent for Washington-based news organization NOTUS, believes that Noma’s dedication to innovation and reinvention since its 2003 opening will help it weather the fallout. But only if its founder stays in the background.

“I think Noma can survive René Redzepi's poor behaviour and egregiousness. I think that there remains curiosity about the restaurant," says Sietsema. "I think he would be wise to sort of stay in the shadows in the distance a little bit.”

Soto says the restaurant is almost fully booked for its first three months, up until the end of October.

Guests will pay a set price of 6,500 Danish kroner (approx. €870) per head for the menu with wine pairing.

A chef shows a new fish dish in fine-dining restaurant Noma's kitchen ahead of its new season in Copenhagen, Denmark, Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Soto says the restaurant conducted an internal audit, and there are “many systems in place” to make sure staff are happy and “can grow.”

“We’ve gone through a period of crisis,” he says. “This means we need to be much more attentive to each individual.”

Noma, a contraction of the Danish words for Nordic and food, opened in 2003 dedicated to “a simple desire to rediscover wild local ingredients by foraging and to follow the seasons.”

While previous offerings were shaped around three distinct seasons, the reopening will see chefs embrace constant change in the menu.

Noma's head of R&D Mette Brink Soberg holds a new berry gazpacho dish topped with flower petals in fine-dining restaurant Noma's test kitchen in Copenhagen, Denmark. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

In the restaurant's test kitchen, Mette Brink Søberg, the head of research and development, delicately tops a berry gazpacho dish with colourful flower petals, recently plucked from the nearby garden.

“We feel that now we’ve done this for so many years, we’ve really become experts in all the flavours, the techniques, the concepts,” Brink Søberg says. “I think we’re ready to take one step further.”

Goodbye to the stars

Redzepi’s fall from grace was hailed by some as a reckoning, in a professional environment which has often been stained by accusations of abuse.

Are the days of bullying and intimidation in kitchen culture over?

Soto believes the industry has evolved.

“People are more aware of what’s fair and what is not,” he says. “People are looking for a little bit more of stability, not only learning a skill, but also something that can mean their lives.”

Aside from Redzepi, another notable absence at the opening is the restaurant's three Michelin stars. The third was awarded in 2021.

In May, the restaurant said it would not be part of this year’s Michelin Guide, saying it didn't meet the guide’s requirements for being open long enough in 2026.

The Copenhagen location shut ahead of the Los Angeles pop-up and remained closed for much of the year.

Asked whether reclaiming Noma’s stars was a priority, Soto shrugs off the idea.

“For us, it’s not about a single marker of excellence. It’s about continuing to push what we’ve done in the past 23 years,” he says. “If this brings something by the door, we’re happy to receive it.”

World.title: Hiroshima survivors warn against Japan's rearmament
World.content:
On the anniversary of the atomic bombings, survivors and activists tell DW Japan's military buildup risks eroding its longstanding commitment to pacifism.

Japan on Thursday commemorates the 81st anniversary of the nuclear attack on Hiroshima.

On August 6, 1945, the US dropped an atomic bomb on the Japanese city of Hiroshima during the last days of World War II, killing close to 80,000 people in the initial blast. Three days later, the US dropped a bomb over Nagasaki.

"Japan adopted a pacifist constitution in reflection on World War II," noted Masako Wada, assistant secretary general of Nihon Hidankyo, or the Japan Confederation of A- and H-Bomb Sufferers' Organizations.

Japan "earned the trust of the international community as a country that promised never to wage a war again," added Wada, who survived the Nagasaki bombing as a 1-year-old.

The dropping of the atomic bomb on August 6, 1945, flattened more than two-thirds of Hiroshima [FILE: September 8, 1945] Image: Stanley Troutman/AP Photo/picture alliance

However, in recent years, Japan has increased defense spending, eased restrictions on weapons exports and expanded the role of its military, citing growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia.

"The current administration is destroying that [trust]," Wada told DW, referring to Japan's recent efforts to pivot away from decades of strict postwar pacifism.

"Japan's recent military buildup is no different from recreating the arms race that led the country toward World War II," said 84-year-old Masashi Ieshima, who survived the Hiroshima bombing at the age of 3.

Survivors warn against rearmament

Ieshima was playing in the entrance of his house, just 1.2 miles (2 km) from the hypocenter, when the blast shattered all the windows in the house, sending shards of glass into his mother.

Hiroshima 'successors' keep telling atomic bomb stories To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Seventy years later, he underwent surgery for thyroid cancer, which was officially recognized as an atomic bomb-related illness. His father, who was also exposed to the Hiroshima atomic bombing, died of laryngeal cancer.

"It makes my blood boil to see Japan justify its military buildup and the easing of arms export restrictions over the possibility of a Taiwan conflict," said Ieshima, who serves as the chairman of Toyukai, the Tokyo affiliate of Nihon Hidankyo.

"If Japan continues down this path, it could lead to war. And if another war breaks out, I believe it will be a nuclear war."

The average age of Japan's atomic bomb survivors, known as "hibakusha," has reached almost 87. They face the urgent challenge of passing on their testimony and calls for peace to younger generations, including their children, grandchildren, and supporters.

Takako Nakamura, a second-generation atomic bomb survivor from Nagasaki, began working actively as a family testimony speaker in February 2026, following her career retirement.

"People were killed without a trace, not even their bones remain. That is the true nature of the atomic bomb," the 73-year-old told DW, her voice breaking.

Wada urged people around the world to recognize that the danger of nuclear weapons is "not something in the past, but in front of us right now."

She said she does not want sympathy for survivors, but empathy. "I want people to think of it as their own issue."

Japan pushes for military buildup, non-nuclear principles at risk

On Tuesday, Japan's Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said the country needs to strengthen its military with a "sense of urgency and crisis" as a new government assessment again highlighted growing risks from China, North Korea and Russia, according to Agence France-Presse (AFP).

In the preface to Japan's latest annual defense white paper , Koizumi said it was "imperative that Japan further reinforce and transform its defense capabilities with a stronger sense of urgency and crisis than ever before."

An atomic bomb explodes after being dropped by a US Air Force B-29 bomber over Nagasaki [FILE: August 9, 1945] Image: U.S. Army Air Forces/Library of Congress/REUTERS

The Defense Ministry told DW that Japan must strengthen its defense capabilities to enhance deterrence while maintaining its exclusively defense-oriented policy.

It cited an increasingly severe security environment, including China's military expansion and activities in the East and South China seas and around Taiwan.

Since taking office in October 2025, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has introduced a series of measures to strengthen Japan's defense capabilities. Her

Her government also relaxed restrictions on arms exports in April 2026, allowing exports of lethal weapons.

It is also considering revising Japan's long-standing commitment to the three non-nuclear principles of not possessing, producing or permitting the entry of nuclear weapons onto Japanese territory.

In November 2025, Takaichi said that a Chinese military attack on Taiwan could constitute a "survival-threatening situation" for Japan, potentially allowing Tokyo to exercise its legal right to collective self-defense.

Many Japanese Gen Zers are opposed to Japan's military expansion Image: Daiki Tateyama/DW

However, the argument that Japan must strengthen its military because China might invade Japan or Taiwan is "not convincing" to the Japanese public, said Koichi Nakano, a professor of political science at Sophia University in Tokyo.

China's military activities, including its maritime expansion, remain limited compared with Russia's war in Ukraine and US attacks on Iran, he told DW.

"Japan is being skillfully drawn into the narrative that it must fall into line with Europe and the US to confront so-called rogue states such as China, North Korea and Russia."

"Japan must responsibly pursue disarmament and establish dialogue," Nakano said. "It must stop demonizing China and recognize it as a country with which meaningful dialogue is possible."

Youth in Japan take to the streets in anti-war protests

Meanwhile, around 27,000 people gathered on July 10 outside the Japanese parliament building in Tokyo, holding colorful illustrated placards with messages such as "No war," and waving glow sticks in the dark.

Reina Tashiro, 36, a member of a civil organization "We Want Our Future," told DW that they aim to "make it as easy as possible for people to take that first step and join a protest."

"It is different from the traditional image of demonstrations, where people raise their fists and shout slogans," Tashiro added. "Our protests may even look stylish."

Nahoko Hishiyama, who has been involved in civic activism for 24 years since the age of 13 and now serves as co-chair of another activist group, pointed out that recent protests have increasingly been led by people in their 20s to 40s, and more women are taking part.

"Japanese women are often said to be too mindful of how others perceive them. In activism, however, that has been turned into a strength, thinking about how to present our message in a way that resonates with the public."

Pacifist Japan is rearming — this is why To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: FIFA president Infantino to stay on after crisis meeting
World.content:
FIFA's leadership has apologized for the controversial plan to open the World Cup to private investment. The plan has since been scrapped.

FIFA's leadership on Wednesday apologized for President Gianni Infantino's plan to open the World Cup to private investment, in a crisis meeting held after growing outrage at the plan and Infantino.

In a statement, the FIFA management board acknowledged "that errors were also made after the proposal was leaked to media." Infantino has since scrapped the plan.

The football body stressed it supported Infantino in staying on as president.

FIFA accused of blackmail in exchange for Infantino support To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did FIFA say?

"Following a meeting in Rabat, Morocco, the FIFA Secretary General and members of the FIFA Management Board in attendance reaffirmed their full support for FIFA President Gianni Infantino, as the only official elected by the 211 FIFA Member Associations," the statement added.

FIFA added that a separate letter had been sent to FIFA Council members and the 211 member associations apologizing and promising a review.

But the football body stressed it would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, ‌good governance and due process" with the plan now withdrawn, vowing to take all necessary measures to protect its reputation.

Calls for Infantino to step down have grown since he abandoned the controversial plan on Saturday.

What was the controversial World Cup sellout plan?

The backlash was centered on a proposal to sell a 20% stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion (roughly €3.6 billion). The plan also came under fire over the involvement of a company with family links to US ‌President Donald Trump, who is considered a close ally of Infantino.

European soccer's governing body UEFA had threatened to boycott the World Cup over the plan.

After the plan was abandoned, UEFA as well as CONCACAF, which runs the game in North and Central America plus the Caribbean, said it had lost confidence in the 56-year-old Swiss Italian’s leadership.

The Asian Football Confederation (AFC) was also critical of the way the proposal was pushed without consultation.

Additionally, European Leagues, which represents more than 1,300 clubs across Europe, said FIFA must not be allowed to "continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions" that affect not just clubs and players, but also fans.

The "impractically short assessment timeline" of four weeks given by FIFA to study the plan to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 tournament was also heavily criticized.

Infantino faces a re-election bid in March at FIFA's next Congress, which will also take place in Morocco — co-hosts of the 2030 World Cup.

Until recently, him claiming a fourth term seemed a formality.

Edited by: Rana Taha

World.title: US: Abdul El-Sayed wins contentious Michigan Senate primary
World.content:
Progressive Abdul El-Sayed defeated moderate Haley Stevens in a contest seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the Democratic party.

US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed scored an important victory against incumbent House Representative Haley Stevens in Michigan's Democratic primary, a closely watched contest that pitted progressives against moderates of the US party.

El-Sayed, who represents the leftwing progressives, narrowly defeated the moderate leaning Stevens 48.5% to 47.5%.

He will go on to face Republican incumbent Senator Mike Rogers in a seat that Democratic party must win if they hope to take control of the US Senate this November in the midterm elections.

If he defeats Rogers in November, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim elected to the US Senate.

Trump insults El-Sayed after primary race

The race between El-Sayed, who was endorsed by the likes of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, and Stevens, who had the backing of the Democratic party establishment was seen as a proxy war for the future ideological direction of the party.

Stevens was also backed with a big fundraising effort of the pro-Israel lobby American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC).

Democrats "have to come together to make sure that we never let Mike Rogers see the inside of the US Senate," El-Sayed said after winning the primary.

Stevens conceded to El-Sayed, saying she would "offer him my full support as we work to defeat Mike Rogers."

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump reacted to the news by calling El-Sayed "a Communist loser who hates Jews and Israel."

Israel at the center of campaign

The 41-year-old doctor focused his campaign on domestic issues like affordable healthcare, the economy and working class people's needs, but he also was vocal on his advocacy to end unconditional military aid to Israel.

The Michigan primary became a battleground between progressives and moderates over US support for Israel, something that has been seen in other Democratic primaries nationwide this year.

Stevens outspent El-Sayed, receiving over $60 million (€51 million) from outside Michigan groups, with more than $30 million coming from AIPAC and its affiliates.

After his primary win, AIPAC signaled said it would oppose El-Sayed and “his radical anti-Israel agenda" in November by supporting Rogers.

World.title: Will Russia start a fresh mobilization drive?
World.content:
Russian authorities are planning to "expand mobilization" in autumn this year, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, citing intelligence services. According to Zelenskyy, Russian President Vladimir Putin is reportedly preparing to recruit additional Russian soldiers to fight in the war against Ukraine.

"He is concealing his intention behind different words and signals, but he is making preparations," Zelenskyy said. "It is important that we, together with our partners, exert sufficient pressure on Russia so that the idea of ending this aggression — the idea of peace, rather than further Russian mobilization — prevails," he added. The Ukrainian president also said Russia's army was losing more fighters at the front than it can recruit, even though Putin wants to intensify the attacks and expand the war.

Putin issued a decree in autumn 2022 launching a "partial mobilization," which remains in effect to this day, as confirmed by the presidential administration in 2023. The document, it said, "regulates additional measures necessary to ensure that the armed forces fulfill their objectives."

Scores of Russians fled abroad after the Kremlin announced a partial mobilization in September 2022 Image: AP/picture alliance

What points to a possible new mobilization drive?

Independent Russian exile media outlet Verstka and Latvia-based Russian-language news portal Vaschnyje Istorii published an investigative report in late June stating that Russia's leadership was secretly "discussing mobilization" given the difficulties in recruiting new conscripts. One source quoted by Verstka said figures by Moscow's mayoral office show the city sent 1,708 people to the front in April of this year and 1,378 in May — around 1,000 fewer people than during the same period last year. This low recruitment rate reportedly continued in June as well.

Vaschnyje Istorii reported that the recruitment rate for soldiers serving on fixed-term contracts more than halved in the last quarter of 2025 compared with the same period the previous year. The outlet said the recruitment rate had dropped even further in early 2026. The news outlet also cited sources from different Russian regions revealing that the number of people applying for army contracts was falling.

Military personnel interviewed by Verstka said that contract soldiers being sent to fight this year were "unfit for combat," with many new arrivals fleeing the front lines. One conscript told the news outlet that "units are staffed at 30 to 40%, at best."

Droves of Russian fighting-age men made also their way to Georgia in 2022 Image: Daro Sulakauri/Getty Images

The US-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported in late July that the Kremlin is laying the groundwork for a fresh mobilization drive. ISW analysts wrote that such a move would be "a personal decision for Putin that is contingent on his personal perception of the battlefield situation and his perception of the stability and integrity of the Kremlin." They added that it "remains unclear whether or how Putin will decide to implement mobilization."

A few days ago, Verstka reported that demand for Armenian rental apartments had shot up, driven by Russian interest — just as it had in 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The outlet said rents in the Armenian capital, Yerevan, have risen by about 30% in recent months. According to the report, Russians are planning to leave the country ahead of the State Duma election, scheduled to be held from September 18 to 20.

One landlord told the outlet that in recent years most of his clients had been Russians who had already been living in Armenia for quite some time. Now, however, 80% of inquiries were from Russians who had recently moved to Armenia or were planning to relocate there.

What has Russia said?

Speaking at a press conference in late July, Russian presidential spokesman Dmitry Peskov chose not to comment on Ukrainian President Zelenskyy's remarks regarding a possible new mobilization drive, saying "it is not Zelenskyy's job to talk about our plans."

Andrei Klishas, a member of the Russian Federation Council, told Russian-language media outlet RTVI in early summer 2026 that a new mobilization was not currently being discussed in the country as it was unnecessary.

Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council, dismissed rumors about a possible new mobilization, calling them "pre-election propaganda." The former Russian president also claimed that in the first half of 2026, some 200,000 people had enlisted in the Russian army.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has refused to comment on rumors of a looming mobilization Image: Ulf Mauder/dpa/picture alliance

"Of course, you can't blindly trust information provided by the Russian authorities," military expert Yan Matveyev told DW. "Information is adjusted to align with their objectives," he added, with regard to Medvedev's statements on the number of new Russian contract soldiers. That said, figures provided by Russian officials are not too far off when compared with analyses by independent researchers, Matveyev said. "Instead of Medvedev's nearly 200,000 new soldiers, that number would probably be closer to 170,000 or 180,000 over six months."

In his view, the current recruitment rate is not sufficient for Russia to secure a military victory over Ukraine. A new mobilization drive would not change that, Matveyev added. "Even if they doubled the size of their army, Russia would not be able to defeat Ukraine, but as can be seen from the statements made by Putin and his officials, that is precisely their goal."

Matveyev believes that, given the losses on the front lines, the strength of Russia's army will dwindle unless a fresh mobilization is launched. This decline, he believes, will continue slowly at first but then accelerate. "Losses are growing and will continue to rise given current trends."

This article was translated from German

World.title: WHO's Tedros vists DR Congo as Ebola outbreak accelerates
World.content:
The head of the World Health Organization warned that "we must urgently and massively scale up all our efforts" against the latest Ebola outbreak, with new cases doubling in some hotspots in the past week alone.

The head of the World Health Organization visited Kinshasa, capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), on Wednesday, warning that the Ebola outbreak in the east of the country was "spreading faster than our scale-up of the response."

The 17th Ebola outbreak in DRC's history is already the fastest-spreading and the second-most deadly outbreak on record.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus has now visited twice this summer since the public health emergency, centered in the eastern Ituri province, was first declared in mid-March,.

His visit coincided with a health scare in the Maluku municipality in northeastern Kinshasa. A passenger on a crowded ship died with Ebola-like symptoms and authorities were rushing to isolate it and conduct checks.

The presence of Ebola was not yet confirmed in the latest scare involving a timber-transporting boat Image: Wendy Bashi/DW

DW correspondent Wendy Bashi reported that the boat was mainly transporting timber, but that roughly 200 people were also on board. The barge had come from Kisangani originally, far to the east in DRC. Bashi reported that the isolation measures were a precaution and that the deceased had not yet been tested for or diagnosed with Ebola.

What did Tedros say in Kinshasa?

WHO's Tedros said that he was holding meetings with health and humanitarian partners supporting the Ebola response in the DRC to "discuss the challenges we face." He noted new cases were "doubling in some hotspots over the past week alone."

"We all agree that we must urgently and massively scale up all our efforts across all pillars of the response and by all partners," he wrote in an online post. "That means reaching every affected community despited insecurity and displacement, strengthening coordination under the Government's leadership, ensuring health workers ahve the protection, training and support they need, and accelerating access to care, surveillance, and safe, dignified burials."

He also said it was crucial that communities be "at the center" of the response, saying the outbreak could only be stopped with their "trust, leadership and partnership."

What are the latest figures on the DRC Ebola outbreak?

According to the most recent data from Congo's Ministry of Health, it had confirmed 3,874 cases, including 1,751 deaths, as of Monday. At least 717 patients were in isolation while 749 patients have recovered.

The vast majority of cases, somewhere in the region of 90%, have been recorded in the eastern province of Ituri bordering Uganda. Only a handful of cases are on record outside DRC's borders.

Authorities and aid groups are racing to construct health care and screening facilities in DRC's eastern regions, as here in North Kivu Province [FILE: July 22, 2026) Image: Xinhua/picture alliance

As Tedros visited on Wednesday, the US State Department pledged another $242 million (roughly €210 million) in funding for a combination of immediate response, preparedness efforts and humanitarian assistance related to the outbreak.

The State Department also said its Travel Advisory status for the DRC, Uganda and South Sudan "remains at Level 4 — Do Not Travel."

DR Congo launches Ebola trial for high-risk contacts To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What other problems are responders encountering?

Medical charity Doctors Without Borders warned on Wednesday that the rare strain was still "spreading at an alarming and unprecedented rate" in a remote area of DRC with poor infrastructure.

"The response is expanding but is still not reaching communities quickly enough to break transmission chains," the group said.

Reports of many front line health workers going on strike, either in disputes over pay levels or non-payment, or a mixture of the two, have only worsened already inadequate access to healthcare.

Health officials are trying to enforce epidemic prevention protocols in a country whose funeral customs lay great value on open coffins and laying hands on the dead Image: Xin Huashefa/Xinhua/picture alliance

Dr. Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa Centers for Disease and Control, warned that "contact tracing is not working" and more and more cases were detected late, reducing the chances of survival.

The rare Ebolavirus strain in this outbreak, known as Bundibugyo, has no approved treatment or vaccine. Hurried trials of candidate vaccines and treatments have since begun.

Researchers believe the outbreak started in remote areas several months before it was identified and officially declared, with early deaths being misdiagnosed as conditions like peritonitis.

Local funeral practices, often involving open coffins and laying hands on corpses, helped the virus to spread.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Germany: Court jails far-right youth terror cell members
World.content:
A Hamburg court has handed down stiff prison sentences to members of the far-right terrorist group "Last Wave of Defense." Politicians are warning that those drawn into extremist violence are getting younger.

The seven members and one supporter of the "Last Wave of Defense" (Letzte Verteidigungswelle) group were found guilty of crimes with the aim of bringing about the collapse of Germany's political system through attacks on migrants and "political opponents." The judge in the Hamburg Higher Regional Court said the group's name reflected their deeply racist and violent mindset. "We are the wave that washes the filth out of our country," the group had written in pamphlets.

The young men sentenced on Wednesday were aged between 14 and 21 when they committed the crimes.

They were sentenced under juvenile criminal law to youth prison terms ranging from one and a half to five years. The sentence for the youngest defendant — one and a half years in prison — was suspended. They had been charged with membership in, or support of, a terrorist organization. The convictions also covered offenses including attempted murder, arson, and dangerous bodily harm.

In May 2025, police raided properties in Altdöbern as part of an investigation into the far-right group Image: Frank Hammerschmidt/dpa/picture alliance

A cultural center was destroyed in an arson attack

According to the ruling, the youths carried out an arson attack on a community cultural center in Altdöbern, a town in the eastern state of Brandenburg, in October 2024. Investigators believe the far-right group mistakenly identified the building — located in a town of only 2,300 residents — as a meeting place for left-wing activists. The building burned to the ground, resulting in property damage amounting to several hundred thousand euros.

Altdöbern's Mayor, Peter Winzer of the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD), told public broadcaster Deutschlandfunk (DLF) that he is still shocked by the attack: "An absolute catastrophe. Because it was a community hub — a place for culture and gatherings. Every local event took place there."

Two of the accused were found to have unsuccessfully attempted to set fire to accommodation for refugees in Schmölln in the eastern state of Thuringia, in January 2025. They also scrawled swastikas and slogans such as "foreigners out" on the facade of the facility.

According to the indictment, three members of the group had also planned an arson attack on an asylum seeker shelter in Senftenberg in Brandenburg.

25 years after the right-wing riots: Rostock’s police chief Thomas Laum speaks to DW To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Parallels with post-reunification events

Brandenburg's Interior Minister Jan Redmann of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) told DLF that he finds it particularly alarming how quickly very young people are radicalizing and banding together online. "We are also observing some surprising continuities — specifically, that the young perpetrators have relatives who had already come to the authorities' attention as right-wing extremists back in the 1990s — the era of the so-called 'baseball bat years.'"

The term "baseball bat years" refers to the period of massive attacks — primarily targeting refugees — that occurred in the territory of the former East Germany in the years immediately following reunification.

A few days after the trial began in Hamburg, federal prosecutors ordered raids on premises in the eastern states of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, but also in the western states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Schleswig-Holstein as part of an operation targeting 10 additional suspects.

In late June, two more youths were arrested in the eastern state of Thuringia as suspected members of the "Last Wave of Defense." In total, authorities estimate that the group has a membership in the "mid-double-digit range" across Germany.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Germany: Leipzig explosive drone 'new level of danger' — Minister
World.content:
Skip next section Interior Minister says armed drone is 'new threat scenario'

08/05/2026 August 5, 2026 Interior Minister says armed drone is 'new threat scenario'

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told reporters that finding an armed drone at a German airport was a new threat situation.

"Drone sightings, drone threats including in a hybrid context, are something we know from the past," Dobrindt said. "That a drone armed with explosives is at an airport is a new threat scenario," he added.

"All the speculation that is currently going on about the explosives, the construction, the question of the drone, the origin and, of course, who is behind it, is now part of the investigation," Dobrindt said.

The interior minister said "it would be short-sighted to believe that this form of threat, which objectively exists, can be combated or countered with simple measures.

"We are dealing with a competition here which may also include foreign powers. This will be part of the investigations," he added.

In June, Dobrindt created a so-called Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats, as Germany has been on high alert for espionage, sabotage and disinformation, particularly from Russia.

"What is happening now also shows that the assessment made months ago — ​that we are dealing with a high level of danger — was justified," Dobrindt added.

On Wednesday, German authorities ‌opened a counterterrorism ⁠investigation into the incident.

World.title: Fears of renewed conflict in Ethiopia
World.content:
Military activity in and around the disputed city of Alamata has sparked concerns that the fragile peace that followed the 2020–2022 Tigray War could unravel.

Residents of Alamata, a city that straddles Ethiopia's Tigray and Amhara regions. say a growing military presence have them fearing renewed fighting.

The city is one of the most contested areas since the Tigray War. Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) forces took control of it at the start of this year, after Ethiopian federal troops withdrew.

One Alamata resident who requested anonymity for safety reasons said: "The TPLF forces have deployed many troops on the Raya front and have been instructed to be ready for war."

"In most areas of the city, you can only see soldiers," another Alamata resident, Ato Gebru TsefaEzigi, told DW. "It seems like a military city."

Alamata is the central hub of the Raya valley, which straddles the Tigray and Amhara regions and alongside. It includes the districts of Raya Azebo in the Tigray region and Raya Kobo in the Amhara region.

Explainer: How did Ethiopia's Tigray war start? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Did Ethiopia forces strike in Western Tigray?

In a statement on August 2, the regional government in Tigray said its forces had repelled an "open military offensive against the Tigray Security Forces in the vicinity of Shererina, Western Tigray" by Ethiopian federal forces.

It also stated that the federal forces were supported by forces belonging to Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). DW could not independently verify the claims.

The Ethiopian federal government has not responded to the Tigray government's statement. However, Ethiopian media reported that Abraham Belay, the federal Minister of Irrigation and Lowland Areas acknowledged that clashes had taken place in western Tigray and blamed the TPLF for intitiating them.

A highly contested area

Alamata lies about 15 kilometers (9 miles) north of Kobo in the Amhara region and sits along a strategic highway linking Tigray with central Ethiopia.

Ethiopian federal forces entered the city in November 2020, at the start of the Tigray War. Forces loyal to the TPLF and deployed TPLF army units have been in control since federal forces withdrew on January 15.

However, the area's status remains unresolved under the African Union-brokered Pretoria Peace Agreement signed in November 2022. Political divisions within the TPLF have also fueled concerns about the durability of the peace process.

An estimated 600,000 people died in the 2020-2022 war. Millions were displaced and essential services collapsed across Tigray and much of northern Ethiopia. The federal government and the TPLF accused each other of having initiated the conflict.

Calls for access and restraint

Although the Pretoria agreement largely ended large-scale fighting, several key provisions remain unimplemented, including the status of disputed areas and the restoration of civilian administration in some of them.

The African Union has repeatedly urged all parties to fully implement the Pretoria agreement and resolve disputes through dialogue. Human rights group Amnesty International has also called for restraint and renewed its calls for independent access to the conflict-affected areas.

"We are also calling for access for human rights observers, investigators, and journalists to Tigray and to all regions impacted by the conflict in Ethiopia," said Suad Nur, Amnesty's Horn of Africa campaigner. "Because we know what happens when perpetrators commit crimes or conduct hostilities where there is no scrutiny or oversight ... We know what happens when hostilities unfold without scrutiny or oversight."

The new crisis facing Tigray’s families To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Regional implications

Renewed instability in northern Ethiopia could have consequences beyond the country's borders. International humanitarian agencies are currently overstretched in countries like Sudan and Somalia.

Analysts warn that renewed fighting in and around Tigray could trigger the displacement of even more people, disrupt trade routes and complicate peace efforts in the region.

For Alamata residents and those in Ethiopian communities still recovering from one of Africa's deadliest conflicts, the latest military movements have revived painful memories of conflict.
