World.title: Government orders blocking of 7,393 links involved in film pirac
World.content:
This was disclosed in a written reply by minister of state for information and broadcasting, L Murugan, to a question on the circulation of pirated films (Representative image)

NEW DELHI: The government has directed online intermediaries to block 7,393 links involved in film piracy, including 4,996 Telegram channels and 1,263 websites, the information and broadcasting ministry told the Lok Sabha on Wednesday.This was disclosed in a written reply by minister of state for information and broadcasting, L Murugan, to a question on the circulation of pirated films, OTT shows and other audiovisual content through Telegram and similar platforms.The government said it had strengthened the legal framework against online film piracy through amendments to the Cinematograph Act in 2023.

World.title: How Chennai’s Zifo Open Quiz outlasted sponsors, a pandemic and changing times
World.content:
What is the fourth letter of the Greek alphabet?

Who was the last Tsar of Russia?

Which is the only sea without any coastlines?

If you go into this quiz expecting such questions, it might be time to read up a little further for Chennai’s iconic Landmark Quiz on Augusr 15.

Now in its 33rd year, the quiz has become as much an Independence Day tradition as the flag-hoisting ceremonies that unfold across the country. Every year, hundreds of teams, from seasoned quizzers to first-timers, school students to families, gather (this time at Sir Mutha Venkata Subba Rao Concert Hall), armed with little more than curiosity and a love for trivia.

What began as the Landmark Quiz in 1994 has grown into one of India’s largest open general knowledge quizzes, drawing participants from across the country and, occasionally, overseas. Today, under the banner of the Zifo Open Quiz, it continues to prove that in Chennai, curiosity is still a spectator sport.

“There is a culture of curiosity and knowledge-seeking in Chennai that isn’t found anywhere else. Maybe Kolkata comes close, but even there the numbers don’t compare,” says Dr Navin Jayakumar, quizmaster, Zifo Open Quiz, adding that a few years ago the quiz received registrations for over 1,000 teams and this year it has crossed 400 already.

The quiz’s longevity, however, has as much to do with the community that has rallied behind it as the questions themselves. For nearly 25 years, it was backed by Landmark and its founder Hemu Ramaiah, who, Dr Navin says, still turns up every year to help mark the answer sheets. When the bookstore chain shut down after the pandemic, he was determined to keep the tradition alive.

“I was not willing to let go of the date August 15. In 2021, even with all the lockdown restrictions, I conducted the quiz online because I wanted to commemorate it in some way. In 2022, I borrowed money from friends and organised the quiz myself. I didn’t want to let go of the tradition even without a sponsor,” he says adding that Raj Prakash G, founder of Zifo came into the picture in 2021. “He told me, ‘We used to come and enjoy the quiz. We don’t want this to die.’ The people who once took part in the quiz are now sponsoring it,” says Dr Navin.

This year’s edition promises a few new additions as well. While the questions will continue to span history, current affairs, science and popular culture, Dr Navin says the quiz has evolved with its audience. “I’m getting older. I started this when I was 30 and now I’m 64. There’s a lot of pop culture that younger people know and I don’t. That’s why, for the past three years, Siddhanth Rao has been the co-quizmaster. The quiz is now more youth-oriented because young people are the future of the quiz.”

He also hints at a surprise for this year’s audience. Unlike previous editions, spectators will not just be watching from the sidelines. “We’re going to allow people to pull out their phones, but only after the preliminary round is over. They will be able to actively take part in the quiz till the very end, and we’ll have prizes for them too,” he says with enthusiasm.

And for those planning to take part, Dr Navin has one piece of advice: don’t prepare for the quiz. “Just be curious. Read the newspaper every day, but don’t stop at the headlines. If you read about the Strait of Hormuz, go and find out where it is, its history and the countries around it. Read what interests you and stay curious,” he says.

The Zifo Open Quiz is not an exam. “The joy lies in discovering something new and saying, ‘I didn’t know that. That’s fascinating.’ Above all, come with your friends and family and have a good time. The community is what keeps this quiz alive.”

World.title: BJD opposes 'government move' to set up private nuclear power plant in Odisha
World.content:
The Opposition BJD has opposed an alleged move to establish a nuclear power plant in Odisha and accused the State’s BJP government of compromising with public safety for the sake of corporate interests.

The BJD’s Opposition came days after a representative of a private company met Odisha’s Deputy Chief Minister K.V. Singh Deo, who is also in charge of the energy department.

Addressing a press conference on Wednesday (August 5, 2026), BJD senior general secretary Lekhashree Samantsinghar claimed that the establishment of a nuclear power plant in Odisha would pose a serious threat to the health and safety of the people.

She alleged that the ‘double-engine government’, driven by its inclination towards private companies, has completely ignored the safety and security of the people of Odisha.

According to the BJD leader, a private company has proposed to establish a 3,000 MW nuclear power plant in Odisha.

“Whenever the subject of nuclear or atomic energy arises, it naturally creates fear in people's minds. In 1945, the nuclear bombings reduced the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki to ruins. In 1986, the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant (in Ukraine) suffered a catastrophic explosion, and in 2011, a similar disaster occurred at the Fukushima Nuclear Power Plant (in Japan),” she said.

The Opposition leader said that the losses and damage caused by these nuclear disasters have still not been fully compensated by the respective governments.

Ms. Samantsinghar added that nuclear energy is inherently hazardous and carries a significant risk to human life, and claimed that in most countries, nuclear energy remains under government ownership and control, and no private entity is entrusted with its ownership.

“However, under the BJP government, this long-standing principle is being altered by transferring nuclear energy into the hands of private companies. For its own interests, the BJP government is showing complete disregard for the lives and safety of the people of Odisha,” she alleged.

Raising questions on the intention of the administration, she said that the BJP government has amended the existing regulations governing nuclear power plants in order to facilitate private participation.

In December 2025, the Central Government passed a law in Parliament paving the way for handing over the nuclear energy sector to private companies, following which private companies have now turned their attention towards Odisha, she said.

Noting that India currently has 8.8 GW of nuclear power capacity under government ownership and that increasing it to 100 GW by transferring ownership to private entities would be extremely dangerous, Ms. Samantsinghar said that matters concerning national security are never entrusted to private organisations.

She alleged that the BJP government is conspiring to privatise a strategically important sector such as nuclear energy.

Despite strong Opposition in Parliament, the government allegedly hurriedly introduced the Nuclear Energy Bill with the intention of handing over ownership to private entities, the BJD leader added.

“Since the formation of the BJP government in Odisha, the state government has been functioning under the directions of the Centre and is unable to take any independent decisions without instructions from Delhi. Acting on the directions of the central government, the state is determined to establish a nuclear power plant in Odisha by compromising the interests of the people,” she alleged.

The BJD urged the BJP government to refrain from establishing a nuclear power plant that would put the lives of the people of Odisha at risk.

“Otherwise, the Biju Janata Dal would launch a mass agitation to safeguard the interests of the people of the State,” she told reporters.

The government did not respond to the BJD’s allegation till the filing of the report.

World.title: Home filmed without my consent: CJP spokesperson Saurav Das
World.content:
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) chief spokesperson Saurav Das on Wednesday (August 5, 2026) alleged that certain YouTubers and media persons had entered his residence and filmed inside without consent, calling it “a serious invasion of privacy” and a security threat to him and his family. He is in Maharashtra to attend a two-day meeting of Citizens for Justice and Peace.

In a post on X, Mr. Das claimed that around 15 to 20 people had gathered outside his residence on Wednesday (August 5) morning, with some camping there since the previous night.

“It’s not just an invasion of my privacy but also a grave security threat to me and my family,” Mr. Das wrote. He said that if “anti-social elements” attacked him at his residence because of the videos, the YouTubers and those allegedly coordinating them would be directly responsible.

‘Police deployed’

An officer from the South district police told The Hindu that security personnel had been deployed outside Mr. Das’s residence after he raised the issue on X.

The officer said that since Mr. Das was not in Delhi, he had authorised someone to submit a draft complaint at the Greater Kailash police station on his behalf. “The complaint would be formally lodged, following which an investigation would be carried out,” the officer added.

Mr. Das’s post drew political reactions, with Aam Aadmi Party national convener and former Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal saying that “this is the real face of Modi”.

Trinamool Congress MP Derek O’Brien said the matter had been raised by his party in the Rajya Sabha onWednesday (August 5) afternoon.

World.title: Tewolde Gebremariam is Air India’s new CEO
World.content:
Air India has appointed Tewolde Gebremariam as its new CEO. A former Ethiopian Airlines chief, he was most recently selected to lead Pakistan International Airlines.

He will succeed Campbell Wilson, the first chief executive appointed after Air India was privatised and handed over to the Tata Group in 2022. Mr Wilson stepped down from the role in April but continued to serve until his successor was appointed.

Also Read | What lies ahead for Air India’s next CEO after Campbell Wilson

“His unique strength lies in managing complex operational landscapes, driving cultural transformation, building competitive global hubs, and developing world-class MRO (Maintenance, Repair, and Overhaul) and aviation training infrastructure,” a press statement from Air India said about the new appointee.

N. Chandrasekaran, Chairman of Air India and Tata Sons said about the new CEO, “Having completed the initial phase of stabilisation, integration, and fleet commitments under Campbell’s guidance, Air India is now entering a critical execution and expansion era. Tewolde’s track record in building one of the world’s most efficient and profitable airline groups makes him uniquely suited to lead Air India. His operational expertise, commitment to safety, and vision for hub development will be instrumental as we establish Air India as a premier global carrier and a source of national pride.”

World.title: Bangladesh government ‘outraged’ over Sheikh Hasina’s press conference in India
World.content:
Bangladesh’s government and public reacted with anger on Wednesday (August 5, 2026) after ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina addressed a press conference in New Delhi, her first public appearance since being deposed, on the very day the country marked the second anniversary of the uprising that forced her from power.

Ms. Hasina, convicted and sentenced to death in absentia by Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal over the deadly crackdown on the 2024 protests, joined virtually from India to address an event organised by the Foreign Correspondents’ Club of South Asia in Delhi. Several of her associates, including her son Sazib Wazed Joy, former Minister Mohibul Hasan Chowdhury Nowfel and former national cricket captain Shakib Al Hasan, joined the event.

Bangladesh’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in a statement issued the same evening, said the country was “outraged” that Ms. Hasina, whom it repeatedly referred to as an absconding, convicted “genocider”, had been permitted to hold a live media interaction on Indian soil, despite New Delhi having been warned in advance of the likely fallout for bilateral ties.

The ministry said the timing made the episode especially painful, calling the address on the anniversary of the July Revolution “an affront to the sovereignty of Bangladesh and a grievous insult to the martyrs” of the movement.

Also Read | Sheikh Hasina’s media event can hurt ties with India: Bangladesh

The statement rejected what it called an attempt by Ms. Hasina and her “criminal cohort” to deny facts established by the United Nations regarding the killing of civilians, including minors, during the crackdown, describing it as a futile bid to “reverse the tide of history.”

It said Bangladeshis had already rejected such attempts and would continue to do so, asserting that the country would never return to what it called the “dark days of fascism” or become a “client state,” and that Ms. Hasina’s “mafia enterprise” would have no future place in Bangladeshi politics.

While affirming that Dhaka sought a “constructive, mutually beneficial and forward-looking” relationship with India based on sovereign equality and non-interference, the ministry said its repeated requests for Ms. Hasina’s extradition under the 2013 Bangladesh-India Extradition Treaty had gone unanswered, and that allowing her to address the media only deepened the hurt felt by the Bangladeshi public.

Shakib Al Hasan’s ancestral home attacked

Shakib Al Hasan, the former national cricket team captain and ex-Awami League lawmaker, had joined the Press Conference in Delhi virtually and shared it on his verified Facebook page. Hours later, his ancestral home in Bangladesh’s Magura district came under attack.

Police said a group of young men gathered outside the house in the town’s Keshabmore area around 9 p.m. on Wednesday and pelted it with stones, breaking window panes, before pouring petrol on the upper section of the iron gate and setting it alight.

Officer-in-charge of Magura Sadar police station Abdullah Al Mamun said residents extinguished the fire before it could spread, and that no member of Shakib’s family was present at the house at the time.

World.title: Mark Zuckerberg sends apologies for ‘errors in operating the platform’, government sources say
World.content:
Meta chief executive officer Mark Zuckerberg conveyed his “apologies” for child sex abuse material (CSAM), “deepfake content and errors in operating the platform,” government sources said, after Joel Kaplan, the technology giant’s global head of public policy, met with officials from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology on Wednesday (August 5, 2026).

“Meta will be called again,” the sources said, indicating that further meetings are on the slate. The delegation led by Mr. Kaplan also met Information Technology Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw.

Mr. Kaplan had been summoned, among other things, to explain why Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s first video message to the youth posted on July 23 was temporarily removed from Facebook. The company had attributed it to an error. The government had insisted on full accounting of the error and a personal apology from Mr. Zuckerberg. The informal readout of the meeting did not include a specific reference to that post’s takedown.

“I apologised to the Minister on behalf of Meta for the error restricting PM Modi’s post,” Mr. Kaplan said in a statement shared by a Meta spokesperson.

The meetings follow heightened concerns around Instagram’s role in amplifying the protests at Jantar Mantar last month, as well as the brief takedown of Mr. Modi’s post on Facebook. Government officials asserted that Meta was “not covered under the Intermediary definition” — a significant statement — since this would make the company liable in court for every single post by users. The government also dressed down the company in a BBC report on s appearing on Instagram promoting CSAM.

The official sources added, “They select who receives the content. Safe harbour under IT Act is not applicable. They admitted that a lot of money was paid for boosting a certain type of content. They apologised and regretted the mistake … Meta accepted the mistake that a lot of illegal content was promoted... Paid promotion carried out for specific audience.”

Standing committee

Earlier in the day, according to a letter from the Lok Sabha Secretariat, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology, headed by the Bharatiya Janata Party’s Nishikant Dubey, demanded that Google India’s safe harbour be lifted, thereby leaving the firm liable for individual users’ posts as a publisher. The letter, seen by The Hindu, cited cybercrime complaints in Hyderabad where complainants lost over ₹48 lakh to cyberfrauds from apps downloaded from Google Play, where Google’s India country manager was named as a co-accused.

This follows a similar demand for Meta, where the committee sought the withdrawal of Instagram’s safe harbour protection following the brief takedown of Mr. Modi’s video. The committee also cited the reporting on CSAM s on Instagram.

The letter was addressed to IT Secretary S. Krishnan and copied to Home Secretary Govind Mohan. The IT Ministry and Meta did not have an immediate response to a query on the letter when contacted by The Hindu. Google declined to comment.

“During the deliberations, the Committee demanded an apology from Mr. Mark Zukerberg, Meta Chief on this issue,” the committee wrote in the letter. “If he fails to tender an unqualified apology within 3 days of receipt of this letter, the protection/immunity given under Section 79(3) of IT Act may be withdrawn and action taken against him as a Publisher.”

Section 79 of the IT Act, 2000 says that “an intermediary shall not be liable for any third party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by” them, subject to certain conditions. The IT Rules, 2021 are the main way those conditions have been expanded by the government, including requirements of taking down content upon notice by law enforcement agencies or designated government officers.

It is unclear if safe harbour can be revoked by the government. “There is no express legal provision under the present legal framework through which the Government can directly remove or revoke the safe harbour protection provided to intermediaries under Section 79 of the IT Act,” Ravi Goyal, a partner at law firm Scriboard, told The Hindu.

“Moreover, the safe harbour protection provided under Section 79 is not a blanket or platform-wide immunity and instead applies in relation to specific content or instances. Therefore, even if an intermediary is found not to be entitled to such protection in respect of a particular piece of content or instance, it could still continue to avail itself of the protection under Section 79 for its services, subject to compliance with law. Thus, such actions are determined on a case-to-case basis by a court of law.”

At a hearing where Meta, Google and X (formerly Twitter) representatives were speaking before the committee on Monday, MPs from the Opposition pushed back against the ruling party’s line of questioning, saying content moderation on social media platforms should not be subject to political influence.

World.title: Collapse of rules-based order calls for total ban on nuclear weapons
World.content:
The world is in a deep crisis. The once sacred “rules based world order” is driven to collapse by those who formulated it, especially the most powerful, the U.S. Countries around the world appear powerless when faced with this onslaught created by men with dangerous ideologies. The self-proclaimed “gatekeepers” of the order have largely fallen silent.

The moral dimension of attacks on people of West Asia, Ukraine, and its impact on the poorest in the rest of the world are swept under the carpet in an atmosphere where military power overrides every other imperative.

In this atmosphere, the media narratives, irrespective of the ideological orientation, end with a common question. What if one of these drivers of the conflict uses the nuclear option? It has been 81 years to this day since the U.S. dropped an atom bomb on Hiroshima — the first time the weapon was used in war, and the first of only two times, and the world seems to be on the brink of a similar mistake today.

An ageing treaty

Russia and the U.S. are declared nuclear weapons powers, Israel is an undeclared one, with no independent oversight of any kind. And Iran may want to have one sooner rather than later under the prevailing circumstances. All these questions would have been hypothetical just a couple of years ago but are now in the realm of possibility.

The one instrument that was supposed to prevent the kind of catastrophe staring at us now is the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). The NPT will undergo a review in 2026, its 11th, as a formality. From its inception, the NPT has been problematic. It divided the world into nuclear haves — the nuclear-weapon states, a.k.a. the P5 group — and the have-nots. The essential pillars of NPT are non-proliferation, peaceful uses of nuclear energy, and, most importantly, disarmament commitments, moving towards the abolition of nuclear weapons.

A majority of nations have followed the first two commitments but the P5, after signing the NPT, moved in the opposite direction, before returning to reduce the size statistically while increasing the effectiveness of the weapons. However, the abolition commitment was never on their horizon. Apart from the P5, there are also outliers that never signed the NPT but possess nuclear weapons, like India, Pakistan, North Korea, and Israel. And of these, Israel maintains a strategic ambiguity and is not subject to any oversight by international agencies, including the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Russia and the U.S. each have more than 5,000 nuclear warheads. All the other P5 countries maintain an arsenal of a few tens to a few hundreds, with China leading with nearly 600 or more. The really dangerous part of these stockpiles is that nearly 4,000 of them are already deployed by various states and a little more than 2,000 are already in ‘high alert’ state of deployment. And only China and India have a ‘no first use’ policy in place; others have completely rejected such a doctrine.

Deterrence means little

Given the ground realities of the present conflicts, there are many signatories of the NPT who are not part of the P5 but close to becoming one within a very short span of time. Recall that North Korea was a signatory but withdrew from the NPT in 2003. The one country that is farthest from any international obligation is Israel. It is, by all accounts, certainly a nuclear weapons state but maintains strategic ambiguity by not declaring itself as such. This creates a deep sense of instability in a region where conflicts are a commonplace. A nuclear tipping point is no more beyond the realm of possibility.

Strategic experts often mention the theory of deterrence in preventing wars. However, there have been wars going on all the time and deterrence means little when the heads of state are despotic or bellicose. The world’s countries urgently need to move towards a treaty on the total abolition of nuclear weapons. Meaningless reviews of the NPT, whose aims are violated with impunity, are not going to help.

Of the nearly 200 countries in the world, only nine have nuclear weapons. The power of the have-nots has to be compelling enough to allow the haves to renounce their nuclear-weapon stockpiles and use nuclear power for the benefit of all, rather than for the destruction of all.

Mundur V.N. Murthy is professor (retired), The Institute of Mathematical Sciences, Chennai. murthymundur@gmail.com

World.title: How excessive police force turns peaceful marches into medical crises
World.content:
When 23-year-old Arhaan (name changed to protect identity) reached his accommodation after attending the Cockroach Janta Party protest march in New Delhi on July 20, his ears kept ringing with pain when he closed his eyes.

He remembers it started when a canister had burst with a loud sound near his head when he was trapped between the barricades and the police. He said he blacked out for a minute when it happened, before running away when the police started lathi-charging.

In the series of protests in Jantar Mantar called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the Delhi police and security personnel have been accused of using lathis, tear gas, pellet guns, and shock batons against peaceful protestors. Several protestors had to be treated for injuries, with one 20-year-old woman requiring ventilator support.

But while security forces have denied the use of many of these devices against protestors, transparency on the crowd control measures has been lacking.

‘Less lethal’

These devices are part of less-lethal crowd control measures. Forces deployed similar devices during the farmers’ protests in 2020-2021, protests against the Citizenship Amendment Bill 2019, and during crackdowns in Manipur and Jammu & Kashmir.

However, their use in excess and misuse is known to have severe long-term consequences for a person’s health, according to the U.S.-based nonprofit Physicians for Human Rights (PHR).

“We completed two systematic reviews looking at the health impacts of so-called ‘less lethal’ crowd control measures,” Madhavi Dandu, director of the University of California Global Health Institute and a member of PHR, said. “Across both reviews, injuries affected nearly every organ system and ranged from transient symptoms to lifelong disability and even death.”

The reviews were published in 2017 in BMJ Open and BMC Public Health.

Deadly gaps

In India, the law requires the intensity and type of less-lethal crowd control measures to escalate only if the crowd does not disperse or becomes violent. However, regulations fall short on what these devices must be made of and on when and who can deploy these measures.

This lacuna can in turn be deadly. For example, tear gas is a lachrymatory — or tear-inducing — agent that the Chemical Weapons Convention classifies as a chemical weapon and has been banned in war. However, the Indian state can use it to control riots in exceptional circumstances.

In India, the most common chemical compound in tear gas is CS gas or o-chlorobenzylidene malononitrile. When in contact, it causes intense coughing, nausea, tightness in the chest, and even physical weakness for a short period of time.

Another compound the Tear Smoke Unit of the Border Security Force produces is pelargonic acid vanillylamide (or PAVA), a synthetic pepper spray. Oleoresin capsicum, a.k.a. pepper spray, is also used.

“Chemical irritants can lead to chronic respiratory disease, persistent eye injuries, skin conditions, and psychological effects such as PTSD,” Dr. Dandu said. Tear gas should never be used in places with poor ventilation or where protesters cannot safely escape from it, she added.

The risk is higher for people with pre-existing respiratory or skin conditions and allergies to these compounds. A 2025 study in Toxicology Reports reported that people exposed to CS spray during a protest in Georgia had significantly higher ECG abnormalities, indicating potential cardiopulmonary effects.

Tear gas canisters, when thrown into a crowd with force, can also cause head injuries and direct contact with the skin can cause burns.

Excessive force

In India, forces have been known to use grenade launchers to deploy tear gas canisters. These launchers can fire around 20 canisters in less than a minute and to up to 400 m. One 21-year-old protestor named Subhkaran Singh died during the farmers’ protests after sustaining a head injury from such a tear gas shell in 2024.

Handheld kinetic weapons, which include lathis or batons, are common less-lethal weapons used to control crowds. They are only to be used on violent protestors after adequate warning from an executive magistrate.

According to the Kerala Police Manual of 1970, personnel must use the lathi only against soft parts of the body — from the shoulder to the thighs — and avoid the neck and the head. The United Nations Guidance on Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement has also said that thorax, spine, throat, kidneys and abdomen should not be struck as they can suffer damage or be ruptured.

“Often we have seen security personnel hit whoever is in front of them,” Harjit Singh Bhatti, a member of Progressive Medicos and Scientists Forum, said. “This is a sign of poor training. Women, children, and the elderly are getting injured because of lathis.”

He added that when excessive force is used, the strikes may also lead to disability or nerve damage that can cause lifelong pain.

Protesters from the CJP march on July 20 alleged that some of the lathis were studded with nails, severely wounding protesters. Many also suffered fractures and head injuries. The incident was also the first known case of shock-batons being used for crowd control in the national capital. These batons release a mild electric shock at the moment of the strike.

Human rights groups have called for such batons to be banned as they can cause permanent disability and even death.

Caught off guard

Kinetic impact projectiles are plastic or rubber bullets with metal fragments, and include those fired by pellet guns. Around five protesters at the CJP march suffered pellet gun injuries, with one protester risking loss of vision. However, these projectiles are inaccurate, particularly at long distances, and can cause indiscriminate harm.

In 2016, more than 6,000 people in Jammu & Kashmir suffered severe pellet-gun injuries. In a study published in the Indian Journal of Ophthalmology, of 777 victims examined, 82% had lost vision to some degree.

“Kinetic projectiles should never target the head, neck or torso and should be fired from recommended distances at the lower extremities only when necessary for safety,” Dr. Dandu said.

Protesters are often caught off guard when confronted with such force and weapons. That can cause fear and panic, heightening the risk of a crowd collapse.

“Ideally, these weapons should only be considered when absolutely necessary and proportionate, after all other de-escalation efforts have failed,” according to Dr. Dandu. “Prioritise communication and avoid indiscriminate deployment.”

She added that rapid access to medical care, officer training, transparency, and accountability are also essential to minimising harm.

In India, information on the crowd control devices that security personnel possess and use is not easily available. Regular audits are necessary to ensure these devices meet quality standards and tests should be conducted in a manner that reveals the weapons’ full impact before they are deployed, per the UN guidance.

Also according to the guidance, the state must monitor the use of force and information about the crowd must be disaggregated to the extent possible on the basis of age, gender, and disabilities before deciding which devices to use. It also requires any serious injuries or deaths caused by such devices to be duly investigated by the competent authority.
