World.title: From “rapid response” to possible law: who are Georgia’s national values being protected from?
World.content:
The Georgian government has not ruled out introducing legislation against what it describes as the erosion of national identity. Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze says the proposed rules could cover insults directed at saints, monarchs and prominent public figures. No draft law has been introduced yet. However, experts argue that the groundwork is already being laid. Members of the ruling team have already begun discussing penalties and possible regulation of the media.

As the ruling Georgian Dream party debates possible punishment for insulting national values, it is worth examining what such measures could cover and what Russia’s experience suggests.

From assaults to a campaign to “protect national values”

The debate over possible legislation followed an attack on comedian Onise Okriashvili over a joke he made on YouTube. Late on 22 July, a man assaulted him near his home in Tbilisi. The attacker, Niko Khurtsilava, said he acted because Okriashvili had insulted Georgian national culture.

Even before the assault, pro-government television channels had launched a media campaign against Okriashvili. They broadcast a clipped excerpt from his YouTube show in which he referred to renowned Georgian writer Nodar Dumbadze using obscene language.

The writer’s grandson, Nodar Macharashvili, publicly backed the attacker. A few days after the incident, MMA fighter Giorgi Kartvelishvili, who also described himself as Khurtsilava’s friend, announced the creation of a new movement that would provide “rapid response” to insults directed at sacred values, ancestors, religion and history.

“If protecting our culture and national identity requires it, we will not shy away from any threat. We are ready to take responsibility for every action we take and, if necessary, even go to prison,” Kartvelishvili said.

He did not specify what he meant by “rapid response”. He also declined to answer journalists’ questions about the use of physical violence and vigilantism.

On 28 July, the group applied to the Public Registry to register its newly established organisation under the name National Generation.

A week after the attack on Okriashvili, on 30 July, another initiative group emerged to “protect national values”. It brought together actor Giorgi Shanidze, director Giorgi Sikharulidze and Kote Mzhavia, director of the Batumi Theatre.

Unlike the first movement, this group called for legal mechanisms rather than “rapid response”. Its members said the law should protect the church, sacred sites, historical heroes and national values.

“Freedom of expression is a fundamental value. However, that right cannot become a tool for insulting the sacred symbols and core values that form the country’s historical, cultural and spiritual foundation,” Giorgi Shanidze said.

The statement refers to “externally funded destructive groups” whose activities, it says, are creating confrontation between the Georgian nation and small minority groups.

“To prevent the situation from escalating further and reaching the point where even the wise Georgian people could lose patience, responsible steps must be taken and the existing problems must be resolved through legal and peaceful means,” the statement says.

The group plans to hold consultations with lawyers, historians, artists and athletes before drafting a legislative proposal.

However, neither the bill nor its concept has been published, so it remains unclear which actions could become punishable. The proposed form of liability and possible penalties also remain unknown.

What could a law on national values include?

On 3 August, Irakli Kobakhidze told journalists that he did not rule out adopting such legislation. However, he said the authorities had not yet discussed any specific proposals.

“There is indeed a need to respond to the coordinated attack against our identity,” Kobakhidze said.

He also identified possible subjects of future regulation, including saints, kings and prominent public figures.

According to Kobakhidze, insults directed at Georgian saints and kings are part of “a chain of coordinated, commissioned actions.”

“These are not simply untalented people. These are people carrying out a specific assignment. The purpose of that assignment is simple: they are trying to weaken our national identity. That is why they are doing all this,” he said.

Kobakhidze did not specify who had allegedly commissioned the campaign. He also provided no evidence to support the claim.

“We must take every possible measure to counter such processes. If that requires adopting a law, we can discuss that as well.”

Kobakhidze’s remarks do not necessarily mean such a law will be adopted. However, they indicate that the initiative has already received political backing from the prime minister.

Meanwhile, MPs aligned with the ruling party have outlined possible restrictions in greater detail.

Georgian Dream MP Irakli Kadagishvili linked the issue to public swearing, abusive language and hooliganism.

“When people use obscene language against a specific individual or institution at a rally, is that freedom of expression or simply abusive language and hooliganism? We cannot just leave it like this.”

Kadagishvili said he did not know what the legislation might ultimately contain. At the same time, he suggested that the media could also fall within its scope.

The MP claimed that certain television channels — referring to opposition broadcasters — had aired 3,500 “anti-church” reports over the past year and a half. He did not explain how he arrived at that figure or what criteria he used to classify the reports as “anti-church”.

Kadagishvili also suggested that “offensive” media content could become subject to legal regulation.

Guram Macharashvili, a member of the People’s Power party, openly called for penalties for public insults. He said the law should protect faith, the church, the patriarch and national traditions.

“When you publicly insult values such as faith, the church, the patriarch or our traditions, that should, of course, be punishable.”

Macharashvili argued that Georgia had offered excessive protection to dissenting views.

“Dissent has always enjoyed a certain degree of protection in Georgia. But recently, I would say it has been protected in an ultra-liberal, excessive way, and that needs to change.”

What counts as an “insult” — and who decides?

Article 17 of Georgia’s Constitution guarantees freedom of thought and expression. It also prohibits persecution for expressing an opinion.

The constitution also guarantees media freedom and prohibits censorship.

The state may restrict freedom of expression only by law and only when necessary in a democratic society. Such restrictions may serve aims including public safety and the protection of other people’s rights. The constitution does not list “insulting national values” as a separate ground for limiting freedom of expression.

At the same time, freedom of expression is not absolute. The law may restrict incitement to violence, threats, harassment or defamation. However, such restrictions must be clearly defined and predictable.

By contrast, “insulting national values” is a far more ambiguous concept. It remains unclear whether the proposed law would protect the reputation of specific individuals or instead safeguard abstract values or historical figures.

It is also unclear who would decide which saints, kings and public figures deserve legal protection. Would the law apply only to historical figures? Where would the line be drawn between legitimate historical criticism and an “insult”?

For example, pro-government television channels also launched a campaign against literary scholar Levan Berdzenishvili after he criticised the policies of Georgian King Erekle II. Berdzenishvili neither joked about the king nor used obscene language. Nevertheless, Georgian Dream MPs and pro-government media sharply attacked him.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed restrictions would apply to satire, works of art or academic research. Another unanswered question is whether critical media coverage of members of the clergy could be treated as an “insult to sacred values”.

Protecting patriotism or deepening political divisions?

Opposition politicians see the initiative as an attempt to mobilise political support.

Giorgi Sharashidze of the For Georgia party argues that the government is trying to claim a monopoly on patriotism.

“They have a very calculated strategy — to gain exclusive ownership of patriotic issues. Everything serves that goal. They want everyone else to appear as opponents of Georgia’s identity, traditions and church, while presenting themselves as the sole defenders of those values.”

Giorgi Shalamberidze of the First Georgia party believes the proposed law could serve another political purpose.

“It could be a political manoeuvre. It may help mobilise a particular segment of voters, or it could mark the beginning of a much broader tightening of legislation in the long term.”

Shalamberidze acknowledged that freedom of expression can be restricted in certain circumstances. However, he pointed to Georgia’s current political environment.

“If this becomes law and is used as a tool, the question is how it will affect political actors, political parties and their freedom of expression, and to what extent it will become a mechanism for restricting their rights.”

Historians’ concerns

It remains unclear where the proposed law would draw the line between insulting a historical figure and offering a critical assessment. That uncertainty raises concerns for historians, researchers and authors.

Assessing historical figures often requires revisiting disputed facts, competing interpretations and long-established narratives.

If the state decides which interpretations are acceptable, the law could become a tool for restricting academic research and scholarly debate.

It also remains unclear whether the proposed rules would apply to academic publications, public lectures, textbooks or documentary films.

Another unanswered question is who would decide where legitimate historical criticism ends and an “insult” begins.

Historian Irakli Khvadagiani argues that placing faith and artistic expression into legal categories contradicts their very nature.

“Faith and creativity do not recognise prohibitions, nor do they accept categories imposed unilaterally. The idea of banning them through legislation is absurd. Humanity went through this centuries ago. It is simply the obsession of a dictator trying to bend society to his will.”

Risk of creating artificial divisions?

Conflict analyst Paata Zakareishvili believes the proposed legislation could fuel ethnic and religious tensions. In his view, the vague concept of “protecting national identity” risks creating new fault lines within society.

“There are not enough supporters of this ideology in Georgia for Georgian Dream to sustain permanent tensions between Christians and Muslims, between Georgians and non-Georgians, or between Georgian speakers and those who do not speak the language.”

Zakareishvili sees elements of far-right ideology in the government’s approach. He argues that it runs counter to the principles of equality and justice.

“This is a classic example of pure far-right ideology. Humanity has gone through this countless times, and it has repeatedly led to catastrophe and world wars, bringing nothing but destruction.”

The conflict analyst also links the initiative to the electoral cycle. Georgia’s next parliamentary elections are not due until October 2028. However, Zakareishvili believes the ruling party has already begun preparing its campaign.

“Georgian Dream is getting ready for the elections. Before the vote, it needs to create exactly these kinds of flashpoints.”

Cases of violence carried out in the name of “protecting traditions” Invoking the need to protect national and religious values is not a new phenomenon in Georgian politics. In 2023, a man attacked Zurab Japaridze, leader of the Girchi – More Freedom party, in the city of Gori. The attacker said he acted because Japaridze had insulted the church and was “corrupting children”.

Later that year, protesters disrupted a lecture by Levan Berdzenishvili in Kvareli. They accused him of insulting King Erekle II and Christian values. In Tbilisi, demonstrators also threw eggs at Berdzenishvili.

On 5 July 2021, opponents of Tbilisi Pride attacked journalists and activists. They justified the violence by saying they were defending the family, the church and traditional values. More than 50 journalists were injured.

In November 2019, far-right and anti-LGBT groups tried to disrupt the premiere of the film And Then We Danced. The Georgian Orthodox Church described the film as “an insult to Georgia’s traditional values”. Protesters attempted to storm cinemas. One of them threw a stone at civil activist Anna Subeliani, causing a serious head injury. Police arrested 12 people that evening.

In January 2024, activist Nata Peradze splashed paint on an icon in Tbilisi’s Holy Trinity Cathedral depicting Saint Matrona of Moscow alongside Joseph Stalin. Far-right groups later gathered outside Peradze’s home, demanding that she be punished.

On 17 May 2013, thousands of people, including members of the clergy, attacked participants in an anti-homophobia rally. At least 17 people were injured. In 2021, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that the violence had taken place in circumstances of the state’s effective acquiescence.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is particularly relevant in this context because the substance and rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia years earlier.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially justified their version as a tool to ensure transparency over foreign funding. They later expanded it into a mechanism used against independent media outlets and civil society organisations.

Lessons from Russia: when the state decides what people can joke about

Russia’s experience is relevant here because both the substance and the rationale behind many legislative initiatives promoted by Georgian Dream resemble measures introduced in Russia in recent years.

The clearest example is the Law on Transparency of Foreign Influence. Russian authorities initially presented their version as a transparency measure for foreign funding. They later expanded it into a tool used against independent media and civil society organisations.

It is therefore worth looking at how Russia gradually developed legislation under the banner of protecting “traditional values”, religious feelings and historical memory.

Russia did not build its legal framework for protecting religion, historical memory and “traditional values” overnight. The system evolved step by step.

Offending religious feelings

In 2012, members of the punk group Pussy Riot staged an anti-Vladimir Putin performance inside Moscow’s Cathedral of Christ the Saviour. A court convicted them of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred.

A year later, Russia toughened Article 148 of its Criminal Code by criminalising public acts that show clear disrespect for society and are committed with the intention of offending the religious feelings of believers.

One of the best-known cases under the law involved blogger Ruslan Sokolovsky, who filmed himself playing Pokémon Go inside a church and posted the video online. In other videos, he also criticised religion and the Russian Orthodox Church.

In 2017, a court gave Sokolovsky a three-and-a-half-year suspended prison sentence. The case involved several criminal charges, including offending believers’ religious feelings and inciting hatred.

In 2024, the European Court of Human Rights ruled that Sokolovsky’s conviction had violated his right to freedom of expression. The court found that offensive or vulgar speech does not automatically amount to hate speech.

“Traditional values” as state policy

In November 2022, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on protecting “traditional Russian spiritual and moral values”.

The document lists patriotism, dignity, life and the traditional family among those values. It also includes service to the fatherland, historical memory and continuity between generations.

According to the decree, external forces threaten these values by acting inside Russia through extremist and terrorist organisations.

The decree also identifies the United States and other “unfriendly states” as sources of those threats.

Russian authorities have explicitly linked cultural and values policy to national security.

A similar narrative has emerged in Georgian Dream’s campaign. Both initiative groups have spoken of a coordinated attack on Georgia’s “national identity”. Prime Minister Kobakhidze has used the same wording.

Legal protection of history

Article 354.1 of Russia’s Criminal Code is titled “Rehabilitation of Nazism”. Lawmakers originally introduced it to prohibit the denial of crimes established by the Nuremberg Tribunal.

However, the law goes much further. It also bans the dissemination of what authorities consider to be “knowingly false information” about the Soviet Union’s actions during the Second World War. The article also protects the honour and dignity of war veterans.

In 2021, lawmakers added a new offence covering the “insulting of the memory of the defenders of the Fatherland”. The law also criminalises offensive use of military glory symbols.

As a result, the legislation does more than prohibit denial of historical facts. It also protects the state’s official interpretation of the Soviet Union’s role in history.

According to a 2025 study by the human rights project OVD-Info, Russian courts handed down 25 convictions under Article 354.1 between 2015 and 2019. Many of the cases concerned interpretations of the Soviet Union’s actions and historical comparisons.

Between 2022 and May 2025, OVD-Info recorded 212 prosecutions under the same article.

A court gave Kazan resident Zulfiya Sitdikova a two-year suspended sentence over posters reading “No to war” and “9 Way”. She replaced the “M” in “May” with a “W”, and investigators interpreted this as desecration of Victory Day symbols.

Authorities also opened a criminal case against historian Mikhail Belousov. Investigators accused him of denying facts established by the Nuremberg Tribunal and spreading false information about the Soviet Union.

Prosecutors also opened two cases against historian Tamara Eidelman. They argued that her video lectures showed disrespect for Russia’s military remembrance days.

Russia has therefore created a system in which historians and society no longer have the final say in historical debates. Instead, investigators, expert witnesses and the courts have become the ultimate arbiters.

Where will Georgia draw the line?

Georgia has not yet introduced such a bill, so it is impossible to say whether it will follow the Russian path.

However, statements by members of the ruling party already suggest a broad range of protected subjects, including the church, the patriarch, saints, kings, public figures, traditions and even media content.

Russia’s experience also suggests that broadly defined protected values can gradually expand over time.

Protecting national values in Georgia

World.title: Georgian scam call centres: old fraudsters, new address? An investigation
World.content:
Georgian scam call centres that came under the spotlight during an international investigative project in 2025 have reportedly resumed operations from a new location. According to the investigative outlet Monitor, people linked to AK Group have relocated to an office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street in Tbilisi.

The outlet says its journalists conducted covert surveillance at the address for six months. They say they identified several of the same individuals who had been seen near AK Group’s previous office last year. According to Monitor, the footage also shows some of the same vehicles that regularly appeared at the company’s former location.

Journalists say they repeatedly spotted vehicles used by Akaki Kevkhishvili, who is widely believed to be the real operator of AK Group. The cars carried the registration numbers AK100KK and AK200KK. Investigators seized one of them in 2025 as part of the ongoing criminal investigation.

According to Monitor, AK Group’s registered owner and director, Meri Shotadze, also regularly visited the same address. She used two different vehicles, one of which investigators have also seized, while the other is registered to another person.

The investigation also claims that several agents who previously worked at AK Group’s former office have reappeared at the new location. They include Anzhelika Chkhapelia, who allegedly used the alias Marina Novikova; Misha Bayramov; Valerian Gigauri; Giorgi Gotman; and Ketevan Malashkhia, who allegedly used the alias Ashley Moriarty. According to Monitor, Malashkhia is a cousin of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife. The outlet also identified a Belarusian citizen, Lita, who had previously denied working at the call centre.

The journalists also say they identified security staff at the new office who had previously been seen outside AK Group’s former premises. They named former law enforcement officer Manuchar Gegia and former Zugdidi traffic police chief Levan Gogia.

According to the outlet, the office on Mirian Mepe Street closed after it announced the publication of its latest investigation. Both floors of the building are now being offered for rent.

Monitor says the premises had been leased since 2022 by RTM Imports, a company owned by Irakli Kvlividze, the brother of Akaki Kevkhishvili’s wife.

The journalists say they informed the Prosecutor’s Office on 1 July 2026 that AK Group’s managers and employees had been regularly operating from the office at 68 Mirian Mepe Street. According to Monitor, prosecutors have not clarified whether they investigated the information or whether the inquiry into the alleged fraud is still ongoing.

Background

In 2025, Monitor and more than 32 international media organisations published an investigation into AK Group’s activities. According to the report, the group employed 85 people and defrauded more than 6,100 people across Europe and Canada between 2022 and 2025. The journalists estimated that the operation generated more than $35 million in revenue over that period.

After the investigation was published, law enforcement authorities opened a criminal inquiry into organised fraud and the laundering of proceeds from crime on an especially large scale. Prosecutors have charged 11 people in the case.

In a separate bribery case, authorities also arrested former Georgian State Security Service chief Grigol Liluashvili. Prosecutors accuse him, in one of the counts, of providing protection to the call centres. A court has also frozen the assets and company shares of the alleged organisers and employees of the call centre network.

Investigation continues

According to Monitor, the Prosecutor’s Office told the outlet that it had requested legal assistance from Germany to help identify potential victims. Prosecutors also said they had sought additional information from journalists involved in the investigation, but claimed they had declined to cooperate.

In a written response, the Prosecutor’s Office said that “the final decision in the case largely depends on information and materials to be obtained from abroad through legal assistance.”

A separate Monitor investigation found that Akaki Kevkhishvili and Meri Shotadze had previously worked at another call centre, 100 Marketing Solutions. Authorities began investigating the company in 2023 and froze its shares as part of the inquiry. However, a court lifted the freeze in 2026.

Are Georgian scam call centres still operating?

World.title: Armenia approves new government as Pashinyan promises appointments based on merit
World.content:
Armenia approves new government

Alongside the opening of Armenia‘s 9th parliamentary term, the country formed a new government. In line with the constitution, Nikol Pashinyan took office as prime minister. He headed the electoral list of the Civil Contract party, which won a parliamentary majority.

The party submitted the required nomination documents for its leader to President Vahagn Khachaturyan, who then signed a decree appointing Pashinyan as prime minister.

On the previous day, at the proposal of Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan and by decree of President Vahagn Khachaturyan, Deputy Prime Ministers Mher Grigoryan and Tigran Khachatryan were reappointed to their posts.

Most cabinet ministers were also reappointed.

Changes were made in the prime minister’s office. Former chief adviser to the prime minister and former Armenian ambassador to the United States, Lilit Makunts, has been appointed chief of staff. Her predecessor, Araik Harutyunyan, became an MP with the ruling Civil Contract faction on August 2.

At the same time, Pashinyan announced that he plans to appoint graduates of leading universities from around the world, selected through the government’s talent pool, to senior positions in the government.

“You will soon see these decisions implemented in practice,” the prime minister said.

Almost all ministers kept their portfolios

At Prime Minister Pashinyan’s recommendation, the following ministers retained their posts:

Defence – Suren Papikyan,

Internal Affairs – Arpine Sargsyan,

Foreign Affairs – Ararat Mirzoyan,

Territorial Administration and Infrastructure – David Khudatyan,

Environment – Hambardzum Matevosyan,

Health – Anahit Avanesyan,

Education, Science, Culture and Sport – Zhanna Andreasyan,

Justice – Srbuhi Galyan,

Labour and Social Affairs – Arsen Torosyan,

Economy – Gevorg Papoyan,

Finance – Vahe Hovhannisyan.

Only High-Tech Industry Minister Mkhitar Hayrapetyan did not keep his post. Pashinyan had previously said that Hayrapetyan himself had decided to step down.

David Tadevosyan replaced him. The prime minister introduced the new minister to ministry staff today. Mkhitar Hayrapetyan also attended the meeting. He said he would remain available around the clock if the new minister or his team needed advice.

“I am ready to contribute my modest knowledge and experience whenever you feel the need,” the former minister said.

David Tadevosyan graduated from the National Polytechnic University of Armenia. Between 2012 and 2014, he studied at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where he earned a Master of Science in Engineering and Management.

Before taking up the ministerial post, Tadevosyan served as acting director of International Radio Network CJSC. Between 2024 and 2025, he headed Afeyan Initiatives for Armenia, an organisation founded by Armenian-American businessman, scientist and philanthropist Noubar Afeyan. Earlier in his career, Tadevosyan worked for the mining company Vallex Group, the Institute of Mining, Metallurgy and Chemical Technologies, and SberSpinoff.

More than 1,000 applications for the government’s talent pool

On 15 June, shortly after his Civil Contract party won the 2026 parliamentary elections, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan invited graduates of the world’s leading universities to join the government. He encouraged them to put their knowledge and professional experience to work in public administration.

Today, the prime minister said the initiative had attracted strong interest, with the government receiving 1,141 applications.

“Following the initial screening, 459 candidates – around 40% of all applicants – advanced to the second stage. The average age of the candidates is 34,” Pashinyan said.

The prime minister announced that the government would create a talent pool based on interview results and professional assessments. Officials will match the selected candidates’ education, work experience and professional skills with the specific needs of the public administration system.

He added that candidates included in the talent pool could receive offers for positions in the public sector or other forms of cooperation during the course of this year.

Armenia approves new government

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘It’s important to understand what kind of hell government is leading us into’
World.content:
Lasha Tugushi, head of the Liberal Academy, has commented on Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s claim that Georgian politicians have never used harsher rhetoric towards Russia than they do today, either before or after the 2008 war. Tugushi argues that the prime minister is repeating a familiar narrative promoted by the ruling Georgian Dream party.

According to Tugushi, the government is trying to present itself as the only force capable of “saving” the country, while linking the events of 2008 and 2022 forms part of that political strategy.

According to Tugushi, the suggestion that Georgia was ever pro-Russian is “nonsense”, as portraying Russia in a positive light has always been regarded as shameful in Georgian society.

Earlier, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy social media statement linking the war in Ukraine to Georgia’s domestic politics and the country’s opposition. According to Kobakhidze, the “Global War Party” needed the war in Ukraine in order to “fuel Russophobia among its agents around the world, including in Georgia, at the highest level.”

Lasha Tugushi said: “Anti-Russian sentiment existed in Georgia long before this. I remember the 1990s, when hostility towards Russia was very strong. The same was true after the war in Abkhazia. I cannot agree with the prime minister’s view that the key turning points were 2008 and 2022.

“I do not remember Georgia ever being pro-Russian. That is nonsense. What’s more, in respectable society it has always been considered shameful to say that Russia is a good country or to speak positively about Russian symbols.

“As for the focus on 2008 and 2022, that is part of a political game in which the leaders of Georgian Dream repeat a familiar narrative: that there is only one benevolent political force capable of saving Georgia – Georgian Dream. Everyone else, they claim, is either an enemy or a traitor seeking to drag the country into a devastating war.”

“But let’s remember who suspended Georgia’s EU integration, who is pursuing an anti-European policy today, who is confronting the ambassadors of Western countries, the European Parliament and the OSCE, who is picking fights with Sweden and France. Who came up with the scare story about the ‘deep state’? Georgian Dream did all of that.

“That does not mean the previous government made no mistakes or that everything was perfect. We need to understand that politics cannot be viewed in black-and-white terms. Things should be called by their proper names. The previous government has plenty of its own sins, and it paid the price for them. But today we see countries that were once on a par with Georgia moving closer to EU membership, while we, instead of advancing towards integration, are drifting further away from the West.”

“There are two main pillars on which the current government relies.

The first is fear – the claim that enemies want to open a second front in Georgia.

The second is the argument that our Georgian identity is under threat.

These are the two narratives they use to frighten people and rely on a fearful public in order to remain in power indefinitely.

But the fact is that they are not succeeding in their campaign against democracy to the extent they would like. It is crucial to see clearly what kind of hell this government is leading us into and what it actually looks like.

Over the past few years, Georgian Dream has taken many steps backwards and not a single step forward. This is an anti-national path. It is building authoritarianism and working against the Georgian people. I have many questions. For example, can Georgian Dream correct the grave mistakes it has made? I would like to believe it can find that path and that at least something will change.”

On Georgian Dream’s policies

World.title: Woman who saved teen from bow and arrow attack given royal bravery award
World.content:
An Ipswich woman has received Queensland's highest civilian bravery award for shielding a teenage girl from a man who was trying to kill her with a bow and arrow.

Nicole Law was doing her fortnightly grocery shop in the Ipswich suburb of Booval in September 2020 when she heard the screams of a 15-year-old girl being chased by a man with a bow and arrow.

While most shoppers ran to safety, the 42-year-old mother walked towards the danger.

"I didn't feel any fear at the time ... all I knew [was] that this young girl was crying for help."

Starting a conversation

Ms Law said she asked the girl, who had an arrow lodged in her hand, to get behind her.

When the man appeared from around the corner, she held her ground and started a conversation.

A man with a bow and arrow attacked a teenage girl at a supermarket in Booval, Ipswich. (ABC News: Anna Hartley)

"I don't know my exact words, but it was just like 'what's happening for you? Why are you doing this?''" Ms Law said.

She said the man, a then 28-year-old named Benjamin Bourke, told her he had been recently hit by a car and was going through a "rough time".

"I just basically said to him 'well that's a really s*** time for you.'"

"He ended up getting down and dropping all his stuff and looking at me and basically telling me that we're ok. It was really weird."

Bourke was then tackled to the ground by two men, before being arrested by police.

Ben Bourke was jailed for 10 and a half years. (Facebook)

What Ms Law did not know at the time was Bourke's intent and the moments that had preceded their encounter.

Bourke later pleaded guilty to attempted murder of the 15-year-old and was jailed for 10 and a half years.

In court, the prosecution said he had earlier fired an arrow at an Indigenous woman for racial reasons, and briefly considered killing another woman with a baby but decided against it.

"I didn't know at the time what pain he was causing, I just saw he was struggling and he was chasing this girl," Ms Law said.

Gold medal for bravery

Ms Law's heroism was recognised at the Royal Humane Society of Australasia's Bravery Medals, sponsored by His Majesty King Charles III, at a ceremony in Brisbane on Thursday.

Ms Law picked up the ceremony's highest honour, the Clarke Gold Medal.

Nicole Law was awarded the ceremony's highest honour, the Clarke Gold Medal. (ABC News)

She was due to be presented with the medal in 2024, but was not able to attend the ceremony at the time.

Organisers postponed the event so Ms Law could be handed the medal by Queensland's governor, Dr Jeannette Young.

"That's unbelievable, thank you, you saved her life," Ms Young told Ms Law as she presented the medal.

Also among the award recipients were three Sunshine Coast surfers who used their boards to help rescue two men caught in a bad storm rip in April 2021.

Ms Law was presented the award by Queensland Governor Jeanette Young. (ABC News)

A 'sense of decency'

Looking back at that day almost six years ago, Ms Law said she thought about the impact on the teenage girl.

"It wasn't fair that that happened to her, and that's something that sticks with you for a long time," Ms Law said.

She said she had recently heard the now-adult woman was doing well and had been supported by her family.

"It was nice to hear that ... it meant a lot to me."

Ms Law plans to hand down the medal to her grandson. (ABC News: Charlie Mclean)

Looking forward, she thinks about her own loved ones.

She said she planned to hand down the medal to her grandson, as a reminder of the family's values and sense of decency.

"I hope they're proud of me, especially my two boys and my grandson ... they will have something to look back on," she said.

" It's just something special for them to have ... [and to know] it's okay to be a decent person. "

"A lot of that gets forgotten these days."

World.title: 'Overly litigious, combative' CIT chief referred for public sector probe
World.content:
The chief executive of Canberra's Institute of Technology (CIT) has been recommended to the Public Sector Standards Commissioner over concerns her "overly litigious and combative" approach to inquiries about her appointment is inconsistent with public sector values.

An ACT Legislative Assembly committee has been looking into whether CEO Margot McNeill gave false or misleading evidence to an inquiry into her recruitment to CIT.

But it was unable to arrive at any conclusion, according to a report tabled on Thursday, because of Dr McNeill's "continued refusal to engage".

Dr McNeill's appointment as CIT chief executive was brought into question earlier this year after revelations to the ACT Integrity Commission that she had failed to disclose an investigation into misconduct in her previous role at TAFE NSW.

CIT board chair Kate Lundy at a previous ACT Legislative Assembly inquiry into the institution's hiring of CEO Margot McNeill. (ABC News: Joel Wilson)

It prompted an assembly probe into her recruitment, at which Dr McNeill gave evidence that she had been instructed by her former employer not to make public details about TAFE NSW's misconduct investigation.

But a day after the report's findings were made public in May, TAFE NSW released a media statement directly contradicting Dr McNeill's evidence, arguing that it had never barred Dr McNeill from disclosing the existence of an investigation.

That triggered a further probe by an assembly committee, tasked with determining whether Dr McNeill was in contempt by giving false and misleading evidence to the committee and failing to produce documents.

But it was unable to get answers.

"Dr McNeill has refused to provide any legal advice she relied upon citing legal professional privilege," the report said.

"TAFE NSW, citing ongoing legal action, has refused to provide any information that could verify their media statement, and to corroborate or refute the evidence provided by Dr McNeill."

CIT's board was unaware of TAFE NSW's misconduct investigation into Dr McNeill until after she was hired. (ABC News: Callum Flinn)

The committee imposed an order on Dr McNeill to produce any advice she had received about disclosing the TAFE NSW investigation to the CIT Board, adding that that was a rare move for inquiries which preferred the wilful cooperation of witnesses.

While Dr McNeill provided some documents, she relied on a letter from her lawyers claiming other material was protected by legal professional privilege, while simultaneously submitting there were no further relevant documents to produce.

The committee described that argument as "confusing at best, and deliberately obstructive at worst."

"The assertion of legal professional privilege over apparently non-existent documents was also fundamentally unhelpful and could be perceived as an attempt to mislead, distract, and obstruct this committee's attempts to seek further information," the report said.

"The committee rejects assertions by Dr McNeill's legal representatives that a claim of legal professional privilege is a valid reason for not complying with an order of a parliamentary committee," the report said.

It also criticised Dr McNeill's "overly legalistic" approach to the initial inquiry, known as the PAA Committee, investigating her recruitment to CIT.

"Tiresome and unwarranted attempts to instruct and threaten this committee about its powers and scope of inquiry were neither helpful nor welcome," the report said.

"Despite Dr McNeill's insistence and consistent attempt to treat this inquiry as a litigious process, the committee has no desire to enter into a further "tit for tat" exchange with Dr McNeill's legal representatives," the report said.

Concerns conduct undermines ACT public service

The committee said it expected senior public servants, including those representing CIT, to engage with the assembly in a way that complies with public sector duties.

In making its two findings, the committee specified that Dr McNeill's conduct raised concerns about whether her conduct undermined the integrity and reputation of the public service.

It recommended the Public Sector Standards Commissioner investigate whether Dr McNeill's conduct was inconsistent with the Public Sector Management Act and the Public Sector Code of Conduct.

Former Commonwealth department secretary Andrew Metcalfe was appointed the Public Sector Standards Commissioner in October last year.

Dr McNeill remains on leave from CIT.

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said the report's findings strengthened his concerns about Dr McNeill's ongoing tenure as CEO.

"Dr McNeill has been afforded every opportunity to clear the air, and yet another committee process has been obstructed by her refusal to do so," he said in a statement.

"Due process is important, but so too is the appropriate use of public funds and the integrity of our public institutions."

Dr McNeill's legal representatives, as well as CIT, have been contacted for comment.

World.title: Dockers not treating trip to MCG any differently as AFL finals loom
World.content:
Since Justin Longmuir took the reigns at Fremantle ahead of the 2020 AFL season, the Dockers have only played at the MCG 12 times.

On Saturday afternoon they face Melbourne at the venue, in what presents as the perfect preparation for the grand final in late September. Unless you're Longmuir, that is.

"I just don't get caught up in dress rehearsals," he said.

"We feel like we've played there enough, had good experiences, had some average experiences there, but beaten teams that have been on top of the ladder.

"We feel like it's not a burden going to the MCG now. [We] go to Melbourne every second week, nearly, so we feel like that's not a burden either."

Justin Longmuir has overseen a record-breaking season for Fremantle, but the ultimate prize is still up for grabs. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

The game is at 1:15pm on Saturday, comparable to the grand final start time of 2:30pm, but Longmuir won't look that far ahead.

"We're going over there to give our best and all we've got, to play and improve our footy against Melbourne, who we know have played some really good footy there," he said.

"[It would] be disrespectful to this game if we got ahead of ourselves.

"It's not the be-all and end-all either. We've had plenty of experiences at MCG and it shouldn't hold any fears for us."

Graham's future no distraction

As the Dockers prepare for the finals, Jaymie Graham will balance his role of assistant coach with the lure of being a potential head coach of a different AFL side.

Graham has reportedly advanced to the final round of interviews for both the vacant Essendon and Carlton jobs, but Longmuir is confident he won't be distracted by that as Fremantle enter the season's home stretch.

Jaymie Graham is fielding considerable interest in his skills from clubs on the east coast. (AAP: Richard Wainwright)

"I've spoken to him regularly about it … we're colleagues, we're pretty good mates away from work, so yeah, of course I've spoken about it," Longmuir said.

"I haven't had to speak to him about getting the balance right. He's professional, he understands his responsibilities at the club, and he's done a great job of managing that.

"The way he's around the club, you wouldn't even know that he's occupied with anything else outside of it."

Battle-worn Freo fans dare to dream flag within reach Hard-bitten Dockers supporters won't want to say it out loud, but hope is slowly turning to expectation that a first premiership could be on the cards.

Should Graham be offered either the Blues or Bombers job, Longmuir said a decision on whether he would remain at Fremantle until the end of its campaign would be made in due course.

"We'll cross that bridge when it comes," he said.

"[I've] got a lot of faith in Jaymie to be able to walk and chew at the same time. I've also got a big understanding that he wants to see this through, and he's enjoyed his time here, he's enjoyed his work here and he loves working for the club.

"If he got a job elsewhere and they announced it and he wanted to see it through, I'd be happy for him to do that."

Longmuir confirmed he had no plans to rest large numbers of players in the run into finals, following a warning from the AFL, although he did say he was slightly surprised by the memo.

Fremantle won't rest large numbers of players in the run to finals, but some may still be managed. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

"I understand that they want to make sure the integrity of every game is there and I get that," he said.

"I also think that it's the club's responsibility to make sure that we're as best prepared to go as long in the season as we can.

"The teams in the top six get a week off. So it's probably not directed at us as much."

World.title: 'Fighting just for a fair go': Elite sport failing on racism, Olympian says
World.content:
Elite sporting organisations are not culturally safe for First Nations athletes and their complaint procedures not fit for purpose, a former Olympic boxer has told a federal racism inquiry.

The final hearings of the parliamentary inquiry into racism, hate and violence against Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people, held in Naarm/Melbourne, has focused on racism in sport and media.

Former Olympic boxer Marissa Williamson Pohlman told the inquiry Indigenous athletes carried the load of racism both on and off the sporting field.

"I'm not only dealing with the racism I experience whilst I'm trying to be an athlete in the arena, but also the systemic failures that are going on for me and my family outside of sport," she said.

"I don't think that I'll ever actually get to witness myself what I could have become as an athlete because all my energy has been wasted on fighting just for a fair go."

Marissa Williamson Pohlman says she has experienced racism in and out of the ring. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Ms Williamson Pohlman, the first Aboriginal woman to represent Australia in Olympic boxing, said she had frequently been on the receiving end of racist slurs during her sporting career.

She also said a Boxing Australia official had called her home coach and threatened "repercussions" if she carried the Aboriginal flag at an Olympic Games qualifier in Solomon Islands.

"Institutions celebrate Blak excellence when it is convenient, but abandon us when it matters most," she said.

"So it's all good when I put some deadly artwork on the uniform, but cultural safety and practice is another thing."

Ms Williamson Pohlmann said she had faced many roadblocks trying to pursue complaints against former national head coach Jamie Pittman.

Mr Pittman is currently employed as Boxing Australia's acting high-performance manager, despite having withdrawn from the Paris Olympics after admitting to sexual misconduct.

Ms Williamson Pohlmann wants an independent investigation into the organisation.

"Through my trials and tribulations I've come to understand that sporting federations investigate themselves," Ms Williamson Pohlmann said.

"Sport Integrity Australia, despite their name, they can only investigate individuals, not the actual organisation.

"The National Sports Tribunal can only take complaints if the federation agrees to it. So they're all just looking out for each other."

The ABC has contacted Boxing Australia for comment.

'You're not in our shoes'

Representatives of Melbourne football and netball club the Fitzroy Stars told the hearing they had experienced racism at the hands of competitors, coaches and umpires, with little recourse.

Esme Bamblett says racism complaints must be adjudicated by people with lived experience. (ABC News: Patrick Stone)

Club president Aunty Esme Bamblett said racism complaints should not be adjudicated by all-white sporting tribunals and must include people with lived experience.

"You can't be impartial [if] you don't know what it feels like to be an Aboriginal person," she said.

"You don't know what it feels like in this country to be an Aboriginal person who has racism directed at them. You don't know because you're not in our shoes."

Torres Strait Islander and former AFL executive Tanya Hosch told the inquiry the responsibility of dealing with racism should not be placed on those who experience it.

"I can't think of a single workplace that I have worked in where I haven't experienced racism and depending on your circumstances in that workplace, [it] drastically impacts your ability to stand up to it," she said.

Ms Hosch said it was "beyond disappointing" that few state and territory government departments across the country had accepted the committee's requests to appear in person.

"It would seem to me that governments of all persuasions are seeking to avoid fronting up to this conversation for fear that they may be politically wedged."

She said the federal inquiry was "one of the few glimmers of hope" among the "ongoing assaults of racism".

Independent senator and committee member Lidia Thorpe said the AFL and NRL had both declined the committee's requests to appear.

The inquiry was announced in the wake of the alleged terror attack on an Invasion Day rally in Perth in January and a violent neo-Nazi attack on Camp Sovereignty in Melbourne last August.

The final report is due to be tabled in parliament by the end of the year.

World.title: 'Harrowing stories of mistreatment and harm' in modern slavery report
World.content:
A NSW parliamentary report into modern slavery has detailed "harrowing stories of mistreatment and harm".

The 188-page document comes after an inquiry into 'Modern slavery risks faced by temporary migrant workers in rural and regional NSW'.

The report said the committee heard "many horrors".

"The committee was shocked to hear the way survivors had been deceived and mistreated, often living in near uninhabitable conditions, forced to work demanding hours and threatened if they spoke up," the report stated.

Sleeping quarters for PALM workers in NSW indicating the absence of storage space for personal belongings. (Supplied: Denise Laverty.)

The committee made 31 recommendations, including urgently introducing a labour-hire licensing scheme and increasing enforcement powers for both police and SafeWork NSW.

During the inquiry migrant workers gave evidence and outlined how those hired under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme faced exploitation and poor treatment by some employers.

The report found their experiences "deviated so dramatically from the expectations these workers had of this country, of what life here could be like and how they would be treated, is a source of great shame".

"What these migrant workers experienced is unacceptable and serves as a stark reminder that we must do better in how we engage with our migrant workforce."

Focus on Coffs Harbour and Nambucca Valley

The report asked the government to investigate allegations of systemic labour exploitation in Coffs Harbour and the Nambucca Valley.

It said the NSW Anti-slavery Commissioner informed the committee some berry pickers on the Coffs Coast were being "systematically exploited by a group of informal labour hire syndicates".

"The committee was alarmed to hear that these labour hire operators may be engaging in coercive and threatening behaviour, to thwart attempts to report their conduct to relevant agencies," the report stated.

That unscrupulous employers in this region have been able to operate largely undetected highlights the urgent need for labour hire reform.

The report found PALM scheme workers were vulnerable to exploitation. (Supplied: Peter Mares)

Other recommendations included adjusting visa settings to allow PALM workers to more easily change employers, and a review of the Working Holiday Maker Program.

The committee found it was "clear from the significant evidence received during this inquiry that too many temporary migrant workers have experienced, or are at a serious risk of experiencing modern slavery, in NSW".

World.title: 'Manosphere' fuelling extremism in boys and young men, inquiry hears
World.content:
Misogyny and its amplification through the "manosphere" may be a key driver of ideologically motivated extremism in young men and boys in Australia, the antisemitism royal commission has heard.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has this week examined the drivers of antisemitism and radicalisation in the community, hearing from lived experience and expert witnesses.

The University of Melbourne's Sara Meger was called to discuss the findings of her recent research into misogynistic attitudes and support for violent extremism.

Dr Meger said her survey of 1,100 boys aged between 13 and 17 and 2,300 adults found misogyny was the most common predictor of men being driven to extremist ideologies.

"More so than how someone places themselves on a political spectrum, more so than their religiosity, their ethnicity, what online things they engage with, the one thing we measured that was most likely to be able to predict if someone any of the forms of violent extremism we measured was their attitudes about the permissibility of violence against women," she said.

"It finds that if you combine the hostile gender attitudes with only the gendered online behaviours [such as] manfluencer engagement, online dating and online pornography, these factors together accounted for between 90 and 97 per cent of all the explained variants in how someone responds to the violent extremism measures."

'We've got to pump those numbers up'

Dr Meger also recounted a discussion with a representative of the Department of Homes Affairs in December and said "more than two thirds of their countering violent extremism case load is taken up by young boys and men between the age of 10 and 24 years old".

"They're massively over-represented in our countering violent extremism efforts," she said.

Dr Meger said after her research was published, she was shocked by the social media reaction to the findings.

"The most common comment made [on social media] was that the frequency of young men expressing misogynistic attitudes was too low," she said.

"The most common sentiment was 'those are rookie numbers, we've got to pump those numbers up'."

Dr Meger says Andrew Tate has been a big influence on students. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Dr Meger said her research also included qualitative and quantitative data provided by more than 500 Australian teachers about the manifestation of misogynistic and extremist views in the classroom.

"It was roughly 25 per cent [of teachers surveyed] said they had experienced sentiments from students that violence to resist government authority was legitimate," she said.

"Teachers frequently noted very hostile misogynistic attitudes expressed by students.

"The teachers independently spoke about [controversial social media influencer] Andrew Tate and the manosphere as having a significant influence on these attitudes.

"They also noted racism and a degree of celebration of overseas political violence being expressed by students, as well as some examples of students drawing swastikas on notebooks or around campus.

"This indicates to us this political polarisation is having very real world impacts on social cohesion at ages perhaps even younger than we had anticipated."

Reformed neo-Nazi speaks at inquiry A reformed neo-Nazi cut ties with his extremist organisation after he realised he was being sold a "load of lies", the antisemitism royal commission has heard.

Dr Meger said early intervention programs for children as young as six years old should be mandated to prevent the spread of misogynistic attitudes.

"If we could more fully integrate an awareness and perhaps risk assessment of how these gender attitudes could be motivating a range of political ideologies, we might be better placed for effective early intervention strategies," she said.

World.title: New errors uncovered at Queensland's troubled DNA lab
World.content:
Murder and rape court cases may have been impacted by simple typos from scientists at Queensland's beleaguered forensics lab.

The mistake was sensationally first discovered as a scientist was in the witness box giving evidence in June.

Forensics Science Queensland (FSQ) was the subject of two commissions of inquiry, which resulted in tens of thousands of DNA samples needing retesting and potential miscarriages of justice.

The latest bungle involved statements the lab provided to police for prosecution, which had typographical errors like the wrong date or case number.

Just over 900 statements dating back to 2023 are being audited, with a third checked so far, and an error rate of 10 to 15 per cent.

Of the statements that had a typo, the government assured none had compromised any criminal court cases.

However, FSQ director Mick Fuller said it would be "impossible" to rule out if the remaining 600 statements had errors that affected cases.

"All we can do is do the audit, do it properly, and be transparent with the outcome.

"If there is an issue that has arrived along the way, we will report that."

Mr Fuller, New South Wales' former top cop, was appointed to the role by the LNP government a year ago, tasked with clearing the massive backlog of samples to be retested and addressing cultural issues.

Former NSW police commissioner Mick Fuller has been appointed as the director of Forensic Science Queensland. (Supplied)

He assured protocols had been put in place to prevent future transcription errors and that the science was "definitively" correct.

"Look, it's not ideal, but from my perspective, it shows that FSQ has grown and can now be better trusted.

"Obviously, we don't want mistakes, and I would love to get all the mistakes out of any aspect of Forensic Science Queensland.

"But of course, if we do make mistakes, then we need to act on them quickly."

Top scientist quietly exits

Esteemed forensic scientist Dr Kirsty Wright led a major review of FSQ, which in August 2025 made damning findings of contamination and unreliable results.

She was appointed to an advisory role to lead reforms at the lab, but it was revealed today she had quietly left the lab in May, just six months into a year-long contract.

"My priority remains to help fix the DNA Lab. I'm available to assist the government as needed," Dr Wright said in a short statement to the ABC.

Queensland's Attorney-General Deb Frecklington did not answer questions about why Dr Kirsty Wright left her advisory role. (ABC News: Luke Bowden)

She has since been replaced, while the progress of the hundreds of recommendations she was helping to implement remains unclear.

Attorney-General Deb Frecklington did not answer questions about why Dr Wright had left, denying there had been a lack of transparency.

"I'm standing right here doing a press conference, like I do whenever we have any other major update.

"Today is an incredible day to think of where we've come from 12 months ago."

Shadow Attorney-General Meaghan Scanlon said the government had serious questions to answer.

"Deb Frecklington promised that she was going to fix the DNA lab, and yet her handpicked adviser has walked off the job halfway through," Ms Scanlon said.

"We only heard about this bungle through the media. The Crisafulli government didn't issue a media release. They didn't stand up and be up front with Queenslanders."

World.title: Investigations underway into surgery mix-up at Melbourne hospital
World.content:
The state government says an investigation is underway into how a Melbourne woman was mistakenly given surgery meant for another patient at a hospital in the city's west.

Debra Buchanan attended Joan Kirner Women's & Children's Hospital in January for a minor procedure to remove a lesion on her pelvic area.

Instead, her lawyer said she woke up from surgery to discover a portion of external tissue from her genital area had been removed, leaving her with permanent scarring.

Ms Buchanan's lawyer Erin Monsalve Fear said the mistake was a "complete systemic failure" on the part of the hospital.

"There's so many safeguards and procedures that should be in place to prevent this from occurring and it's evident that those have simply failed or not been followed in Deb's instance," Ms Monsalve Fear said.

A lawyer representing Debra Buchanan says the hospital is yet to apologise for the mistake. (Supplied: Western Health)

Beyond physical pain and permanent disfigurement, Ms Monsalve Fear said her client had now lost trust in the medical profession entirely.

"Deb has now had to go back into surgery to deal with the original cancerous lesion that she was supposed to have operated on," she said.

"So the trauma that has followed that, she's obviously been terrified to go back into surgery after this experience occurred."

Ms Monsalve Fear said her client was seeking damages, and also wanted to raise awareness by sharing her story.

Government says investigation underway

The Department of Health confirmed the incident was being reviewed by Safer Care Victoria, the agency which oversees patient care in the state.

Government minister Vicki Ward said the incident was "extraordinary" and extended her sympathies to Ms Buchanan.

"What has happened to her is just awful, and it is not acceptable," she said.

"I know that there will be a review, Safer Care Victoria is working with Western Health now."

Healthcare quality and safety improvement agency Safer Care Victoria has now engaged with Western Health. (ABC News)

In a statement, Western Health's chief operating officer John Ferraro said the company was "committed to open and transparent communication with patients" during any investigation.

"Due to our obligations to protect patient privacy and confidentiality, we are unable to comment on the care of any individual patient," he said.

"In line with Victoria's Statutory Duty of Candour requirements, where a patient adverse event has occurred, we provide an apology, meet with the patient, undertake a review of the incident, and share the findings and actions taken to help prevent a recurrence."

Ms Monsalve Fear said despite the surgery taking place in January, Western Health was yet to apologise.

"There [has] been some acceptance from the hospital that the wrong procedure was performed, it hasn't really amounted to an apology to Deb," she said.

ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton on his phone during the budget estimates hearing on July 31. ACT Opposition Leader Mark Parton addressed the media on Thursday after being accused of texting a sex worker on the clock. 9News Footage from last week’s hearing shows Parton, who holds the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Affairs portfolio, frequently on his phone. World.title: Revealed: The AFL club that signed secret concussion deal with at-risk player
World.content:
Geelong allegedly struck an agreement with one of its players, who had a history of concussion, that would see him assume legal responsibility for future on-field head trauma, this masthead has confirmed. The AFL Players’ Association has condemned the deal, which involved an unnamed player signing an agreement that acknowledged his elevated risk of concussion. The AFL is facing mounting legal actions over its liability for head trauma sustained on-field. AFL Photos Three industry sources, speaking anonymously because of the sensitivity of the situation, confirmed Geelong was the club involved. The Cats were contacted for comment.



Related Article Exclusive

AFL injury ward ‘Vague and embarrassing’: Cats’ doctors hit back at Rooke class action concussion claim “The game has a duty to provide a workplace that protects the health, safety, and wellbeing of players and all clubs hold this duty as employers,” AFLPA chief executive James Gallagher said. “Clubs cannot unilaterally contract out of their obligations under the CBA and standard playing contract, nor attempt to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws. Importantly, no player is permitted to return to play or train unless they have been deemed medically fit to do so.” AFL chief executive Andrew Dillon and executive general manager of AFLW, health and football operations Laura Kane appeared at mental health media round table on Thursday morning but did not answer questions about the initial report in the Herald Sun, which did not name the player or the club that struck the agreement two years ago. The league was expected to make a statement later on Thursday.



The agreement reportedly acknowledged that the player was at a higher risk of more concussions and more serious damage because of his history, and required him to “take upon yourself the physical and legal risk of loss, damage or injury” arising from future concussions. Melbourne coach Steven King responded to the report at his media conference on Thursday. Concussion is a growing issue for the AFL. Marija Ercegovac “All I’ll say about that is, as a club, or me personally, I would never do anything or ask my players to put themselves at risk,” King said.



“I think what we are doing, and the things we have implemented in the game to help look after players’ safety and wellbeing has been really positive. “As a coach, my opinion is, I would never ask a player to put himself at risk to play. Those decisions are with our doctors and medical team and that’s where, as a coach, I leave them to be honest.” The revelation comes as the AFL and its clubs face a number of lawsuits relating to the long-term impacts of repeated head trauma. These include a $1 billion class action set to go to trial next year, involving more than 100 former AFL players, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke. Former Geelong defender Max Rooke is the lead plaintiff in a class action against the AFL. Paul Rovere WorkSafe is also investigating the AFL’s concussion management protocols.



Related Article Opinion

AFLW The first generation raised on AFLW has arrived – and they are taking over Libby Birch AFL columnist Sports law expert Leon Harris, who is doing his PhD in head trauma and concussion liability, said he was not surprised to hear such a contract had been drawn up. He said whether it was enforceable was another matter. “You can’t contract your way out of a statutory liability. If you have breached workplace health and safety requirements, you can’t say, ‘oh no we got them to sign a waiver for any injury they suffer at any point, we’re in the clear’,” Harris said. “So under the civil liability legislation in theory you would have rights still even if you were encouraged to contract your way out of those rights, but it just becomes a fight you don’t really want. “If the player as an adult knows the risk that they’re running by continuing to play and is willing to voluntarily assume that risk then, in a way, that’s up to the player. But the question then becomes, is it OK for a professional sporting organisation to allow somebody in that situation to assume that risk of harm, and that potentially is more of a moral question than a legal question.”



Harris said part of the problem was that there was still a grey area around the issue as it was yet to be fully decided in court. There remained limited research around the prolonged effects of repeated sub-concussive head trauma, he added. While numerous legal actions have been brought in Australia and overseas, most have resulted in settlements. “I think eventually it will end up going to a court to make a decision, whether it’s here, whether it’s in England … and they will make a ruling and a variety of sports will have decisions to make, unless those sports start putting rules in place now to deal with sub-concussive events, not just concussion.” The AFL was contacted for comment. World.title: ABC boss apologises for ‘Race Around the World’ Gina Rinehart episode
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ABC boss apologises for ‘Race Around the World’ Gina Rinehart episode Calum Jaspan August 6, 2026 — 1:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content ABC boss Hugh Marks has apologised for an episode of the new Race Around the World program, where a contestant joked of turning billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart’s “guts” into a “big sausage roll,” as the ABC’s independent ombudsman also threw out a series of complaints. The short film titled A Very Relaxing Video was deemed to have not breached the ABC’s editorial policies according to the Ombudsman, who concluded that any reasonable audience member would view the remarks as “satirical and exaggerated commentary”, as opposed to a genuine call or endorsement of violence, as Rinehart has alleged. The ABC found no breach in relation to complaints made about a program which made reference to Gina Rinehart. ABC The short film titled “A Very Relaxing Video” aired during an episode of the ABC program on July 12. Presented as an avant-garde production in the Scottish Highlands, contestant Kate McGuinness concluded by saying: “When the revolution comes, will you hide under the bed or will you know exactly how to shove a stick right up Gina Rinehart’s butt hole, stirring it round, mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll to make something out of nothing.”



Rinehart has threatened the ABC with legal action following a campaign from News Corp outlets. The Ombudsman said the program initially received eight complaints, but after several media outlets criticised the content, the ABC received a further 988 complaints. Marks apologised despite the Ombudsman’s findings, saying the episode’s content fell short of the community’s expectations of the broadcaster. “While the Ombudsman has found that the film did not breach the ABC’s editorial policies, the ABC acknowledges the episode has fallen short of community expectations,” Marks said in a statement. “The ABC apologises to Mrs Rinehart and to anyone else affected or upset by the publication of the film.” Marks said the ABC has considered whether its existing policies and guidance “sufficiently distinguishes between news and non-news content”.



“As a result, the ABC will amend its guidance as it applies to violence,” Marks said. McGuinness apologised to anyone offended by the program last week, but said her film was in no way intended to be taken literally. “The sense of humour featured in each of my films on the Race Around The World program is farcical. In no way was it my intention to promote violence. My writing is cartoonish and always satirical. Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone,” she said. Numerous politicians have weighed in on the story since it was first publicised by The Herald Sun two weeks ago. Federal Health minister Mark Butler called the content “revolting” in comments made to News Corp at the weekend. On Friday, a statement from Hancock Prospecting, the company which Rinehart chairs, said the program posed an ongoing risk to her, placing ABC chair Kim Williams, managing director Hugh Marks and deputy chair Lisa Caffery on legal notice. World.title: Toddler rescued as two found dead in outback murder-suicide
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandTragedy Toddler rescued as two found dead in outback murder-suicide Eleanor Wilson , Robyn Wuth and and William Davis Updated August 6, 2026 — 1:56pm ,first published August 6, 2026 — 8:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A toddler has been rescued from a siege that left two adults dead and forced an outback town into lockdown for hours. The incident unfolded in Charleville, about 740 kilometres west of Brisbane in south-west Queensland, after police rushed to reports of a serious assault at a home about 6pm on Wednesday. Loading Residents across a three-street block were ordered to stay inside for nearly eight hours as specialist police swarmed the area and declared an emergency situation. Inside the home, officers found the bodies of a 45-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman, while a toddler only just old enough to walk was found alive at the property.



Southern region assistant commissioner Matthew Vanderbyl said on Thursday morning the scene had become dangerous for police. “The situation became quite dynamic and quite threatening to police quite quickly, and … they withdrew to a point of safety,” he said. He said negotiators were then brought in, as were specialist police from Brisbane. Vanderbyl added reports the woman were pregnant had not been verified by investigators. Police are treating the deaths as a murder-suicide. A crime scene was established and a report would be prepared for the coroner.



The young child was talk to hospital, but was not seriously injured. Police have not confirmed if the man was armed. “It will take some time to try and piece together the events of what happened last night,” Vanderbyl said. The case will be investigated by the Ethical Standards Command. Charleville mayor Shaun Radnedge said the survival of the child was a rare shard of hope in a heartbreaking day for the tight-knit community.



“Our community is devastated by the tragic events that unfolded in Charleville overnight,” he said. “We are a close-knit town, and an incident of this nature is felt deeply by many people. “The little baby has survived. I don’t know how or don’t know why, but it’s there.” The council is organising support for the community through the days ahead. “We encourage anyone affected by this tragedy to reach out to family, friends, neighbours or local support services,” Radnedge said.



“Please do not carry this alone. Charleville is strong because its people look out for one another. “In the coming days, I ask everyone to show compassion, avoid speculation and give those directly impacted the privacy and respect they need at this incredibly difficult time.” Police were expected to provide more information in a press conference on Thursday morning. AAP If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). These include a $1 billion class action set to go to trial next year, involving more than 100 former AFL players, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke. Former Geelong defender Max Rooke is the lead plaintiff in a class action against the AFL. Paul Rovere WorkSafe is also investigating the AFL’s concussion management protocols.



Related Article Opinion

AFLW The first generation raised on AFLW has arrived – and they are taking over Libby Birch AFL columnist Sports law expert Leon Harris, who is doing his PhD in head trauma and concussion liability, said he was not surprised to hear such a contract had been drawn up. He said whether it was enforceable was another matter. “You can’t contract your way out of a statutory liability. If you have breached workplace health and safety requirements, you can’t say, ‘oh no we got them to sign a waiver for any injury they suffer at any point, we’re in the clear’,” Harris said. “So under the civil liability legislation in theory you would have rights still even if you were encouraged to contract your way out of those rights, but it just becomes a fight you don’t really want. “If the player as an adult knows the risk that they’re running by continuing to play and is willing to voluntarily assume that risk then, in a way, that’s up to the player. But the question then becomes, is it OK for a professional sporting organisation to allow somebody in that situation to assume that risk of harm, and that potentially is more of a moral question than a legal question.”



Harris said part of the problem was that there was still a grey area around the issue as it was yet to be fully decided in court. There remained limited research around the prolonged effects of repeated sub-concussive head trauma, he added. While numerous legal actions have been brought in Australia and overseas, most have resulted in settlements. “I think eventually it will end up going to a court to make a decision, whether it’s here, whether it’s in England … and they will make a ruling and a variety of sports will have decisions to make, unless those sports start putting rules in place now to deal with sub-concussive events, not just concussion.” The AFL was contacted for comment.
