World.title: ABC boss apologises for Race Around the World Gina Rinehart episode
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMedia & marketing ABC boss apologises for Race Around the World Gina Rinehart episode Calum Jaspan August 6, 2026 — 1:58pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: Graphic content ABC boss Hugh Marks has apologised for an episode of the new Race Around the World program, where a contestant joked of turning billionaire mining magnate Gina Rinehart’s “guts” into a “big sausage roll”, as the ABC’s independent ombudsman also threw out a series of complaints. The short film titled A Very Relaxing Video was deemed to have not breached the ABC’s editorial policies, according to the ombudsman, who concluded that any reasonable audience member would view the remarks as “satirical and exaggerated commentary”, as opposed to a genuine call or endorsement of violence, as Rinehart has alleged. The ABC found no breach in relation to complaints made about a program which made reference to Gina Rinehart. ABC The video was aired during an episode of the ABC program on July 12. Presented as an avant-garde production in the Scottish Highlands, contestant Kate McGuinness concluded by saying: “When the revolution comes, will you hide under the bed or will you know exactly how to shove a stick right up Gina Rinehart’s butthole, stirring it round, mixing her guts up nice and smooth, to make one big sausage roll to make something out of nothing.”



Rinehart has threatened the ABC with legal action following a campaign from News Corp outlets. The ombudsman said the program initially received eight complaints, but after several media outlets criticised the content, the ABC received a further 988 complaints. Marks apologised despite the ombudsman’s findings, saying the episode’s content fell short of the community’s expectations of the broadcaster. “While the ombudsman has found that the film did not breach the ABC’s editorial policies, the ABC acknowledges the episode has fallen short of community expectations,” Marks said in a statement. “The ABC apologises to Mrs Rinehart and to anyone else affected or upset by the publication of the film.” Marks said the ABC has considered whether its existing policies and guidance “sufficiently distinguishes between news and non-news content”.



“As a result, the ABC will amend its guidance as it applies to violence,” Marks said. Related Article Graphic content

Australian TV ABC Race Around the World contestant apologises after Gina Rinehart complaint McGuinness apologised to anyone offended by the program last week, but said her film was in no way intended to be taken literally. “The sense of humour featured in each of my films on the Race Around The World program is farcical. In no way was it my intention to promote violence. My writing is cartoonish and always satirical. Unfortunately, jokes do not land with everyone,” she said. Numerous politicians have weighed in on the story since it was first publicised by The Herald Sun two weeks ago. Health Minister Mark Butler called the content “revolting” in comments made to News Corp at the weekend.



On Friday, a statement from Hancock Prospecting, the company which Rinehart chairs, said the program posed an ongoing risk to her, placing ABC chair Kim Williams, managing director Hugh Marks and deputy chair Lisa Caffery on legal notice. World.title: Toddler rescued as two found dead in outback murder-suicide
World.content:
Updated NationalQueenslandTragedy Toddler rescued as two found dead in outback murder-suicide Eleanor Wilson , Robyn Wuth and and William Davis Updated August 6, 2026 — 1:56pm ,first published August 6, 2026 — 8:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A toddler has been rescued from a siege that left two adults dead and forced an outback town into lockdown for hours. The incident unfolded in Charleville, about 740 kilometres west of Brisbane in south-west Queensland, after police rushed to reports of a serious assault at a home about 6pm on Wednesday. Loading Residents across a three-street block were ordered to stay inside for nearly eight hours as specialist police swarmed the area and declared an emergency situation. Inside the home, officers found the bodies of a 45-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman, while a toddler only just old enough to walk was found alive at the property.



Southern region assistant commissioner Matthew Vanderbyl said on Thursday morning the scene had become dangerous for police. “The situation became quite dynamic and quite threatening to police quite quickly, and … they withdrew to a point of safety,” he said. He said negotiators were then brought in, as were specialist police from Brisbane. Vanderbyl added reports the woman were pregnant had not been verified by investigators. Police are treating the deaths as a murder-suicide. A crime scene was established and a report would be prepared for the coroner.



The young child was talk to hospital, but was not seriously injured. Police have not confirmed if the man was armed. “It will take some time to try and piece together the events of what happened last night,” Vanderbyl said. The case will be investigated by the Ethical Standards Command. Charleville mayor Shaun Radnedge said the survival of the child was a rare shard of hope in a heartbreaking day for the tight-knit community.



“Our community is devastated by the tragic events that unfolded in Charleville overnight,” he said. “We are a close-knit town, and an incident of this nature is felt deeply by many people. “The little baby has survived. I don’t know how or don’t know why, but it’s there.” The council is organising support for the community through the days ahead. “We encourage anyone affected by this tragedy to reach out to family, friends, neighbours or local support services,” Radnedge said.



“Please do not carry this alone. Charleville is strong because its people look out for one another. “In the coming days, I ask everyone to show compassion, avoid speculation and give those directly impacted the privacy and respect they need at this incredibly difficult time.” Police were expected to provide more information in a press conference on Thursday morning. AAP If you or anyone you know needs support, you can contact the National Sexual Assault, Domestic and Family Violence Counselling Service on 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732). World.title: Why free-range eggs might not actually be from free-range hens
World.content:
Shoppers buying free-range eggs are being warned that they may not strictly be from free-range chickens, while the threat of bird flu hangs over the industry.

Many egg suppliers that have the ability to do so have put their hens into lockdown, restricting their roaming, as a precaution to protect them from bird flu, which has been discovered in a native bird in Wairarapa.

Australia is facing a wider outbreak. It was reported this week that the country had had its first mass mortality event in a group of native seabirds in South Australia.

There, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has paused enforcement measures for free-range egg labelling, to allow free-range producers to keep hens inside to protect them from disease.

Do I have to buy that extended warranty? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

The Commerce Commission said it would take a similar approach in New Zealand.

Simon Pope, head of fair trading and product safety investigations, said it recognised the current difficulties faced by the industry and sympathised with those who were affected.

"The Fair Trading Act does not allow us to give exemptions to egg and poultry producers in relation to free range claims, even when there is an outbreak.

"However, we can exercise discretion in deciding whether to investigate or take enforcement action. We would consider all relevant circumstances in a situation where such a decision was required.

"The Commission has produced guidance for egg and poultry meat producers related to how we exercise this discretion."

It said it would expect producers and retailers to consider things like a public awareness campaign so shoppers understood why birds might not be free-ranging for health reasons. They could also use temporary packaging or add stickers on the free-range labels.

Woolworths is displaying signage around its free-range eggs. A spokesperson said it was monitoring the situation and working with suppliers and the Ministry of Primary Industries.

World.title: Expansion of citizen's arrest powers to take effect within a week
World.content:
An amendment to the Crimes Act has passed its final reading in Parliament.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith says the majority of the legislation will take effect within a week.

That includes an expansion to citizen's arrest powers, allowing members of the public to intervene in any Crimes Act offence at any time of day.

A person making an arrest would be allowed to use restraints "when reasonable," but is also required to contact police and follow their instructions.

The bill is intended to crack down on retail crime by allowing security guards to detain thieves.

"Retailers and security guards face abuse and assault that no New Zealander should be subjected to, and we know the economic cost of retail crime is in the billions," Goldsmith said in a statement.

The amendment also specifies a number of new, more specific offences, including for assaulting first responders and front-line corrections workers, and three new offences for "coward punches".

"Where others may flee, first responders and front-line corrections workers run towards danger to help those who need urgent assistance. Assaulting them puts multiple lives at risk, so there must be greater consequences for these terrible acts of violence," he said.

"We know how dangerous coward punches are. People can be killed or suffer lifelong brain injuries, yet perpetrators often receive lenient and insufficient sentences. That changes with this legislation."

World.title: Māori roll grows by almost 15,000 voters since last election
World.content:
Doctor Lara Greaves discusses Maori roll enrolment deadline Midday Report Download MP3 5m

Enrolled Māori voters wanting to switch between electoral rolls have until midnight on Thursday (August 6) to decide before this year's election.

The latest Electoral Commission figures show there are currently 305,124 voters registered on the Māori Roll, which is an increase of 14,824 since the 2023 general election.

Within the same timeframe, the number of Māori on the general roll has dropped by more than 20,000 to 255,900.

The gap between the two rolls has more than tripled since the last election with more than 49,224 on the Māori roll than the general roll.

The latest data indicates the growth in numbers on the Maori roll has largely been driven by voters already enrolled who have switched from the general, to the Māori roll.

Associate professor in politics at Victoria University of Wellington, Dr Lara Greaves told Midday Report she expects the Māori roll to keep growing over the next three years.

"We've got this very young group that are ageing into voting more and more every day, the Māori population is kind of shaped like a triangle so what we're expecting to see is more rangatahi Māori age into voting, and what we know about rangatahi Māori is that many are very proud of their culture, of their language, they want to uphold Te Tiriti, they want to uphold Māori rights."

People who want to represent Māori rights in politics generally go on the Māori roll, she said.

Greaves said there has been a number of public campaigns by Māori organisations and political parties to encourage people to switch to the Māori roll.

"Generally we've seen a lot of people try to campaign to get more Māori on the Māori roll, the Hīkoi mō te Tiriti that was another one where people were talking about 'hey go on the Māori roll that's a way to exercise your political rights.' So there's been quite a few campaigns and ways of trying to get people to learn more about the Māori roll.

"My own research shows that actually there's not a lot of knowledge out there, fewer than half of a survey that we conducted knew that more Māori on the Māori roll means more Māori electorates."

One unorthodox campaign that has been turning heads online is from Green candidate for Waiariki Tania Waikato, it features images of young Māori women in bikinis and shirtless Māori men.

"If bikinis mean people take a moment to think about the Māori roll than so be it," Greaves said.

The chief Māori advisor Hone Matthews said the Commission has sent letters, follow up emails and text reminders to entitled voters.

Thousands have taken the opportunity to change rolls, enrol, or update their address on the electoral roll.

"If you are happy with the roll you're on, kei te pai. If you would like to change rolls before the election, you need to do it now."

The Electoral Commission expects to see enrolment numbers continue to increase as the election draws closer.

It has also advised anyone who experiences technical difficulties with enrolment to call 0800 36 76 56. From overseas, the number is +64 9 909 4182 (international call rates may apply).

World.title: Hamilton City Council votes against submitting Head Start proposal
World.content:
Being forced to put forward an amalgamation process now, a Hamilton City councillor says is like getting stuck in a tent "which is not desirable when the tent is a brothel with the minister who wants to pimp us out".

In May, the government gave councils three months to come up with a Head Start proposal for merging into larger unitary councils.

The Head Start process was "voluntary" but if council's did not participate, the government said it would step in to ensure reform still happened through a backstop process. That process had not yet been finalised.

Despite this, Hamilton City Council today decided, with 12 votes in favour and 3 against, that it did not want to submit a proposal.

Mayor Tim Macindoe said he had a phone call with Local Government Minister Simon Watts on Wednesday night, where Watts stressed that opting in with a Head Start proposal was just stage one of a process that would enable council's to keep developing models over the months ahead.

"However he was also quite clear during our discussion that backstop council's will not be at the table for that process.

"His messages were fairly clear, his tone was pleasant throughout, it wasn't threatening, but it didn't leave me with hope we could still be at the table to negotiate if we are a backstop council."

But Macindoe said he told the minister that he expected to be able to be a part of discussions no matter what councillor's decided.

"I still think its inconceivable that we wouldn't be. How could we possibly be in a position where other council's are making decisions that have a profound impact on the future direction of New Zealand's fastest growing and fourth largest city."

He said following the vote, they would either be at the table or "have to push that very very firmly".

Councillor Andrew Bydder said the minister was telling them to put their car keys in the bowl or be left out in the cold.

"It feels like a sleazy hook up. This is not a criticism of our neighbours, it's like kissing your sister.

"I don't want a one night stand, but a lasting relationship, not an imminent divorce. I think Hamilton is the most attractive council, with sexy gardens, but the other players know our credit card is maxed out.

"The underlying problem is that we have urban issues and our dance partners have rural issues. A problem shared may be a problem halved but any partnership with us will be like Paddy Gower, having both issues.

"If we go with the western block now, the government match makers might think we are actually happy with it. Getting into the tent might leave us stuck in the tent, which is not desirable when the tent is a brothel with the minister who wants to pimp us out."

Deputy mayor Geoff Taylor said it was a shame they were left with the option of a western authority], with Waikato, Waipā, South Waikato districts and an unwilling Taupō.

He called it a "coalition of the unwilling" and said the process had not been collegial or particularly constructive.

They would not, he said, look back at choosing that option with any pride.

"We are making the biggest decision in Hamilton's history, with no financial due diligence whatsoever. There's no business case, it's there in black and white, they will do that work after you've made the decision. By then, I think we are committed.

"And we haven't asked our people what option they prefer, and my fear is if we go with the west we will never get the chance to genuinely ask them. I don't want to see any more pretend consultation, where we only go out for views once a direction has been set and there's no realistic opportunity for change."

He said they needed to stand their ground and take the time they needed to find the right solution.

World.title: El Niño's 'spiky' temperatures could harm or even kill people this summer, health official warns
World.content:
Hot weather driven by "spiky" temperatures from El Niño could harm and even kill people this summer if they are not prepared to cope, a senior health official says.

After years of coping with severe flooding, agencies are now turning their minds to heatwaves, drought and wildfire, as what could be the strongest El Niño event on record develops.

Earth Sciences New Zealand (ESNZ) declared El Niño was underway at the beginning of July, and was expected to peak during the southern hemisphere summer.

At a National Emergency Management Agency forum on Thursday, ESNZ and MetService meterologist Jon Tunster said measurements from July were already at record strength for that month, "which is pretty concerning".

"It was worthy of a bit of a fuss earlier in the year, but what's happened now is that we also have observations starting to back it up," he said.

El Niño forms when warmer-than-normal ocean temperatures in the eastern Pacific slow down the trade winds that would normally carry moisture across to Australia, New Zealand and other countries on the western side of the ocean.

For New Zealand, an El Niño generally means wetter conditions in the south-west of the South Island, and drier, windier conditions in most other parts of the country, especially the east and north-east.

Earth Sciences New Zealand

Unlike places like Australia and Indonesia, though, El Niño does not necessarily mean a hot summer in New Zealand.

However, ESNZ chief weather scientist Chris Brandolino said temperatures could be "spiky", soaring for a few days before dropping back down.

The organisation had analysed data from the strong El Niño of 1997-98, when very hot temperatures were recorded in Canterbury.

It found that MetService's current heat alert system - which warns of one- and two-day regional temperature spikes - would have been triggered nearly a dozen times that summer for Canterbury residents.

Te Whatu Ora medical officer of health Cheryl Brunton said heatwaves were relatively rare in New Zealand, but even a mild heatwave could have negative effects on people's health.

"Heat is a silent killer and it also harms people relatively silently."

How much harm extreme heat caused depended on the timing, intensity and duration of hot weather, but also how acclimatised a population and its infrastructure and institutions were, Brunton said.

"The evidence suggests that the effects of heatwaves on health are actually greater in temperate areas because extreme heat occurs less frequently and so people simply aren't used to it."

Recent heatwaves in Europe had already caused an estimated 10,000 excess deaths in June, she said.

People in Bordeaux, France, wear face masks to ptrotect themselves from smoke from wildfires, driven by extreme temperatures across parts of Europe. AFP / Ed Jones

Health effects could include heat rash, heat exhaustion and heat stroke, and could increase the risk of death for people with cardiovascular, respiratory and other chronic diseases because of the strain on their body's systems.

Anyone who might struggle to cool themselves was at risk - including babies, people who were bed-bound, and those struggling with living costs, Brunton said.

"Lower socioeconomic groups ... might not be able to afford the things that would enable them to adapt, think for example air conditioning."

Renters might not be able to adapt as easily, along with those living in new builds "where it's very difficult to actually open a window even to allow air through".

Brunton raised particular concerns about homeless people, who were currently struggling with freezing temperatures in some places.

"The homeless are going to find it difficult in very hot temperatures as well, because they tend to be within urban areas and that urban heat island-type effect, which can increase those temperatures in that area, is also going to be relevant to them."

Te Whatu Ora had information about keeping cool in extreme heat on its website, she said.

Agencies monitoring wildfire, drought conditions

Representatives from Fire and Emergency and the Ministry for Primary Industries told the forum they were closely monitoring soil moisture levels.

MPI national response manager Andrew Curtis said there were already "a couple of spots" around the country that were experiencing a winter drought.

"Parts of the North Island are already starting to go quite dry - they're not getting the precipitation that they would be expecting this time of the year," he said.

"Going into summer, if they start in a hard place, what are they going to look like in mid-January?"

El Niño's typical combination of drying, westerly winds and a lack of rainfall could combine to flip regions into drought "quite quickly", Curtis said.

The good news was that there was still plenty of time for rural communities to prepare, he said.

"We have about six months to do what we can do on-farm, on-property in order to get ready for this."

Sheep during a previous Canterbury drought RNZ / Patrick Phelps

Farmers should develop a plan now, he said.

That included checking and carrying out maintenance on water supplies and infrastructure, creating livestock and cropping plans for dry conditions, working out where supplementary feed supplies might come from, and how to manage risks to human and animal health from hot or dry weather.

El Niño's effects could be made worse by increased import costs and supply chain difficulties, he said.

"There are commodities, things like [fertiliser], where things may become scarce," he said.

"Things that were available may not be available and that's part of planning - making sure that if you don't get what normally [you can get], where can you get it from? What would that look like for you carrying on through summer?"

Fire and Emergency wildfire manager Tim Mitchell said fire conditions were normal for this time of year at the moment.

Based on previous experience though, the fire season could start as early as September and run longer than usual, he said.

During 1997-98, heightened fire risk had persisted on the eastern side of the country into early April.

Monsoon helicopters fight a fire in the Port Hills, February 2017 Supplied

The strong winds associated with El Niño contibuted to both drying out wildfire fuel, and driving fires when they sparked, he said.

They could also hamper fire crews' ability to get wildfires under control.

"That [wind] may pose some real operational challenges to particularly our aerial tactics that we may deploy for fires over the season."

New Zealand typically experiences 4,300 wildfires a year. While most were small, 98 percent were caused by human activity, Mitchell said.

Not all areas would experience heightened fire risk, but FENZ was developing a national campaign to raise awareness and encourage people to comply with fire bans and other regulations.

World.title: Luxon catches caucus off-guard with promise to hold MMP referendum if re-elected
World.content:
Christopher Luxon has caught his caucus off-guard with a seemingly off-the-cuff campaign promise to hold a referendum on the MMP voting system if re-elected.

On Newstalk ZB on Thursday morning, the National leader said a referendum on MMP was "something we should consider" and he wanted to see it happen next year.

"I actually think it's quite right to check-in constitutionally and say, is this the system New Zealanders still want ... is it still where you want to be?" he said.

The announcement certainly took his coalition colleagues ACT and New Zealand First by surprise, but it also appears his National colleagues were unaware as well.

On their way into the House on Thursday afternoon, Luxon's National colleagues would not say whether they knew he was going to announce the policy.

Louise Upston said the prime minister was "reflecting a conversation" that many people were having around potential changes to MMP.

Asked whether she knew Luxon was going to make those comments on Thursday morning, she repeated he was reflecting conversations that were had with constituents.

Louise Upston. RNZ / Mark Papalii

"Well, there'll be lots of things that I don't know what the prime minister is going to say. He is the prime minister. He's been out engaging with the public, reflecting what the conversations are."

Tama Potaka said what the prime minister said was up to the prime minister, and his focus was on serving the people of Hamilton West.

He would not say if the caucus had endorsed the policy.

"What goes on tour stays on tour, and it's the same with the caucus."

Simon Watts said the position had been "outlined clearly" by Luxon.

Asked whether it was National Party policy before 9am on Thursday morning, Watts said he had been doing speeches all day and was not involved in the timing.

"But I've seen the announcement, and that's consistent from where we are."

But National's campaign chair Simeon Brown said it was not a formal announcement.

Simon Watts. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"He was on radio giving a view, and that's great."

Brown said National had long been open about having a conversation on a four-year term, which "raises other questions" around New Zealand's electoral system.

"The prime minister was saying very clearly, if you're going to have that conversation, you know, every 20 years or so, we also have a conversation around the type of electoral system that we have as a country as well."

He would not answer questions on whether a referendum on MMP was National Party policy, or whether it had been discussed in caucus.

As justice minister, Paul Goldsmith would be responsible for legislating the referendum.

Like Brown, he said it was "pretty obvious" National was interested in a four-year term, and it "probably makes sense" to look at MMP at the same time.

"We always talk about constitutional reform," he said.

Goldsmith was not sure if it was an announcement from the prime minister, saying Luxon was simply answering a question.

Mark Mitchell said it was not something that was relevant to this election.

"But certainly, if we're successful in being returned to government, then it's something to talk about in the next term."

Mark Mitchell. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

It was put to Mitchell that if it was something to be talked about next term, then it was relevant to this election.

He then admitted he had not seen the prime minister's comments.

"I know that he has made a comment and he has shared his opinion around the fact that he thinks the country should have a chance to be able to have a say on MMP, and he's been, from what I understand, he's been very clear about the fact that would not happen this term."

Speaking at the government's announcement on new industry-led subjects for secondary schools, National's deputy leader Nicola Willis said the party had "previously reflected" that it thought a four-year term was a good idea, and the prime minister had "expressed interest in getting feedback" on MMP.

"I was aware that these were views that he held and that we've discussed in our caucus, and that we've discussed with everyday New Zealanders whose doors we knock on and whose businesses we visit."

Coalition partners respond to "yahoo or numpty" comments

During his interview, Luxon made the case for wanting as many National ministers in Cabinet as possible.

"The question is, I keep saying, I don't need some yahoo or numpty from some other party around that table. I can do a lot more to get the centre-right agenda, centre being the operative word, done and out the door so think about your vote, November 7. It's important."

He then denied that he was referring to his coalition partners as yahoos and numpties.

Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour said that sort of commentary did not help New Zealand, but put in a dig of his own.

"I don't want to be pointing the finger at them, but it's a simple fact that, you know, he's had to move on at least five of his own ministers for different reasons. So you know, it's the old thing, once you start throwing stones, sometimes you end up finding the glass houses a bit shaky."

Deputy Prime Minister David Seymour. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Fellow ACT minister Nicole McKee defended her party's performance.

"It's not offensive to me. I'm going about trying to do the work that New Zealanders want done, that they voted us here to do. We are successful in that. I think it reflects more on him than it does on those that are actually achieving."

McKee was in favour of keeping MMP.

New Zealand First minister Casey Costello said she was surprised by Luxon's comments, and hoped he was not talking about her.

"I hope he's not. I wouldn't think so. Well, I hope it's not New Zealand First, because I think we're doing a great job."

Her leader Winston Peters said previous referendums on MMP were "decisive", and put his foot down on any changes to the electoral system.

World.title: 'Pretty harrowing': Climbers rescued from ravine told family they were safe throughout ordeal
World.content:
The young Kiwi climbers rescued from a ravine in the Solomon Islands told their families they were okay throughout their ordeal.

Keanu Isaksson, 25, and Luca Zylstra-Law, 19, were trapped in a ravine on Mount Popomanaseu for eight days before their rescue in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

"They certainly were being very kind to their mothers ... they were telling us that they were warm and dry, which absolutely was not the case," Deni Holl, Isaksson's mother, told RNZ.

As a week of torrential rain battered the mountain, the climbers fell into a crevasse and found themselves stuck on an perch above a sheer 30-metre drop.

There, they faced rock falls, a dwindling satellite phone battery, and the uncertainty of whether rescue was possible.

The pair, exhausted but uninjured from their "pretty harrowing" ordeal, are currently recovering in Honiara.

Holl said they are in good spirits and are even talking about their next trip to the Amazon.

"There will be no stopping them," she said.

Eight days on the precipice

Isaksson and Zylstra-Law, both avid outdoorsmen, had moved their climb forward to make room for a trip to the Amazon nearer the end of the year.

Guided by locals up the mountain, they messaged their parents every day via their satellite phone.

"They had to part company with the guides because those guides could not cross into other tribal land," Holl said.

"We had gotten one of these EPIRB (Emergency Position Indicating Radio Beacon) messages every single day just saying 'checking in, everything's fine, love you'."

The peak of Mt Popomaneseu in the distance. Reddit

But one day passed and neither mums were messaged. Then another day passed.

"We had no idea that anything adverse was wrong, just maybe they had forgotten to send that message."

Three days passed before the next message came through: "Urgent. Urgent. Requiring helicopter evacuation, cannot go forwards, cannot go backwards."

The mothers knew nothing of the chasm that the boys had found themselves in. They had tried for three days to climb out on their own, before calling for help.

"Keanu is employed by a skills company in Australia, and he is sent to various places where those skills are required ... one of them is ropes access."

"So if the boys could have gotten themselves out using ropes, that would have been happening."

Holl recalled her shock at seeing a birds-eye photo of them taken from a helicopter, shown to her after the rescue.

"They certainly were being very kind to their mothers ... they were telling us that they were warm and dry, which absolutely was not the case."

The boys were camped on a tiny rock outcrop, on the precipice of a more than 30-metre sheer drop, under a waterfall. The river below had swollen, and they dealt with waves of torrential rain and rock falls which threatened serious injury at any moment.

The pair were stuck in a ravine for eight days. Paul Hubbard

"They were wet and very cold the whole time, they had to snuggle up to each other to keep themselves warm," she said.

"They had quite a plan for making sure that they were mentally sharp, and in tact the whole time. It was very frightening for them for the first few days, with the rock falls, because there was no getting away from them."

Communication via the satellite phone was fraught. The pair had to conserve their battery, anticipating well over a week before their rescue. And little did they know, they were sending messages too long to be received by the boys under those conditions.

"That communication system only works if there is a satellite directly going over ... for it to seek signal, they were in too steep a place.

But Holl and Zylstra-Law's mum Tanya raised their boys on the great outdoors - one has a rock climbing dad, both were mentored by neighbours in the bush, and were well practiced on the nearby Mount Tamahunga and Aotearoa's great walks.

Isaksson was only months out of a trip to Mt Everest base camp. The pair were not novices.

"So deep down, of course, we were very worried ... but I know my boy."

Long-time friends Keanu Isaksson (right) and Luca Zylstra are preparing for an upcoming trip to the Amazon. Supplied

A gap in the weather

Rescue would not come for another five days.

Police told Holl and Tanya that, thanks to several rainless months (likely due toEl Niño conditions), the boys were caught in "some of the worst weather (authorities) had seen in decades".

The space they were trapped in could not fit a helicopter at all, and the one on hand did not have a winch. But even if it did, a clear baring to lower a net was simply impossible.

It meant all they could do was wait for gaps in the weather to go up and make drops - food, fresh water, gear, and a radio.

Holl said she was grateful for the support she received from police, which included regular weather updates and the latest on their condition.

"They were doing everything within their power, they were very good to us," Holl said.

Time went by with seemingly no progress, causing Holl and Tanya to go to the media and ask for re-enforcements from New Zealand and Australia.

The families had even discussed taking matters into their own hands.

"Keanu's dad, he is a climber, my son has exactly the same qualifications as his father," she said.

"He was booked for a flight to go over there himself, and to try and organise to be dropped as close as possible wherever there was access, and he was going to attempt to abseil to the boys, and to hoist them out somehow.

"We had no idea, but we just could not sit and wait any longer ... if Tanya and I were fit enough, that is what we would be doing."

But by early Tuesday morning, a new helicopter and a new pilot were on the scene. They came, made a drop, went back to Honiara and waited for a gap in the weather.

The boys felled an intervening tree, clearing space for a long-awaited pickup.

"What can I tell you? It was just overwhelming," Holl said.

"I am still over at Tanya's each day ... we are very lucky to have a community like this in our little valley here, hopefully at some stage the boys will be home."

After recovering, Holl said Isaksoon had to head back to Australia for work, but Zylstra-Law would be on the next flight home.

"All I want to be able to do is to give [Isaksson] a big hug."

World.title: The trade-off between te reo Māori and big tech companies
World.content:
For years te reo pronunciation on global tech platforms has made Māori speakers cringe, a Māori tech expert says, and while there are trade offs, a new tool for Google Maps will help change that.

In July, Google and Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori launched an AI-powered text-to-speech (TTS) model that could correctly pronounce cities and towns with te reo Māori names.

University of Waikato computer science professor Te Taka Keegan was blunt in his assessment of te reo pronunciation on tech platforms in the past: "Our Māori place names have been bastardised for 150 years and I believe this tool, more than anything else, will start correcting that."

Keegan worked at Google for six months in 2008 and 2009 helping to develop the Google Translator Toolkit.

Ultimately that tool was deprecated, meaning Google withdrew its support for it. Keegan said that showed him while Google may have the best intentions ultimately those intentions were not the same as Māori.

"I consider myself a Māori language activist, I'm actively trying to build tools to support te reo Māori. Google aren't Māori language activists. They are a large computer science for-profit company. And even though they have a famous historic motto, 'don't be evil,' profit is their underlying goal. Whereas when Māori are working to support Māori language, other considerations will always be more important than profit."

However, Keegan said he has worked on many projects over the last 30 years to do with Māori language and technology and this was one of the first where a large international company had taken Māori data seriously.

"If you listen to the tool, the way it pronounces Māori language is beautiful. It's a beautiful pronunciation, it's not a loud punch you in the face, boisterous, it's a real subtle, real ngāwari, relaxing pronunciation.

"And its beauty will draw people in. When I say people, I mean Pākehā New Zealanders, because Māori language speakers in Aotearoa already understand the value of te reo and already pronounce Māori place names correctly. So in that sense, it is really a tool for transformation among non-Māori language speakers, and that transformation happens through subtlety."

Non-Māori speakers would only need to hear it maybe four or five times before, hopefully, they will start saying Māori place names correctly, he said.

Places will now have their names pronounced correctly. Google Maps / supplied

Country Director of Google New Zealand Caroline Rainsford said Māori data sovereignty was an incredibly important part of the project.

"Because we don't actually want to own the models, you know, we very much believe in doing the work to enable them. But so what we've done at the moment is Te Taura Whiri will be the guardian of the Māori lexicon. And Google has actually a licence from them to use this for the purposes of the text-to-speech model, starting with Google Maps and hopefully over time other products."

Beyond that the plan was that a group of interested parties would become the guardians of the data to ensure academics, researchers and local communities would be able to access the data and share in the benefit, she said.

Keegan said some Māori, with good reason, were hesitant to engage with big tech companies, however in this instance the positive benefits outweigh the negatives.

"There are always trade-offs when working with big tech, but in this case Google has agreed that Māori retain intellectual property rights over Māori language data. That's unique. This is an example of engaging with big tech to develop a solution that, ultimately, I believe will be better for the long term health and attitude towards te reo Māori."

Maybe a little further down the track Māori will have their own version of Google Maps they completely controlled under a mana motuhake governance, that speaks te reo from start to finish, he said.

In the meantime we now had Google Maps that spoke Māori places names way better than it used to, he said.

"Ultimately, it should be Māori that are building technology for Māori, and especially for Māori language. It should be Māori AI engineers that are building Māori AI for Māori."

When the new tool went live, Keegan decided to test it out on a drive with his nine-year-old moko, after the first word her eyes widened and by the fourth she was laughing.

"She was laughing with happiness and laughing with joy that finally it's pronouncing reo Māori names correctly. And I think that's what this tool can do, I think it can bring joy to Māori language speakers to hear our language spoken as it should be spoken."

Te Taura Whiri chief executive Ngahiwi Apanui-Barr told Sunday Morning recently he had difficulties getting his own staff on board with working with a tech giant.

Authentic new voice for Google Maps NZ Sunday Morning Download MP3 10m

But, he said their job was to normalise te reo and all learners needed to see the language reflected back at them.

Apanui-Barr said they were aiming to get place names pronounced correctly, however there were tens of thousands of place names and hundreds of thousands of street names.

"So some of them won't be quite correct, but we'll be working with people and we encourage people to feed back where there are mispronunciations of street names."

World.title: Court asked to jail disgraced AFL great Nicky Winmar for assaulting woman
World.content:
The future of disgraced AFL great Nicky Winmar hangs in the balance, with prosecutors calling for him to be jailed for assaulting a woman.

Winmar, who was recently removed from the league's Hall of Fame, was last month found guilty of bashing the woman in the town of Cohuna in 2025.

Winmar smashed the woman's head against a door, pulled her hair and twisted her arm during the attack.

She said the assault left her "a shadow of the person I once was".

Bendigo magistrate Trieu Huynh said he had not decided whether to impose a jail term.

Annina Tropea (left) told the Bendigo court Nicky Winmar needed to be sent to jail to learn the consequences of his actions. (ABC News: Nate Woodall)

Prosecutor Annina Tropea said Winmar had prior convictions for violence and said jail was needed to make him understand that there were consequences for his actions.

"Engaging in that conduct was a conscious and persistent choice," she said.

However, Winmar's barrister, Dermot Dann KC, said his prison should be a punishment of "last resort", and a community corrections order was more appropriate.

A sentencing date has been set for August 28.

Winmar was found guilty last month of assaulting a woman in northern Victoria last year. (ABC News: Nate Woodall)

Winmar, who sat alone, slumped forward and covered his ears as the victim read out a statement about how the crime affected her life.

The woman said she felt "extreme pain" in her arm, leaving her unable to complete daily duties or simple tasks.

She said the attack also had an "immense impact" on her mental health and that she constantly felt paranoid, scared and frightened.

"The visions and reminders of being overpowered and powerless are so detailed," she said.

"Not being able to stand up for myself — I was so helpless."

Former AFL great Nicky Winmar found guilty of assaulting woman The woman previously told the court she was "fearful" for her life on the night of the incident last year.

Winmar pleaded not guilty during the case; however, the magistrate found the charges guilty beyond reasonable doubt after hearing evidence from the victim and other witnesses.

Mr Dann, for the defence, said his client had a storied AFL career whose most important achievement was standing up to racism, when he famously lifted his jumper and pointed to his skin in a match against Collingwood in 1993.

After Winmar was found guilty, he was stripped of numerous playing accolades and a bronze statue of him outside Perth Stadium was taken down.

"They can erase his statue and they can erase his names from their hall of fames," Mr Dann said.

"What they'll never be able to erase … in the hearts of minds of the many, many people who care about racism and intolerance and injustice, is the memory of his courageous stand that day at Victoria Park."

Winmar endured a difficult upbringing in WA and currently struggled with depression, PTSD and alcohol disorders, Mr Dann said.

"This is a man who's had plenty of highlights but also plenty of lowlights," he said.

"Of course, this proceeding is one of the real lowlights.

"He has undergone significant efforts towards rehabilitation."

Mr Dann said his client suffered numerous concussions in his playing days and investigations were under way to determine whether he had acquired a brain injury or developed CTE.

Winmar's priors include multiple convictions for assault, including an attack on a taxi driver in 2019, the court heard.

Winmar made no comment outside court.

World.title: Birthday boy Popyrin wins in Montreal
World.content:
Alexei Popyrin has celebrated turning 27 by booking his place in the Montreal Masters' round of 32 for the third year running.

The shock 2024 champion progressed in just 76 minutes, beating the 32nd-seeded Belgian Raphaël Collignon 6-4, 6-3 on Wednesday (Thursday AEST).

Former world number 19 but currently ranked 139, Popyrin beat fellow Australian Thanasi Kokkinakis to earn his place in the main draw and saw off Román Andrés Burruchaga in round one to notch his first ATP-level win since May.

And with another crack looming at the US Open in New York — where he beat Novak Djokovic in 2024 en route to his best finish at Flushing Meadows — Popyrin can largely credit another win in Canada to his booming serve.

Popyirn fired down 10 aces, won 84 per cent (27/32) of first-serve points and did not face a break point, while also converting three of nine break-point opportunities of his own.

The Sydneysider will next face another Argentine in Thiago Tirante, who upset world number 9 and seventh-seeded American Taylor Fritz 7-5, 6-3.

At the women's WTA event in Toronto meantime, Australian world number 61 Daria Kasatkina suffered a lengthy, 6-3, 5-7, 6-4 loss to second seed Elena Rybakina.

The two-time grand slam champion from Kazakhstan survived after a two-hour and 22-minute scare to progress and tee up a clash with 28th seed Anna Li of the US.

Later on Wednesday, 20-year-old Aussie qualifier Maya Joint beat 14th-seeded Romanian Sorana Cîrstea 6-4, 6-4 to join compatriot Talia Gibson in the third round.

AAP

World.title: AFLPA responds after report says player signed concussion deal with club
World.content:
The AFL Players Association says it is in discussions with the league after reports a Victorian club signed a deal with a player with a history of concussions that required him to assume all legal responsibility for future brain trauma.

According to a report in News Corp newspapers on Thursday, the club made the player sign the agreement in a bid to exonerate itself and its medical staff from future court action.

The deal with the unnamed footballer, who is still an active AFL player, was signed two years ago.

The report said the club viewed such an agreement as the only way the player could continue his career given his history of concussions.

Loading...

The disclosure agreement required the individual to "take upon yourself the physical and legal risk of loss, damage or injury" arising from future concussions.

It also acknowledged the player was at higher risk of more concussions and could face more serious damage if they suffered further head knocks.

The reported deal has been slammed by concussion campaigners, experts and the AFL Players Association (AFLPA), who were reportedly unaware of the agreement.

"Clubs cannot unilaterally contract out of their obligations under the CBA and Standard Playing Contract, nor attempt to avoid their responsibilities under health and safety laws," AFLPA boss James Gallagher said in a statement provided to ABC Sport.

'I have lost basically everything': Ex-AFL player opens up on compensation fight Head trauma ended Aiden O'Driscoll's promising AFL career before he could play his first game. Now, like many former footballers affected by brain injuries, he faces an uncertain future as he fights for compensation.

"Importantly, no player is permitted to return to play or train unless they have been deemed medically fit to do so.

"We are in discussions with AFL to better understand the circumstances of this case and ensure this issue is not replicated further at the elite level."

Concussion and head trauma is one of the most pressing issues facing the AFL today.

Multiple players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and premiership Magpie Nathan Murphy, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley and Shane Tuck, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multi-million dollar concussion class action case against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
